btree-double-fsync-per-mutation.text: B-tree mutations pay for `os.fsync()` twice: once when writing the WAL entry (`btree.py:137`) and again when committing the page to the data file (`btree.py:105`), with the WAL truncated only after the data file sync confirms durability.

btree-durability-protects-data-not-struc.text: The B-tree's durability model protects user data but not structural integrity: mutations pay double fsync for data pages (WAL entry + data write) while structural metadata is never fsynced, AND structural integrity silently erodes during normal operation (leaked pages, ever-growing height, dangling parent pointers after free_page) with no defensive checks in the I/O layer to detect or prevent degradation.

justifications.label: Fsync asymmetry protects the values but not the tree shape, while the tree shape degrades monotonically — durability effort is precisely misallocated

btree-durability-via-wal-commit.text: Covered by existing `btree-wal-no-data-fsync` (page writes intentionally not fsynced) and `wal-commit-sync-before-truncate` (commit is the durability barrier).

btree-empty-leaf-freed-on-delete.text: When all keys are removed from a non-root leaf, the page is returned to the free list via `PageManager.free_page()` rather than persisting as an empty node

btree-empty-tree-operations-return-sane-.text: All operations on an empty B-tree return `None`, `0`, `False`, or `[]` and never raise an exception.

btree-file-never-shrinks.text: The B-tree data file only grows (via `next_free` bump in `allocate_page`) and never shrinks; no truncate, compact, or defrag operation exists anywhere in the module.

btree-fix-plan-all-crash-safety.text: All six bugs documented in `fix-plan.md` concern single-writer WAL/fsync crash safety; none involve concurrent access races, illustrating that even without concurrency the WAL protocol has subtle correctness requirements

btree-fix-plan-execution-order.text: This describes dependency ordering within a planning document, not a code invariant — it will become irrelevant once the fixes land.

btree-fix-plan-scopes-out-merge-redistri.text: b-tree-storage-engine/fix-plan.md Bug 5 scopes the page-freeing fix to freeing empty leaves and removing parent pointers, explicitly leaving full merge/redistribute out of scope.

btree-free-list-exists-unused.text: Contradicts existing accepted belief `free-page-only-called-from-delete`, which confirms the free list IS called from the delete path; the code was updated after the entry was written.

btree-free-list-immediate-reclaim.text: Covered by the combination of `btree-empty-leaf-freed-on-delete` (pages are freed immediately) and `btree-single-threaded-assumption` (no concurrent access makes deferred reclamation unnecessary).

btree-free-list-intrusive.text: Freed pages store the "next free" pointer in their own body at `HEADER_SIZE` offset, forming an intrusive singly-linked list with no separate allocator data structure.

metadata.example:
def free_page(self, page_num):
    data = struct.pack(HEADER_FMT, 0, 0) + struct.pack(">I", free_head)
    self.write_page(page_num, data)  # freed page stores next-free pointer
    self.write_meta(..., new_head=page_num)

btree-free-list-unused-by-logic.text: Contradicted by existing belief `btree-empty-leaf-freed-on-delete`, which states that empty leaves are returned to the free list via `free_page()`.

btree-free-page-bypasses-wal.text: `pm.free_page()` called during deletion writes directly to the data file without WAL logging, creating a crash-consistency gap if the process fails between the free and the WAL commit

btree-free-page-links-singly-linked-list.text: `PageManager.free_page(page_num)` links the freed page into a singly-linked free list stored in page headers.

btree-free-page-no-parent-fixup.text: `PageManager.free_page` adds a page to the free list without removing the parent's downlink to it, creating a dangling-pointer risk on crash

btree-free-page-writes-link-before-metad.text: free_page writes the free-list link into the page before updating metadata, creating a crash window where a page can be orphaned from both the tree and the free list.

btree-get-reads-at-most-height-plus-one-.text: Duplicate of `btree-lookup-reads-bounded-by-height` proposed from the sibling test entry.

btree-has-page-io-counters.text: The B-tree's `PageManager` tracks `pages_read` and `pages_written` with a `reset_counters()` method (multiply by `page_size` for bytes), but WAL writes are not counted by any existing counter

btree-height-never-shrinks.text: Since delete never merges internal nodes or demotes the root, tree height only increases (on splits) and never decreases, regardless of how many keys are deleted.

btree-impl-asymmetric-split-vs-merge.text: The reference implementation fully propagates splits upward through `_insert`'s return value but swallows the `'empty'` signal in `_delete` after one level of cleanup, making insertion structurally complete but deletion structurally incomplete

btree-insert-delete-cycle-recycles-pages.text: During insert/delete cycles, freed pages are reused from the free list before extending the file, preventing unbounded growth as long as free_page is called during deletion.

btree-insert-no-wal-commit.text: `_insert` never calls `wal.commit()`; the caller (`put`) is solely responsible for committing after all page writes and metadata updates complete, making the entire `put` atomic with respect to crash recovery

btree-internal-split-promotes-key.text: Internal node splits promote the midpoint key into the parent (removing it from the child), unlike leaf splits which copy it (the key remains in the right child); this asymmetry allows uniform `bisect_right` routing at all internal levels.

btree-keys-decoded-as-utf8.text: Leaf deserialization always decodes keys as UTF-8 strings while values remain raw bytes; invalid UTF-8 in key bytes causes UnicodeDecodeError at read time, not write time (since serialize accepts both str and bytes).

btree-keys-sorted-within-every-node.text: Keys within every B-tree node (both leaf and internal) are sorted; all lookup, insert, and range-scan logic depends on this ordering.

btree-leaf-next-sibling-sentinel-fffffff.text: B-tree leaf nodes use the sentinel value `0xFFFFFFFF` (`NO_SIBLING`) to indicate no next sibling.

btree-leaf-overflow-trigger-max-keys.text: In _insert's leaf case, a leaf with len(keys) <= max_keys is written without splitting, while len(keys) > max_keys triggers a split.

btree-leaf-page-format-starts-with-type-.text: The serialized leaf page format begins with a 1-byte page type, 2-byte key count, and 4-byte next_sibling pointer, followed by entries.

btree-leaf-search-bounds-check-before-ma.text: Leaf lookup uses bisect_left and checks idx < len(keys) before comparing keys[idx] == key.

btree-leaf-sibling-chain.text: Leaves store a `next_sibling` pointer forming a left-to-right chain terminated by `NO_SIBLING` (0xFFFFFFFF), enabling range scans without touching internal nodes.

btree-leaf-sibling-chain-forward-only.text: Leaf pages store a `next_sibling` forward pointer (`NO_SIBLING = 0xFFFFFFFF` sentinel) but no backward pointer, so unlinking a leaf from the sibling chain requires locating the predecessor via parent traversal rather than direct backlink.

btree-leaf-sibling-not-updated-on-delete.text: Contradicts existing accepted belief `btree-leaf-sibling-patched-on-remove`, which confirms that the predecessor leaf's `next_sibling` IS updated when a leaf is freed; the bug described in the entry was fixed.

btree-leaf-sibling-patched-on-remove.text: When an empty leaf is removed during deletion, `_delete` patches the previous sibling's `next_sibling` pointer to splice the empty leaf out of the linked list used by `range_scan` and `__iter__`

btree-leaf-split-at-half.text: In a leaf split, _insert uses mid = len(keys) // 2, keeps keys[:mid] in the left page, and places keys[mid:] in the new right page.

btree-leaf-split-copies-key.text: Leaf splits copy the midpoint key into both the parent and the right leaf (key remains searchable in the leaf), while internal splits promote the midpoint key out of both children into the parent only

btree-leaf-split-promotes-first-right-ke.text: When a B-tree leaf splits, the first key of the new right leaf is promoted to the parent internal node.

btree-len-reads-total-keys-from-metadata.text: `BTree.__len__` reads the `total_keys` field directly from the page 0 metadata rather than counting entries in the tree.

btree-lookup-reads-bounded-by-height.text: A single `BTree.get()` reads at most `height + 1` disk pages, verified via `pm.pages_read` after counter reset.

btree-lookups-read-at-most-height-plus-o.text: The test_page_io_counts test validates that B-tree lookups read at most height + 1 pages.

btree-max-keys-forces-splits.text: With `max_keys_per_page=4`, inserting a 5th key into a leaf triggers a page split; tests use this small fanout to exercise multi-level tree structure with few keys.

btree-meta-page-five-u32-fields.text: The B-tree metadata page (page 0) stores five 4-byte unsigned integers: root_page, height, total_keys, next_free_page, and free_list_head.

btree-metadata-bypasses-wal.text: `BTree._write_meta` writes root pointer and free list head directly to the data file without logging through the WAL, making metadata updates not crash-safe.

btree-metadata-page-tracks-root-height-t.text: The B-tree metadata page (page 0) maintains `root_page`, `height`, `total_keys`, `next_free_page`, and `free_list_head`, updated on every structural change.

btree-metadata-tracks-height-and-total-k.text: Overlaps with existing belief `btree-page-zero-is-metadata` which already establishes that page 0 is the metadata page

btree-mutation-fsync-is-asymmetric.text: B-tree mutations pay double fsync costs for user data (WAL entry + data page) but skip fsync entirely for structural metadata, creating an asymmetry where key-value pairs survive crashes but the free-page list and allocation state may not.

justifications.label: User data gets two fsyncs per mutation while metadata gets zero — a durability asymmetry hidden from callers

btree-mutations-call-wal-commit.text: The BTree class calls WAL.commit at the end of every mutating operation, including put, delete, and close.

btree-needs-latches-not-transaction-lock.text: Concurrent B-tree access uses page latches held for microseconds to protect physical page structures, separate from transaction locks held for logical isolation.

btree-next-free-page-vs-free-list-head.text: next_free_page only increases (high-water mark), while free_list_head is the recycling mechanism that prevents file growth by pointing to freed pages.

btree-next-sibling-for-range-scans.text: Duplicates existing beliefs `range-scan-follows-sibling-chain` (range scans use sibling pointers) and `btree-sibling-pointers-unused-for-merge` (sibling pointers not used for merge).

btree-no-block-size-parameter-or-test-la.text: No block_size parameter or test_large_dataset test exists in the B-tree codebase.

btree-no-delete-operation.text: Contradicted by multiple existing beliefs (`btree-delete-skips-free-page`, `btree-empty-leaf-freed-on-delete`, `btree-delete-no-commit-on-miss`, `btree-leaf-sibling-patched-on-remove`) that describe delete behavior in detail. The entry's grep likely missed the method.

btree-no-merge-or-redistribute.text: Duplicates existing beliefs `btree-impl-asymmetric-split-vs-merge` and `btree-sibling-pointers-unused-for-merge`, which already establish that merge/redistribute logic is absent.

btree-no-merge-redistribute-underflow-re.text: Grepping for `merge|redistribute|underflow|rebalance` across the B-tree implementation returns zero matches, confirming no merge or redistribution logic exists.

btree-no-sibling-sentinel-is-0xffffffff.text: The rightmost leaf uses the sentinel value `NO_SIBLING = 0xFFFFFFFF` to mark the end of the sibling chain.

btree-no-underflow-rebalancing.text: Delete does not rebalance underfilled nodes; the only cleanup is freeing empty non-leftmost leaves at depth 2 — a deliberate simplification over production B-trees.

btree-page-alignment-enables-corruption-.text: Fixed-size page addressing provides natural resync boundaries for recovering from data file corruption.

justifications.label: Page alignment only isolates corruption when the reader knows the page size; since page size is not persisted, reopening with wrong size silently misaligns all pages

btree-page-alignment-isolates-corruption.text: The B-tree's fixed-size pages (`page_num * page_size` addressing) provide natural resync boundaries for the data file — corruption of one page does not affect reads of other pages, unlike the streaming WAL formats

btree-page-io-has-no-defensive-checks.text: The B-tree's page I/O layer lacks defensive validation at every stage: deserialization accepts any bytes, leaf-finding doesn't verify node types, and page writes silently truncate oversized data — a single corrupted byte can cascade through the tree undetected.

justifications.label: Three independent observations at different stages of the page lifecycle (read, navigate, write) reveal a consistent absence of safety checks

btree-page-manager-defers-fsync-to-sync-.text: B-tree PageManager defers fsync to explicit sync() or close() calls; individual page writes end with flush() only.

btree-page-manager-sync-and-close-fsync.text: The B-tree PageManager sync() and close() methods call flush() followed by os.fsync() on the data file.

btree-page-manager-sync-on-committed-wri.text: b-tree-storage-engine/btree.py PageManager.sync() is called on every committed write path.

btree-page-overwrite-no-size-change.text: B-tree PageManager overwrites pages at fixed offsets within a pre-allocated file, so most write+sync cycles do not change file size and would benefit from `fdatasync` skipping metadata I/O

btree-page-size-default-4096.text: The B-tree uses fixed-size pages of 4096 bytes by default, with every page (leaf, internal, or free) occupying exactly that size on disk.

btree-page-size-not-persisted-in-data-fi.text: The B-tree page size is not persisted in the data file, so reopening the database with a different page_size value silently corrupts page reads.

btree-page-split-requires-at-least-three.text: A B-tree leaf split requires at least three full page writes: the two leaves and the parent.

btree-page-write-always-full-page-size.text: PageManager.write_page() always writes exactly page_size bytes (4096 default), padding with zeroes regardless of payload size.

btree-page-writes-not-individually-durab.text: Duplicates existing belief `btree-wal-no-data-fsync` — both capture that `PageManager.write_page()` does not fsync

btree-page-writes-unbuffered-by-app.text: `PageManager` has no application-level page cache — every `read_page` reads from the file and every `write_page` writes immediately, relying entirely on the kernel page cache for performance

btree-page-zero-is-metadata.text: Page 0 is always the metadata page (root_page, height, total_keys, next_free_page, free_list_head); the root page is never page 0.

metadata.example:
# Page 0: root_page(4B), height(4B), total_keys(4B), next_free(4B), free_head(4B)
META_FMT = ">5I"
self._f.seek(0)
self._f.write(struct.pack(META_FMT, root, height, total_keys, next_free, free_head))

btree-partial-split-replay-orphans-right.text: If a crash occurs after the right page and left page are WAL-logged but before the parent update, recovery produces a consistent sibling chain but the right page is unreachable from tree descent — range scans find the keys but point lookups silently miss them

btree-put-does-not-validate-value-is-byt.text: `BTree.put` does not type-check `value`; passing a `str` fails later inside `_serialize_leaf` when concatenating with bytes.

btree-put-is-upsert.text: `BTree.put()` on an existing key updates the value in-place without incrementing `len(tree)` — it is an upsert, not a blind insert.

btree-put-metadata-reread.text: `put` must re-read metadata after `_insert` returns because `PageManager.allocate_page` mutates `next_free` and `free_head` as a side effect during splits, and those changes are not threaded back through the return value.

btree-put-resets-io-counters.text: `BTree.put` calls `pm.reset_counters()` before reading metadata, zeroing `pages_read` and `pages_written` for per-operation stats.

btree-put-root-split-handling.text: When _insert returns a (mid_key, new_page) tuple at the root, put allocates a new root page, creates an internal node with the old root and new page as children, and increments the tree height.

btree-range-scan-excludes-end.text: Duplicate of `range-scan-half-open-interval` proposed from the range_scan entry.

btree-range-scan-provides-ordered-access.text: B-tree range scans provide correct ordered sequential access by walking the actively maintained sibling chain with support for unbounded end keys, traversing all matching keys in sorted order.

justifications.label: Sibling chain maintenance ensures ordering but no cycle detection means a corrupt pointer could cause infinite traversal

btree-range-scan-uses-search-to-find-sta.text: The B-tree range scan's first phase uses `_search` to descend from the root through internal nodes to the leaf containing `start_key`.

btree-range-scan-walks-leaf-chain-via-ne.text: The B-tree range scan's second phase walks the leaf chain by reading `next_sibling` from each leaf and calling `PageManager.read_page(next_sibling)` until the sentinel or an out-of-range key is reached.

btree-recovery-follows-same-sync-truncat.text: The B-tree WAL's `recover` method follows the same sync-then-truncate ordering as `commit`: it replays entries, fsyncs the data file, then truncates and fsyncs the WAL.

btree-recovery-is-crash-safe.text: Duplicate of `wal-recover-then-truncate` which states recovery fsyncs the data file before truncating the WAL, so a crash during recovery leaves the WAL intact for re-replay

btree-recursive-insert-returns-union.text: `_insert` returns a discriminated union: `None` (updated existing), `'inserted'` (new key, no split), or `(mid_key, new_page)` (split happened); root splits are handled in `put()`, not inside the recursion.

btree-reimplements-wal-internally.text: b-tree-storage-engine/btree.py contains its own WAL and PageManager classes internally rather than importing from write-ahead-log/wal.py.

btree-reusable-after-deleting-all-keys.text: After deleting every key from a B-tree, the tree remains in a usable state and accepts new inserts normally.

btree-search-is-read-only.text: Too trivial — a search/get function being read-only is the expected default

btree-selective-fsync.text: Covered by combination of `btree-wal-fsync-per-entry` (WAL fsyncs) and `write-meta-no-fsync` (PageManager metadata does not)

btree-sibling-chain-fixed-offset.text: The `next_sibling` field sits at a fixed byte offset (bytes 3–6) in every serialized leaf page, making the sibling chain walkable without fully deserializing page contents

btree-sibling-chain-gives-o1-leaf-traver.text: The B-tree sibling chain gives O(1) leaf-to-leaf traversal, making range scans proportional to the number of results rather than the tree height.

btree-sibling-chain-maintained-across-mu.text: The B-tree sibling chain is actively maintained during all structural mutations with a fixed wire format: splits write the new right page with the old leaf's next_sibling pointer before rewriting the old leaf, deletions patch the previous sibling's pointer to splice out the removed leaf, and the next_sibling field sits at a fixed byte offset (bytes 3-6) enabling reliable traversal without full page deserialization.

justifications.label: Split, delete, and read operations all respect and maintain the sibling chain through coordinated ordering and format invariants.

btree-sibling-pointers-unused-for-merge.text: Leaf pages serialize a `next_sibling` pointer (via `_serialize_leaf` and `NO_SIBLING` sentinel) providing infrastructure for merge/redistribute, but no code path reads sibling pointers during deletion.

btree-single-file-avoids-dir-fsync-gap.text: The B-tree's PageManager writes to a single pre-existing data file opened at construction, so normal operations never create new files and avoid the directory fsync gap that affects segment-based engines during rotation and compaction.

btree-single-threaded-assumption.text: The B-tree implementation has no locking, latching, or concurrency control; all crash-safety gaps exist even without concurrent access

btree-single-writer.text: `put` (and `delete`) assume single-threaded access: metadata is re-read after `_insert`/`_delete` without any locking or compare-and-swap, creating a TOCTOU window under concurrent writers.

btree-split-asymmetry-leaf-vs-internal.text: The leaf-copy side duplicates `btree-leaf-split-copies-key`; the internal-promote side is captured in the accepted `btree-internal-split-promotes-key` above.

btree-split-logic-not-in-first-200-lines.text: The first 200 lines of `b-tree-storage-engine/btree.py` cover `PageManager`, `WAL`, and leaf serialization helpers, but do not contain the split or delete logic.

btree-split-propagates-mid-key-return.text: In btree.py, _insert_into propagates splits upward by returning (mid_key, new_page_num) for the parent to insert, rather than using Lehman-Yao detect-and-finish.

btree-split-serialization-cost-scales-wi.text: B-tree splits serialize entire nodes, so larger max_keys_per_page values increase serialization and rewrite cost.

btree-split-uses-recursive-return.text: Duplicate of existing belief `btree-recursive-insert-returns-union`, which captures that `_insert` returns either `'inserted'` or `(mid_key, new_page_num)` to propagate splits upward.

btree-split-write-order-protects-chain.text: During a leaf split, `_insert` writes the new right page to the WAL before the modified left page, ensuring the sibling pointer target is durable before any pointer references it — so the chain never points to a nonexistent page after crash recovery

btree-splits-are-crash-safe.text: Multi-page B-tree operations (splits, deletes) are made crash-safe by writing all modifications to the WAL before applying them to data pages.

justifications.label: Split atomicity requires that recovery replays only complete operations, but the WAL applies all CRC-valid entries without commit verification — partial splits can be applied

btree-stdlib-only.text: The B-tree module uses only stdlib imports (os, struct, zlib, bisect) with zero external dependencies.

btree-structural-integrity-silently-erod.text: B-tree structural integrity silently erodes over time: deletions cause monotonic degradation (leaked pages, ever-growing height) while the I/O layer performs no validation to detect or report the resulting inconsistencies.

justifications.label: Degradation from deletion combines with absent I/O validation to create an unobservable structural decline

btree-survives-close-reopen.text: Data written before `BTree.close()` is fully recoverable by constructing a new `BTree` on the same directory, including updates and deletes.

btree-test-delete-frees-empty-leaf-no-fi.text: The test test_delete_frees_empty_leaf verifies that pages move to the free list but does not assert that the file size decreases.

btree-test-metadata-consistency-after-sp.text: The test `test_metadata_consistency_after_split` was not found in `test_btree.py` (grep returned 0 matches).

btree-tester-main-block-prints-all-tests.text: `b-tree-storage-engine/tester_test_btree.py` has a `__main__` block that calls every test function sequentially and ends with `print("\nAll tests PASSED")`.

btree-tester-requires-no-test-framework.text: `b-tree-storage-engine/tester_test_btree.py` requires only Python, `tempfile`, and the `btree` module; it does not require pytest or any test framework.

btree-tester-tests-assert-on-public-api-.text: The standalone tester tests assert on both the public API contract and observable internals like `tree.stats.height` and `tree.pm.pages_read`.

btree-tests-default-max-keys-per-page-4.text: The B-tree tests use a default max_keys_per_page=4.

btree-tests-do-not-verify-reclaiming-hal.text: `test_delete_and_reinsert` and `test_delete_frees_empty_leaf` do not verify space reclamation or merging of half-empty leaves.

btree-tests-probe-internal-state-via-pag.text: B-tree tests such as `test_page_io_counts` and `test_metadata_consistency_after_split` reach into internal state like `tree.pm.pages_read` and `_read_meta()` to verify invariants that a pure API test cannot catch.

btree-tests-stress-page-size-128-max-key.text: The B-tree test suite configures BTree with page_size=128 and max_keys_per_page=4 to stress the tightest page boundary.

btree-tests-use-temp-directory-isolation.text: Every B-tree test uses `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory` as a context manager to give the tree a fresh, isolated filesystem namespace with automatic cleanup.

btree-traversal-is-forward-only.text: B-tree sequential access is strictly forward-only: iteration descends the left spine (following children at index zero at every internal level) to reach the leftmost leaf, then walks the forward-only sibling chain, with no backward pointer, reverse iterator, or random leaf access mechanism.

justifications.label: Both the descent path and horizontal walk are unidirectional, constraining all sequential access to forward traversal

btree-tree-structure-change-rewrites-ful.text: _write_meta() rewrites the full metadata page whenever tree structure changes, including key count, root pointer, and free list.

btree-underfull-leaves-persist.text: Direct consequence of existing belief `btree-no-underflow-rebalancing`; the space amplification follows mechanically from the lack of merge/rebalance

btree-update-amplification-does-not-comp.text: B-tree updates overwrite leaf pages in place, so write amplification does not compound with subsequent updates to the same key, unlike LSM compaction.

btree-uses-bisect-not-linear-scan.text: In-node key lookup uses `bisect_left`/`bisect_right` (binary search), making within-node search O(log B) rather than the textbook O(B) linear scan — shifting the optimal branching factor higher than classical B-tree analysis predicts.

btree-wal-appends-require-size-sync.text: B-tree WAL writes are appends that extend the file, so `fdatasync` would still need to sync the file-size metadata.

btree-wal-before-data.text: Every page mutation is logged to the WAL (with fsync) before being written to the data file; recovery replays the WAL, so no committed write is lost on crash.

metadata.example:
# WAL entry written before page modification
wal_entry = struct.pack(">II", page_num, len(data)) + data
self._wal_fd.write(wal_entry)
os.fsync(self._wal_fd.fileno())
# then write data page

btree-wal-checksum-excludes-page-num.text: In `b-tree-storage-engine/btree.py`, the WAL entry checksum covers only `page_data`, so a corrupted `page_num` during recovery writes a valid page to the wrong disk location without detection — the most dangerous integrity gap in the codebase

btree-wal-commit-resets-sequence-counter.text: After truncating the WAL, WAL.commit() resets _seq to 0.

btree-wal-correct-commit-order-is-fsync-.text: The correct WAL commit sequence is to fsync the data file before truncating the WAL, ensuring protected data is durable before discarding the log.

btree-wal-entry-format-is-seq-page-len-d.text: Each B-tree WAL entry is structured as `(seq, page_num, data_len, data, crc32)`.

btree-wal-entry-header-format.text: The B-tree WAL entry format is: sequence number (4 bytes), page number (4 bytes), data length (4 bytes), page data, and a 4-byte checksum.

btree-wal-entry-includes-full-page.text: Each B-tree WAL entry is `16 + page_size` bytes (12-byte header with seq/page_num/data_len, full page image, 4-byte CRC32), making WAL writes the dominant cost for small key-value updates

btree-wal-fsync-pagefile-deferred.text: Covered by existing beliefs `btree-wal-fsync-per-entry` (WAL fsyncs per entry) and `write-meta-no-fsync` (PageManager defers sync)

btree-wal-fsync-per-entry.text: Each `WAL.log_write()` call performs an `fsync`, guaranteeing that WAL entries are durable before any data page writes proceed

btree-wal-has-no-commit-marker-in-wal.text: The B-tree WAL does not contain a commit marker; its correctness relies on truncating the WAL only after syncing all data pages to the data file.

btree-wal-is-physical-redo-only.text: The B-tree WAL in `btree.py` stores full after-image page data (physical WAL) and supports only redo recovery; there is no undo capability

btree-wal-is-reference-implementation.text: Comparative judgment across implementations rather than a testable factual claim about a specific module

btree-wal-log-write-fsyncs-each-entry.text: The B-tree WAL log_write method calls both flush() and os.fsync() on each logged page image.

btree-wal-no-commit-record.text: Duplicate of existing `btree-wal-replays-without-commit` which captures the same structural fact that the B-tree WAL has no commit marker and replays all valid entries unconditionally

btree-wal-no-data-fsync.text: `PageManager.write_page` calls `flush()` but never `os.fsync()`, so written pages may not be durable on crash even after the WAL has committed.

btree-wal-no-operation-boundaries.text: The WAL logs individual page writes and commits by full truncation; it cannot represent a multi-step structural operation as an atomic unit

btree-wal-provides-split-atomicity.text: Multi-page operations (splits, deletes that free pages) are made crash-safe by writing all page modifications to the WAL before applying them to the data file

btree-wal-recover-ignores-metadata.text: WAL.recover replays page data writes but does not validate or restore the metadata page's next_free or free_head fields.

btree-wal-recovery-redoes-then-truncates.text: WAL.recover() redoes valid page images into the data file, syncs the data file, and then truncates the WAL.

btree-wal-recovery-test-simulates-crash-.text: `test_wal_recovery` simulates a crash by closing raw file handles (`tree.pm._f`, `tree.wal._f`) without calling `tree.close()`, then reopens the tree to verify recovery.

btree-wal-recovery-writes-to-wrong-locat.text: During B-tree WAL recovery, a corrupted `page_num` passes the payload-only CRC and causes a valid page to be written to the wrong disk location.

btree-wal-replay-idempotency-enables-com.text: WAL replay is safe to run at any time because page writes are idempotent; this idempotency eliminates the need for a commit marker in the WAL.

btree-wal-replay-is-idempotent.text: Because the B-tree WAL stores complete page images, replaying entries already applied to the data file produces identical results, making the crash window after `sync()` but before `truncate()` harmless

btree-wal-replays-without-commit.text: The B-tree's WAL replays all valid (CRC-passing) entries on recovery regardless of whether a commit marker is present — uncommitted entries are applied without distinction.

btree-wal-syncs-data-file-defers.text: Covered by existing `btree-wal-fsync-per-entry` (WAL fsyncs every log entry) and `btree-wal-no-data-fsync` (data file defers fsync).

btree-wal-three-phase-commit.text: The B-tree WAL commit follows a strict three-phase protocol: (1) write WAL entries + fsync, (2) fsync data file via `page_manager.sync()`, (3) truncate WAL + fsync WAL fd — crash-safe at every interleaving because WAL entries are physical page images making replay idempotent.

btree-wal-truncate-before-data-sync.text: `WAL.commit()` truncates the WAL before the data file is fsynced, creating a crash window where both the log and the data can be lost.

btree-wal-truncate-is-safe.text: The B-tree's WAL `commit()` only truncates after fsyncing the data file, making truncation idempotent — a crash mid-truncation simply replays the WAL entries again on recovery

btree-wal-truncation-is-commit-point.text: The WAL truncation in `commit()` is the atomic linearization point: before truncation, recovery will redo the transaction; after truncation, the transaction is committed

btree-wal-uncommitted-entries-test-appen.text: `test_wal_uncommitted_entries` manually appends a WAL entry via `WAL.log_write` without a commit marker, then reopens the tree to verify uncommitted entries are replayed without corrupting committed state.

btree-wal-uses-full-page-images.text: The WAL logs complete page images (physical logging) rather than logical operations, which eliminates incomplete-split states during recovery but increases write amplification compared to PostgreSQL's logical WAL entries.

btree-wal-uses-trailer-crc.text: The B-tree WAL places its CRC32 checksum as a trailer after `page_data`, while the standalone WAL and Bitcask embed CRC in the record header — a structural difference that affects torn-write detection behavior

buffer-bounded-by-window-plus-lateness.text: Join buffer size is bounded by events within `window.duration` of the current watermark; `_expire_events` garbage-collects everything below that cutoff on every event arrival or `advance_time` call

bully-assumes-full-connectivity.text: The Bully Algorithm requires any node to message any other node directly via `all_node_ids`; there is no ring or tree overlay topology

bully-candidate-half-timeout.text: Candidates wait `election_timeout // 2` for ALIVE responses before deciding, shorter than the follower's full `election_timeout`, to avoid cascading election delays.

bully-cascade-causes-quadratic-messages.text: Receiving an ELECTION from a lower-ID node triggers both an ALIVE response and a new `start_election` call, creating the O(n²) message cascade in worst-case elections

bully-coordinator-from-lower-id-triggers.text: A node rejects a COORDINATOR from a lower-ID sender by starting its own election.

bully-coordinator-is-broadcast.text: `declare_victory` sends a COORDINATOR message to every other node in the cluster (O(n) messages), not just to nodes that participated in the election

bully-election-alive-nodes-agree-on-lead.text: After `run_until_leader()`, all alive nodes agree on the same leader.

bully-election-terms-monotonic.text: Election terms in `get_election_history()` are enforced to be monotonically non-decreasing across successive elections, validated by `test_terms_increase_monotonically`

bully-has-four-message-types.text: The Bully leader election implementation defines four message types: ELECTION, ALIVE, COORDINATOR, and HEARTBEAT.

bully-highest-id-wins.text: The Bully Algorithm always elects the highest available node ID as leader; `start_election` only sends ELECTION to higher-ID nodes, and `declare_victory` only fires when no higher node responds.

bully-no-external-dependencies.text: Subsumed by existing beliefs `ddia-pure-python-stdlib` and `ddia-modules-self-contained` which already capture the repo-wide pattern of zero external dependencies.

bully-node-has-three-states.text: Each `BullyNode` is in one of three states: follower, candidate, or leader.

bully-recovery-triggers-election.text: When a failed node recovers via `recover_node`, it immediately starts an election, potentially preempting the current leader — this is the defining "bully" behavior.

bully-run-until-leader-returns-none-afte.text: `run_until_leader(start_time, max_ticks)` ticks until all available nodes agree on a single leader, or returns `None` after `max_ticks`.

bully-sends-election-to-higher-only.text: Covered by existing belief `bully-highest-id-wins` which already states "start_election only sends ELECTION to higher-ID nodes"

bully-split-brain-resolved-post-hoc.text: Split-brain is detected and resolved by `_resolve_split_brain` in the cluster harness after each tick (forcing lower-ID leaders to re-elect), not prevented by the node-level protocol alone.

bully-standalone-runner-exits-1-on-failu.text: The standalone runner in `test_leader_election.py` prints PASS/FAIL per test and exits with code 1 if any test fails.

bully-start-election-declares-victory-wh.text: `start_election` declares victory immediately if no higher-ID nodes exist.

bully-state-machine-handles-four-message.text: `receive_message` in the Bully implementation handles exactly four message types: ELECTION, ALIVE, COORDINATOR, and HEARTBEAT.

bully-synchronous-delivery.text: All messages generated within a single `tick()` call are delivered and fully resolved (including cascading responses) in a `while all_messages` loop before the tick returns.

bully-term-never-decrements.text: `_current_term` is incremented on every `start_election` call and is never decremented.

bully-test-imports-unused-symbols.text: Trivial import detail, not an architectural invariant that would break things if violated

bully-tests-use-deterministic-simulation.text: Leader election tests control time via an explicit `start_time` parameter to `run_until_leader()` rather than real timers or sleeps, making the entire test suite deterministic with no flaky timing

bully-unavailable-nodes-return-empty-fro.text: `receive_message` and `tick` both early-return `[]` when a node's `_available` field is `False`.

bully-unavailable-nodes-return-empty-res.text: In `receive_message`, a node with `_available` false returns an empty list and sends no response.

byzantine-equivocating-sends-peer-sequen.text: The EQUIVOCATING Byzantine mode sends each peer a digest derived from the peer identifier and message sequence number.

byzantine-mode-is-immutable-after-constr.text: The `byzantine_mode` field is set in `__init__` and never modified during protocol execution, so a node's fault behavior cannot change mid-protocol — simplifying reasoning about safety guarantees

byzantine-wrong-digest-sends-prefixed-no.text: The WRONG_DIGEST Byzantine mode sends a string formed by prefixing the node ID with bad_digest_.

cassandra-compaction-throughput-config.text: Cassandra exposes `compaction_throughput_mb_per_sec` to rate-limit compaction I/O.

cassandra-defaults-to-stcs.text: Cassandra uses size-tiered compaction as its default compaction strategy.

cassandra-has-time-window-compaction-str.text: Cassandra provides `TimeWindowCompactionStrategy` for time-aware compaction scheduling.

cassandra-phi-keeps-inter-arrival-window.text: Cassandra's phi accrual detector keeps roughly the last 1000 heartbeat inter-arrival intervals per peer and fits them to an exponential or normal distribution.

catch-up-read-all-returns-snapshot.text: `catch_up()` obtains events via `read_all()`, which returns a snapshot of the event list at the moment of the call.

catch-up-resets-snapshot-counter-after-s.text: When the snapshot interval threshold is reached during `Projection.catch_up`, it calls `save_snapshot()` and resets `_events_since_snapshot` to zero.

catch-up-returns-processed-event-count.text: `Projection.catch_up` returns the integer count of events processed during the call, returning zero if the projection was already caught up.

catch-up-save-snapshot-deep-copies-state.text: `Projection.catch_up` triggers `save_snapshot()`, which deep-copies the projection state before storing it in the store's `_snapshots` mapping.

catch-up-then-subscribe.text: `LiveProjection` implements the catch-up subscription pattern: replay historical events via `read_all(from_position=...)`, then switch to push-based updates for future events, bridging pull/push at a known position with no gap

catch-up-uses-event-id-filtering.text: `catch_up()` calls `read_all(from_position=self._position + 1)` to skip already-processed events, but `_on_event` has no equivalent position guard — an asymmetry that enables duplicate processing

catch-up-uses-position-plus-one.text: `Projection.catch_up()` calls `read_all(from_position=self._position + 1)`, so loading a snapshot sets the exact boundary — only events after the snapshot's position are replayed, making reconstruction cost proportional to events-since-snapshot

cbf-8x-memory-vs-standard.text: `CountingBloomFilter` uses one byte per counter position (`bytearray(self._m)`) versus one bit per position in `BloomFilter`, an 8x memory overhead for deletion support

cbf-count-tracks-calls-not-cardinality.text: `CountingBloomFilter.__len__` returns `add` calls minus `remove` calls, not distinct element count; adding the same item twice and removing once leaves `len == 1`

cbf-membership-requires-all-counters-pos.text: `CountingBloomFilter.__contains__` returns true only when every hashed counter position is greater than zero.

cbf-one-byte-per-counter.text: Each `CountingBloomFilter` counter uses a full byte in a `bytearray` regardless of `counter_bits`, using 8x more memory than a bit-packed representation

cbf-remove-can-introduce-false-negatives.text: Unlike standard Bloom filters which never have false negatives, `CountingBloomFilter.remove()` can cause false negatives when two items share a hash position — removing one decrements the shared counter, potentially making the other appear absent

cbf-remove-false-accept.text: `CountingBloomFilter.remove` can silently succeed for an item never added if all its hash positions have non-zero counters from other items, corrupting the filter state

cbf-remove-raises-on-absent-item.text: `CountingBloomFilter.remove()` raises `ValueError` if any hash position has a zero counter, providing a safety check against removing items that were never added

cbf-remove-two-pass-atomicity.text: `CountingBloomFilter.remove()` validates all hash positions have non-zero counters in a first pass before decrementing any in a second pass, preventing partial state corruption when removing an absent item

cbf-saturated-counters-are-permanent.text: When a `CountingBloomFilter` counter reaches `_max_val` (default 15), it is never decremented, preventing false negatives at the cost of a slight false positive rate increase

cbf-saturated-counters-never-decrement.text: When a `CountingBloomFilter` counter reaches `_max_val` (default 15 for 4-bit counters), it is permanently frozen: neither `add` nor `remove` will change it

cdc-and-event-sourcing-share-projection-.text: `CDCConsumer`/`MaterializedView` in `cdc.py` and `Projection` in `event_store.py` implement the same structural pattern — track position, pull new events, apply handlers — against different event sources (database mutations vs. domain events)

cdc-backbone-both-heuristic-and-insuffic.text: The CDC backbone that all derived systems depend on has two independent reliability gaps: event type semantics are determined by reconstruction heuristics rather than explicit markers (insert vs update distinguished by old_value presence, tombstones reported as None, snapshots use sentinel sequence numbers), AND the consistency requirements of derived systems (explicit flush to make mutations visible, old values for index maintenance) aren't reliably met by the CDC infrastructure.

justifications.label: CDC event semantics are heuristic-based AND derived systems need guarantees CDC doesn't provide — the consistency backbone is unreliable at both the semantic and operational levels

cdc-before-after-contract.text: Every `ChangeEvent` follows a strict before/after convention: INSERT has `before=None`, DELETE has `after=None`, UPDATE has both populated as full row copies, making events self-contained without querying the source database.

cdc-compact-returns-removed-count.text: `CDCLog.compact()` returns the number of events removed.

cdc-compaction-preserves-relative-order.text: `CDCLog.compact()` retains the latest event per `(table, key)` and preserves the relative order of surviving events.

cdc-consumer-and-database-share-process.text: In this CDC implementation, `CDCConsumer` and the database share the same process.

cdc-consumer-poll-is-at-least-once.text: If a CDC consumer crashes mid-`poll()`, the position is not advanced, so all events from that batch will be reprocessed on the next call — providing at-least-once delivery with no deduplication.

cdc-consumer-position-is-next-sequence.text: A CDC consumer's `_position` tracks the *next* sequence number to read (not the last one read); after processing, it advances to `last_event.sequence_number + 1`.

cdc-consumer-position-is-volatile.text: CDCConsumer tracks its read position as an in-memory integer (`_position`) with no durable offset storage, meaning position is lost on process restart

cdc-consumer-seek-moves-cursor.text: `CDCConsumer.seek()` allows the consumer cursor to be rewound or fast-forwarded.

cdc-determines-insert-vs-update-by-old-v.text: The CDC layer distinguishes `insert` from `update` events by checking whether `old_value is None`; the WAL only knows `PUT` and `DELETE`, so the semantic enrichment happens at the CDC boundary

cdc-event-semantics-depend-on-reconstruc.text: CDC event semantics are determined by reconstruction heuristics rather than explicit markers: insert vs update is distinguished by checking whether old_value is None, tombstones are reported as None values indistinguishable from missing data in conflict records, and snapshots use a sentinel sequence number (-1) to distinguish bootstrapped state from real events.

justifications.label: Event type, deletion state, and bootstrap origin are all inferred from value-level conventions

cdc-insert-update-distinction.text: Insert vs. update is determined solely by whether `CDCStream.emit()` receives a non-None `old_value`; the WAL itself only records `PUT` operations for both cases

cdc-log-compact-keeps-latest-event-per-t.text: The `CDCLog.compact()` method keeps only the latest event per `(table, key)`, implementing log compaction while allowing new consumers to bootstrap from current state.

cdc-log-compact-keeps-latest-per-key.text: CDCLog.compact() retains only the most recent event per (table, key) pair, matching Kafka log compaction semantics but without concurrent-reader safety

cdc-log-compaction-keeps-latest-per-tabl.text: `CDCLog.compact()` keeps only the latest event per `(table, key)`, bounding log growth while preserving the ability to bootstrap new consumers.

cdc-log-sequence-numbers-survive-compact.text: `CDCLog.compact()` preserves the original sequence numbers of surviving events; it does not renumber them, so consumer positions remain valid references after compaction.

cdc-materialized-view-transform-none-del.text: When a `MaterializedView`'s transform function returns `None` for an INSERT or UPDATE event, the row is removed from the view rather than stored, acting as a filter on the derived table.

cdc-old-value-required-for-consistency.text: Duplicates the combination of existing beliefs `unbundled-db-cdc-events-carry-old-value` and `secondary-index-stale-entry-cleanup`

cdc-old-value-required-for-index-consist.text: `SecondaryIndex.process_event` depends on `CDCEvent.old_value` to remove stale index entries during updates; without before-images, incremental index maintenance produces phantom references

cdc-read-operations-do-not-generate-even.text: `CDCDatabase.select` and `scan` do not append `ChangeEvent`s to the CDC log.

cdc-search-index-full-reindex-on-update.text: `SearchIndex` removes all old tokens and re-adds all new tokens on every UPDATE event, even if only non-indexed columns changed — correct but not optimized for partial changes.

cdc-search-index-tokenization-whitespace.text: `SearchIndex` tokenizes specified columns by whitespace splitting and lowercasing.

cdc-snapshot-uses-sentinel-sequence-numb.text: `create_snapshot` assigns `sequence_number=-1` to all synthetic INSERT events, distinguishing bootstrapped state from real log entries and enabling new consumers to load current state then seek to the live tail.

cdc-write-and-log-are-synchronously-coup.text: Every CDCDatabase mutation (insert/update/delete) writes to in-memory state and appends to CDCLog in the same synchronous call with no failure boundary between them

ch-md5-masked-to-32-bits.text: The consistent hash ring's `_hash` function truncates MD5's 128-bit output to 32 bits via `& 0xFFFFFFFF`, matching the `RING_SIZE` of 2^32

metadata.example:
def _hash(key):
    return int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) & 0xFFFFFFFF

ch-preference-list-skips-duplicates.text: `get_nodes` walks clockwise past virtual nodes belonging to already-seen physical nodes, ensuring exactly `replication_factor` distinct physical nodes in the preference list

result = []
while len(result) < self.replication_factor:
    node = self._ring_nodes[idx % n]
    if node not in seen:
        seen.add(node)
        result.append(node)
    idx += 1

ch-ring-sorted-invariant.text: `ConsistentHashRing._ring_positions` is maintained in sorted order at all times via `bisect`; all key lookups depend on this invariant

self._ring_positions.insert(idx, pos)

ch-transfer-maps-are-descriptive.text: `add_node` and `remove_node` return transfer map descriptions of which arcs move between nodes but do not move data themselves; the caller must act on the map

ch-vnode-count-is-weighted.text: A consistent hash ring node with weight `w` gets `int(num_vnodes * w)` virtual nodes, so weight=0.5 produces half the default ring presence

chained-checksums-trade-random-access-fo.text: Chained frame checksums (as in SQLite's WAL) prevent mid-log splicing, deletion, and reordering but require sequential validation from the chain start, eliminating the ability to validate or replay a single record in isolation

checkpoint-empty-payload.text: Checkpoint records are encoded with zero-length key and value fields; the record's semantic role is carried entirely by its `OP_CHECKPOINT` type and sequence number

checkpoint-filtered-from-replay.text: `replay()` filters out CHECKPOINT records (along with COMMIT records), returning only PUT and DELETE — checkpoint records serve as truncation boundaries, not data operations visible to recovery consumers

checkpoint-force-syncs.text: Duplicate of existing `force-true-bypasses-sync-mode` which already captures that `force=True` unconditionally syncs regardless of sync mode setting

checkpoint-is-just-marker.text: checkpoint() writes an OP_CHECKPOINT record and forces a sync, but it does not trigger any data flush or WAL truncation on its own; a caller must coordinate those steps.

checkpoint-record-not-used-in-recovery.text: `OP_CHECKPOINT` records are written to the WAL but recovery (`_recover_seq_num`) does not search for them; the caller must supply the checkpoint sequence number externally via `replay(after_seq=)`

checkpoint-record-unused-for-truncation.text: The WAL supports `OP_CHECKPOINT` records that could serve as a durable truncation watermark (skip records below the watermark during replay), but `truncate()` physically removes records instead of using this mechanism

checkpoint-requires-prior-durability-of-.text: The caller is responsible for ensuring the primary storage is durable before calling checkpoint(); the WAL itself does not enforce this ordering.

checkpoint-seq-increment-before-sync-fai.text: If _do_sync() raises an OSError during checkpoint, _seq_num has already been incremented, leaving a gap in the sequence.

checkpoint-shares-sequence-space.text: Duplicate of existing `wal-checkpoint-consumes-sequence` which already captures that checkpoint records consume from the shared monotonic sequence counter

checksum-mask-is-python2-compat.text: The `& 0xFFFFFFFF` mask in `WAL._checksum` is a Python 2 portability idiom — Python 3's `zlib.crc32` already returns unsigned values, making the mask technically redundant but kept as defensive code

client-holds-stale-token-after-lock-expi.text: The `Client._held_tokens` dict is never cleared on lock expiry — the client retains and may use a token whose corresponding lock has already been acquired by another client

client-write-attaches-cached-fencing-tok.text: `Client.write_to_resource()` automatically attaches the client's cached fencing token for the named lock to the write.

code-expert-directory-contains-only-topi.text: The `.code-expert/` directory contains only `topics.json`, with no templates, specs, or generation scripts.

code-expert-has-no-codegen.text: The code-expert workflow is read-only against the target repository — it scans, explores, and extracts beliefs but never generates or modifies source files

code-expert-has-no-test-generation-step.text: Describes the code-expert tool's workflow, not a code invariant of the target repository; tool behavior belongs in tool documentation, not the belief registry

code-expert-tool-state-only-topics-json.text: The `.code-expert/` directory contains only `topics.json`; it has no templates, specs, or generator configuration.

code-expert-tooling-has-zero-tester-test.text: A grep for `tester_test` across all code-expert tooling returned zero matches.

code-expert-workflow-steps-sequence.text: The documented code-expert workflow consists of the steps scan, explore, explain, propose beliefs, review, and derive.

codebase-does-not-explicitly-model-gc-pa.text: The codebase contains no explicit modeling of GC pauses or network delays; there are zero grep matches for `gc_pause`, `sleep`, `delay`, `frozen`, `network_delay`, or `latency`.

codebase-has-13-fsync-calls-and-zero-fda.text: The codebase contains 13 os.fsync() call sites and zero os.fdatasync() calls.

codebase-lacks-compaction-filters.text: Neither compaction module implements RocksDB-style compaction filters, user-defined callbacks that transform or drop entries during compaction.

codebase-never-uses-fdatasync.text: The codebase contains zero uses of `fdatasync`; all durability calls use `os.fsync()`.

codebase-uses-no-steal-policy.text: All implementations use NO-STEAL buffer management: uncommitted transaction data is never written to the persistent data store, eliminating the need for undo logging at the cost of requiring all dirty data from active transactions to fit in memory

combiner-does-not-affect-map-output-stat.text: `map_output_records` is incremented before the combiner runs (line 108), so stats reflect pre-combiner volume; the test at line 68 asserts this explicitly

combiner-groups-by-key-with-sort-groupby.text: `_apply_combiner` sorts pairs by key and uses `groupby` to collect values per key before invoking the combiner.

combiner-has-no-negative-test.text: The test suite contains no negative test showing a non-associative or non-commutative combiner producing wrong results.

combiner-not-type-checked.text: The combiner's callable signature matches the reducer's, but no runtime or static check verifies associativity or commutativity — a non-associative combiner (e.g., average) produces silently wrong results that vary with `num_mappers`

combiner-output-indistinguishable-from-m.text: The reducer reads combiner output from intermediate JSON files identically to raw mapper output, with no metadata distinguishing pre-aggregated values from raw emitted pairs

combiner-requires-associativity-and-comm.text: Correctness of a MapReduce combiner requires the combine function to be associative and commutative.

combiner-runs-per-mapper-partition.text: Duplicates existing belief `mr-combiner-is-map-side-only` which already states the combiner runs inside `_run_mapper` on each mapper's output for a single partition independently

combiner-test-asserts-same-result-with-a.text: The combiner test uses `word_count_reducer` as the combiner and asserts the result is identical with and without the combiner.

commit-aborts-on-conflict.text: On write-write conflict, `commit()` calls `abort(tx)` internally and returns `False`, so callers never need to manually abort after a failed commit; the transaction is dead after a `False` return.

commit-aware-replay-requires-sequence-ra.text: A correct crash-recovery replay would track which records belong to which batch by sequence-number ranges and only replay batch records when a corresponding COMMIT record exists.

commit-conflict-check-not-atomic.text: The conflict-check-then-commit sequence in `MVCCDatabase.commit()` is not atomic — no locking protects the window between checking versions and marking committed, requiring single-threaded execution for correctness.

commit-conflict-only-for-concurrent-writ.text: In commit(), a version conflicts only if its creator is different, not aborted, committed, and was either active at the observing transaction's start or has tx_id >= tx.tx_id; writers committed before the snapshot are not conflicts.

commit-conflict-scans-all-versions.text: The write-write conflict check in `commit()` scans all versions of each key in the transaction's write set (not just the latest), making conflict detection O(versions) per written key.

commit-means-data-sync-then-wal-truncate.text: Duplicates existing `wal-commit-sync-before-truncate` which already captures the ordering invariant that data is fsynced before the WAL is truncated

commit-only-in-batch.text: `OP_COMMIT` is written exclusively by `append_batch()` in `write-ahead-log/wal.py`; single `append()` calls never produce a COMMIT record, so individual operations are their own atomic unit

commit-raises-on-inactive-transaction.text: commit() raises TransactionError if the transaction is not active, meaning it has already committed or aborted.

commit-read-only-skip-conflict-check.text: Read-only transactions bypass write-write conflict detection entirely in `commit()` and always commit successfully, since they cannot produce write-write conflicts.

commit-timestamp-unused-by-visibility.text: Commit timestamps are assigned by `commit()` and stored in `_commit_timestamps`, but `_is_visible` never references them — visibility is determined purely by transaction IDs and the committed/active-at-start sets.

compact-closes-handles-before-keydir-ful.text: In `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py`, cached file readers for old immutable files are closed at the start of the merge-write phase, before all keydir entries have been updated to point to new locations, creating a window where reads would fail even without concurrent access

compact-deletes-old-data-and-hint-files.text: After merging, `compact` deletes both `.data` and `.hint` files for every old immutable file ID.

compact-deletes-old-sstable-files.text: `compact()` removes old SSTable files from disk after merging, meaning any concurrent reader holding a reference to a deleted SSTable reads stale data (on Unix) or crashes (on Windows)

compact-empty-log-advances-base-by-old-l.text: When compaction removes all messages and new_log is empty, _base_offsets[partition] is set to the previous base plus len(log).

compact-filters-against-live-index.text: During log-structured-hash-table compaction, records in frozen segments are only kept if `_index` still points to that exact `(path, offset)`, correctly excluding keys that were overwritten in the active segment after the frozen segment was closed.

compact-merged-file-ids-start-after-acti.text: `compact` assigns new merged data file IDs starting at `active_file_id + 1`.

compact-newest-wins-by-seq.text: During compaction, the entry with the highest SSTable sequence number wins for each key; sequence numbers are per-SSTable (all entries in one SSTable share the same seq), not per-entry

compact-no-concurrency-safety.text: `compact()` mutates `self._sstables` without locking; concurrent `_flush` or `get` calls during compaction can produce incorrect state or lose newly flushed SSTables

compact-no-immutable-files-returns-immed.text: `compact` returns immediately when there are no immutable files, meaning all existing file IDs equal the active file ID.

compact-not-crash-safe.text: Log-structured-hash-table compaction is non-atomic: the sequence of write-new, update-index, delete-old, rename-active has no transaction boundary, and a crash mid-compaction can leave orphaned segments or a misnamed active file.

compact-partition-returns-removed-count.text: Topic.compact_partition returns the number of messages removed by compaction.

compact-preserves-active-highest-id.text: Substantially duplicates existing belief `bitcask-compaction-renumbers-active` — the invariant that the active segment has the highest ID is maintained by the renumbering mechanism that belief already describes.

compact-purges-tombstones.text: Tombstones (`b""`) are permanently removed during compaction and never written to the output SSTable; deleted keys disappear entirely after merge

compact-rotates-merged-files-at-max-file.text: `compact` rotates merged data files at `max_file_size`, just like active files are rotated.

compact-sets-base-offset-absolutely.text: `Topic.compact_partition` overwrites `_base_offsets[partition]` with the first surviving message's offset (absolute assignment), discarding whatever the previous base was, because compaction removes messages from arbitrary positions.

compact-single-threaded-assumption.text: Log-structured-hash-table compaction has no synchronization protecting the index, file handles, or segment counter during its multi-step mutation sequence; concurrent access during compaction would corrupt state.

compact-skips-crc-validation.text: Log-structured-hash-table compaction reads records from frozen segments without verifying CRC checksums, unlike `_scan_segment` which stops at the first CRC mismatch; a corrupted record could be silently copied into the compacted segment.

compact-triggered-explicitly-by-caller.text: Compaction is triggered explicitly by the caller; there is no automatic background compaction.

compact-uses-explicit-timestamp-comparis.text: During scanning, `compact` keeps an entry if its timestamp is newer than a previously seen entry for the same key, handling out-of-order cases.

compaction-avoids-direction-complexity.text: Design rationale comparing to LevelDB, not a testable codebase invariant; the actual constraint is captured by `sstable-merge-forward-only`.

compaction-buffers-all-entries.text: `lsm.py:compact` collects all merged entries into an in-memory list before writing the output SSTable, requiring O(n) memory proportional to total data rather than O(k) proportional to number of input SSTables

compaction-crash-can-resurrect-deleted-k.text: A crash during LSM compaction after tombstones are stripped from the merged output but before old SSTables are deleted can resurrect previously-deleted keys, because the tombstone that suppressed them no longer exists in any surviving SSTable.

compaction-deletes-before-fsync.text: Covered by existing `lsm-compaction-deletes-without-fsync-barrier` which captures the same missing fsync barrier between output write and input deletion

compaction-deletes-before-reader-release.text: `compact()` deletes old SSTable files immediately after replacing `self._sstables`, with no mechanism to defer deletion until active readers holding references to the old list finish their iterations

compaction-hazard-within-broken-durabili.text: Compaction is the highest-risk operation yet operates within a durability pipeline broken at both ends: crash-unsafe compaction can permanently lose data or resurrect deletes, AND the surrounding infrastructure has fsync gaps (data may never reach disk) and unrecoverable integrity checks (corruption detected but not repaired) — the most dangerous operation has the least protection.

justifications.label: Critical data lifecycle hazard compounded by broken surrounding durability infrastructure

compaction-is-critical-data-lifecycle-ha.text: Compaction is the critical junction where crash safety and data lifecycle intersect: crash-unsafe compaction can permanently lose data or resurrect deleted keys (no write-temp/fsync/rename, delete-before-rename ordering), and fragmented tombstone semantics mean those corruptions propagate inconsistently through derived systems that require flush and old-value tracking for correctness.

justifications.label: Crash-unsafe compaction corrupts the very operation (tombstone processing) that derived system consistency depends on

compaction-is-explicit-not-background.text: Both the LSM and SSTable modules trigger compaction via explicit synchronous method calls (`compact()` / `run_compaction()`), not background threads — removing the write-amplification pressure that motivates least-overlap selection in production systems.

compaction-is-unsalvageable-as-designed.text: Compaction is unsalvageable as designed: it is the highest-risk operation within a durability pipeline broken at both ends (crash-unsafe writes that are unverifiable by testing), AND it triggers two independent failure modes under the concurrent access that production workloads produce (concurrent readers see inconsistent state, concurrent writers corrupt shared data structures), making it simultaneously the most critical and most dangerous operation.

justifications.label: Compaction is critical for data lifecycle yet hazardous under both crash and concurrency

compaction-lacks-crash-safety-across-imp.text: No storage engine implementation uses the write-temp/fsync/rename pattern for file creation, and both Bitcask implementations delete old segments before renaming replacements, creating crash windows where data exists in neither old nor new files.

justifications.label: Three observations across Bitcask and LSM establish that non-atomic file operations are a codebase-wide pattern, not implementation-specific

compaction-manager-never-deletes-old-fil.text: `CompactionManager` removes compacted SSTables from the in-memory `_sstables` list but never deletes their underlying files on disk; cleanup is the caller's responsibility.

compaction-manager-never-removes-tombsto.text: The `CompactionManager` in `sstable-and-compaction/sstable.py` always calls `merge_sstables` with the default `remove_tombstones=False`, making it conservatively correct but causing unbounded tombstone accumulation

compaction-manager-requires-existing-dat.text: CompactionManager requires data_dir to already exist and be writable; it never creates the directory itself.

compaction-manager-supports-partial-merg.text: The `CompactionManager` supports both size-tiered and leveled strategies with partial compactions, so a merge may include only a subset of SSTables and cannot always guarantee full key coverage.

compaction-manager-supports-two-strategi.text: `CompactionManager` implements both `'size_tiered'` and `'leveled'` compaction strategies, selected by a string parameter.

compaction-not-atomic.text: `LSMTree.compact()` performs a multi-step file swap (write new SSTable, update in-memory list, delete old files) with no mechanism to make the transition atomic across crashes

compaction-output-filename-uses-counter-.text: Every CompactionManager merge writes a new .sst file to data_dir with a monotonic counter plus a millisecond timestamp in the filename.

compaction-preserves-keyless-messages.text: Topic.compact_partition keeps all keyless messages in addition to the latest message for each key.

compaction-preserves-original-offsets.text: After `compact_partition`, surviving messages retain their original offset values, creating non-contiguous gaps in the offset sequence; offsets are never renumbered.

compaction-propagates-corruption.text: `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py:compact` copies records without integrity validation, so silently corrupted data survives compaction into new files

compaction-rename-reverts-without-dir-fs.text: Without directory fsync, a compaction rename can revert on crash, and deleted files can reappear, causing index/disk mismatch.

compaction-requires-full-read-for-update.text: General CS fact about read-modify-write workloads, not a testable claim about this codebase's behavior

compaction-respects-size-limit.text: Bitcask compaction output is itself subject to `max_file_size` rotation, so smaller size limits produce more post-compaction files — feeding back into recovery cost.

compaction-result-assigned-level-1.text: `CompactionManager.run_compaction` with leveled strategy assigns merged output to level 1 but does not verify that the new file's key range is disjoint from existing L1 files

compaction-strategy-vs-scheduling-decoup.text: The `sstable.py` `CompactionManager` separates *which* SSTables to merge (size-tiered vs. leveled strategy) from *when* to merge, but neither the manager nor any caller implements scheduling, rate-limiting, or load-aware deferral logic.

compaction-threshold-controls-overlap-wi.text: The `compaction_threshold` parameter (`lsm.py:204`) directly controls how many overlapping SSTables can accumulate before compaction, setting the worst-case missing-key probe count to `threshold - 1`

compaction-trigger-is-count-only.text: Duplicate of existing `compaction-triggered-by-sstable-count` which already captures that compaction triggers on SSTable count thresholds.

compaction-triggered-by-sstable-count.text: LSM compaction runs automatically when `len(self._sstables) >= self._compaction_threshold` (default 4), triggered at the end of `_flush` after the new SSTable is registered

compare-join-strategies-normalizes-outpu.text: `compare_join_strategies` strips `_mapper_id` and sorts records before comparing the three join strategies' outputs.

compare-returns-four-states.text: `VectorClock.compare` returns exactly one of `BEFORE`, `AFTER`, `EQUAL`, or `CONCURRENT`, implementing the partial order defined by component-wise comparison.

metadata.example:
def compare(self, other):
    # Returns "BEFORE", "AFTER", "EQUAL", or "CONCURRENT"
    if has_less and has_greater: return "CONCURRENT"
    if has_less: return "BEFORE"
    if has_greater: return "AFTER"
    return "EQUAL"

compare-strategies-runs-identical-worklo.text: `compare_strategies` runs the same document insert and field query workload against both DB types and returns their stats side-by-side.

concurrency-check-is-pre-mutation.text: The `expected_version` optimistic concurrency check in `append_batch` runs before any state mutation, so a `ConcurrencyConflict` exception is safe and leaves the store completely unchanged.

concurrency-detection-uses-origin-mismat.text: The multi-leader module treats a write as concurrent if `local_origin != remote_node`, using origin mismatch as a heuristic instead of vector clocks.

concurrency-unsafe-on-both-read-and-writ.text: Concurrency safety is absent from both mutation and query paths: core components (B-tree, garbage collector, consistent hash ring) silently assume single-threaded write access with no locks or assertions, and range scans lack snapshot isolation, cycle guards, or concurrent modification protection, meaning concurrent workloads can corrupt state through both writes and reads independently.

justifications.label: Neither writes (silent single-thread assumption) nor reads (no snapshot isolation) are safe under concurrency

concurrent-access-during-compaction-is-d.text: Compaction under concurrent access is unsafe in two independent failure modes: concurrent readers and writers have no synchronization (no locks, latches, or snapshots on either path), AND compaction itself has no crash-safe file operations — concurrent access can corrupt live state silently, and a crash during this unsynchronized compaction produces irrecoverable data loss.

justifications.label: No concurrency control on either path plus no crash-safe file operations equals two independent failure modes

concurrent-compaction-can-resurrect-dele.text: If range_scan() reads an old SSTable before compaction deletes a tombstone but reads the compacted SSTable after the tombstone is gone, the merge logic may resurrect a deleted key.

concurrent-flush-and-compact-can-cause-d.text: If _flush() appends a new SSTable while compact() is iterating the list, the new SSTable may be included in the merge and also remain as a separate SSTable (duplicate data), or be excluded from the merge and lost when compact() overwrites self._sstables (data loss).

concurrent-range-scan-skips-keys-on-spli.text: Without latching, a range scan that caches a `next_sibling` pointer can miss keys moved to a new sibling page by a concurrent split — the core phantom problem at the physical level.

concurrent-scan-split-can-skip-keys.text: Theoretical failure mode about concurrent access that cannot occur in the single-threaded implementation; not a testable claim about the code as it exists

conflict-requires-different-origins.text: A conflict in `apply_remote_change` is only detected when `local_origin != remote_node`; two writes from the same origin at different timestamps are treated as sequential updates and resolved by tuple comparison without generating a `ConflictRecord`.

conflict-resolution-architecture-is-spli.text: Conflict resolution is implemented in two disconnected modules: CRDTs encode resolution in their merge semantics (self-resolving), while the strategy enum covers only LWW and custom-merge — leaving no unified API and no bridge between the two approaches.

justifications.label: The enum explicitly tracks that CRDTs are a third strategy but delegates to a separate module, creating an architectural seam where composition should exist

consensus-accept-requires-geq-promised.text: `ConsensusInstance.accept(proposal_number, value, proposer_id)` accepts only if `proposal_number >= self.promised`.

consensus-and-membership-use-incompatibl.text: Gossip-based failure detection and Raft consensus interact in a way that can compound partition hazards: gossip's timeout-driven liveness set determines cluster membership, while Raft's partition behavior means an isolated leader silently accepts uncommittable writes and its inflated term forces re-election upon rejoining — if gossip's failure detection misclassifies a partitioned-but-live leader, it may trigger membership changes that interact with Raft's already-disruptive partition recovery.

justifications.label: Gossip's timeout-based failure detection can trigger Raft's partition hazard (stale leader + forced re-election) even without a real partition

consensus-architectures-are-inverse-opti.text: Raft and Total Order Broadcast represent contrasting approaches to Paxos optimization: Raft centralizes proposal authority in a single elected leader (one election per term, then Phase-2-only replication), eliminating dueling proposals within a term, while TOB allows any node to propose for any slot using full two-phase Paxos each time, making it susceptible to competing proposals. These represent different points in the leader-based versus leaderless tradeoff space.

justifications.label: Leader-based and leaderless consensus are inverse optimizations of Multi-Paxos

consensus-correctness-doubly-unverified.text: Consensus protocol correctness is doubly unverified: both Raft and TOB represent untested inverse optimizations of Multi-Paxos whose safety properties diverge specifically under asynchrony and crash failures, AND the testing methodology covers neither crash nor asynchronous failure modes — the exact conditions under which the two optimization strategies would reveal different safety profiles.

justifications.label: The test methodology's blind spots exactly coincide with the conditions that would differentiate the consensus variants, making their safety claims maximally unfalsifiable.

consensus-prepare-promises-if-greater.text: `ConsensusInstance.prepare(proposal_number, proposer_id)` returns a promise only if `proposal_number > self.promised`.

consensus-safety-unverified-across-optim.text: Both consensus mechanisms represent inverse optimizations of Multi-Paxos (Raft centralizes proposal authority in a leader, TOB decentralizes it to allow any node to propose), but neither variant's safety has been validated under the asynchronous conditions it is designed for — all protocol tests use deterministic synchronous delivery with no real network I/O, message loss, or reordering.

justifications.label: Two inverse Paxos optimizations share the same verification gap — both are designed for asynchronous networks but tested exclusively under synchronous simulation

consistent-hash-add-node-is-idempotent.text: Adding a node that already exists silently returns an empty transfer map and does not change the ring's node count, vnode positions, or key assignments.

consistent-hash-default-150-vnodes.text: `ConsistentHashRing` defaults to 150 virtual nodes per physical node, and exposes `load_imbalance` (max_load / avg_load) to measure distribution quality

consistent-hash-get-node-walks-clockwise.text: `ConsistentHashRing.get_node` walks clockwise from the key's hash position to the next virtual node.

consistent-hash-get-nodes-collects-repli.text: `ConsistentHashRing.get_nodes` walks the ring collecting `replication_factor` distinct physical nodes, implementing a Dynamo-style preference list.

consistent-hash-get-nodes-first-equals-g.text: `get_nodes(key)[0]` always equals `get_node(key)` — the preference list's head is the primary replica.

consistent-hash-load-balance-test-requir.text: The load balance test with 150 vnodes and 3 nodes asserts ring imbalance remains below 1.5x.

consistent-hash-minimal-redistribution.text: Adding an Nth node to the ring moves approximately 1/N of keys, not a full reshuffle — the defining property that makes consistent hashing useful for dynamic cluster membership.

consistent-hash-replication-requires-suf.text: `get_nodes()` raises `ValueError` rather than silently under-replicating when `replication_factor` exceeds the number of physical nodes on the ring.

consistent-hash-ring-get-load-distributi.text: ConsistentHashRing.get_load_distribution returns fractions of ring address space per node that sum to 1.0.

consistent-hash-ring-get-node-empty-ring.text: ConsistentHashRing.get_node and get_nodes raise ValueError when called on an empty ring.

consistent-hash-ring-get-node-uses-bisec.text: ConsistentHashRing.get_node uses bisect.bisect (bisect_right) on the sorted position list to locate the clockwise successor vnode for a key hash.

consistent-hash-ring-get-node-wraps-to-i.text: ConsistentHashRing.get_node wraps to ring index 0 when the key hash is greater than all vnode positions.

consistent-hash-ring-get-nodes-worst-cas.text: ConsistentHashRing.get_nodes can traverse up to len(_ring_positions) entries in the worst case when most vnodes belong to a small number of physical nodes.

consistent-hash-ring-lookup-is-olog-v.text: Key lookup via `get_node` is O(log V) where V is total virtual nodes, using `bisect` on the sorted position list; node addition is O(V) per vnode due to `list.insert`.

consistent-hash-ring-no-positive-validat.text: `ConsistentHashRing` does not validate that `num_vnodes`, `weight`, or `replication_factor` are positive; zero or negative values silently produce degenerate ring states (e.g., a node with zero vnodes exists in `_nodes` but owns no ring arc).

consistent-hash-ring-nodes-registry-maps.text: ConsistentHashRing stores physical node IDs in the _nodes dict mapping to their float weights.

consistent-hash-ring-not-thread-safe.text: `ConsistentHashRing` has no synchronization; concurrent `add_node`/`remove_node` calls corrupt the sorted `_ring_positions` and `_ring_nodes` lists.

consistent-hash-ring-remove-node-absent-.text: ConsistentHashRing.remove_node raises ValueError when the requested node is not present.

consistent-hash-ring-remove-node-iterate.text: ConsistentHashRing.remove_node iterates indices in reverse when deleting vnodes to avoid index invalidation during removal.

consistent-hash-ring-sorted-invariant.text: `_ring_positions` is maintained in sorted order at all times via `bisect` insertion; `_ring_nodes` is kept parallel to it with `len(_ring_positions) == len(_ring_nodes)` always holding.
