consistent-hash-ring-uses-32-bit-space.text: The ring's hash space is `[0, 2^32)`, as validated by `test_ring_position_valid_range`.

consistent-hash-ring-uses-md5.text: All consistent hash ring positions are computed via MD5 truncated to 32 bits; the hash function is not pluggable

consistent-hash-ring-uses-md5-truncated-.text: The ring hashes keys and vnode identifiers using `hashlib.md5` truncated to 32 bits via `& 0xFFFFFFFF`, chosen for distribution quality rather than security.

consistent-hash-ring-vnode-position-is-h.text: Each virtual node position is computed by hashing the string formed by node_id, a colon, and the vnode index.

consistent-hash-routing-correct-under-si.text: Consistent hash routing provides correct minimal-redistribution key assignment with proper deduplication: adding an Nth node moves approximately 1/N of keys (not a full reshuffle), and the preference list correctly skips virtual nodes of already-seen physical nodes to return exactly replication_factor distinct physical nodes.

justifications.label: Minimal redistribution and deduplicated preference lists ensure correct routing, gated on the ring having no synchronization for concurrent add/remove operations

consistent-hash-test-suite-is-flat-pytes.text: The consistent hashing test suite is a flat collection of pytest test functions with no test classes.

consistent-hash-tests-use-10000-keys-for.text: The consistent hashing statistical tests use populations of 10,000 keys to obtain stable key distribution measurements.

consistent-hash-vnode-count-test-sweeps-.text: The vnode count test sweeps vnode counts [1, 10, 50, 150, 500] and asserts 500 vnodes produce better balance than 1 vnode.

consistent-hash-weight-scales-vnodes.text: The `weight` parameter on `add_node` scales virtual node count proportionally, supporting heterogeneous nodes with different capacities

consistent-hash-weighted-nodes-get-propo.text: The weighted node test asserts that a node with 3x weight receives roughly 3x the keys of a normal-weight node.

consistent-hashing-ring-uses-threading-l.text: The consistent hashing ring guards add_node, remove_node, get_node, and get_nodes with a threading.Lock using a public/private method split.

consumer-group-offset-resume.text: A new consumer joining a group loads committed offsets from the broker (tested at `test_partitioned_log.py:152`), enabling offset-based resume but also duplicate redelivery on crash

consumer-group-rebalance-redistributes-p.text: `partitioned_log.py` redistributes partitions among consumers when consumers join or leave a consumer group.

consumer-independent-positions.text: Each `DerivedSystem` tracks its own LSN position independently via `_position`, allowing consumers to fall behind or catch up at different rates without blocking each other

context-parameter-establishes-causality.text: Passing a vector clock as `context` to `VersionedKVStore.put` declares the write descends from that version; omitting context treats the write as concurrent with all existing versions

convergence-rate-asymmetry-membership-vs.text: Membership and data convergence operate at fundamentally different rates: gossip-based membership changes propagate in O(log N) rounds via epidemic-style random peer selection, but data convergence in ring topology requires O(N) sync rounds because each round advances changes by exactly one hop via store-and-forward requeuing — creating a window proportional to cluster size where the membership view is current but data remains stale.

justifications.label: O(log N) membership convergence vs O(N) data convergence creates a growing window where the cluster knows who's alive but hasn't finished replicating — the gap widens with cluster size

correct-sync-pattern.text: Already captured by individual per-implementation beliefs: `rotation-always-fsyncs`, `wal-batch-always-fsyncs`, `btree-wal-before-data`, `bitcask-fsync-per-record-default`.

correctness-gap-widens-under-failure.text: The gap between expected and actual system correctness widens under failure: distributed protocols require storage-layer guarantees (crash-safe compaction, atomic writes, complete CRC coverage) that no implementation provides, and the resulting divergence accumulates without bound because anti-entropy can detect but not fully reconcile the inconsistencies.

justifications.label: Unmet storage guarantees produce divergence that distributed compensating mechanisms cannot fully resolve

correctness-unachievable-and-unfalsifiab.text: System correctness is both unachievable and unfalsifiable: the gap between specification and implementation widens under every failure mode (distributed protocols require unmet storage guarantees, replica divergence accumulates without bound, storage degrades monotonically), and the testing methodology cannot detect these gaps (crash paths untested, protocols validated only under synchronous simulation) — the system cannot be correct and cannot discover that it is not.

justifications.label: The depth-4 conclusion that correctness gaps widen under failure combined with the depth-3 conclusion that protocol safety is unfalsifiable produces a depth-5 epistemic closure: the system's incorrectness is provable from analysis but invisible from testing

corruption-detection-on-read-not-write.text: Subsumed by the more specific `bitcask-crc-validated-on-read-only` above

corruption-is-terminal-across-all-reader.text: Corruption is a terminal condition across every binary record reader in the codebase: each stops at the first CRC failure with no resync capability, and the WAL specifically halts all replay rather than skipping the corrupt record, meaning any single corrupt byte truncates the recoverable history.

justifications.label: Stop-on-first-error without resync is universal — corruption in any record silently discards all subsequent records

corruption-propagates-through-all-data-p.text: Corruption propagates silently through every data transformation pipeline: both Bitcask compaction implementations copy records without CRC validation, and hint file generation reads source records without integrity checks — every transformation step amplifies corruption rather than filtering it.

justifications.label: Three independent base beliefs each show a transformation step that skips integrity verification, forming a pipeline where corrupted data survives every stage

corruption-terminates-scan.text: In `_scan_segment`, a CRC mismatch or short read stops scanning the entire segment; records after the corrupt point are silently lost from the index even if they are individually valid.

metadata.example:
expected_crc = zlib.crc32(payload) & 0xFFFFFFFF
if crc != expected_crc:
    raise CorruptionError(f"CRC mismatch")
# caller breaks on CorruptionError, losing remaining records

corruption-test-checks-count-not-continu.text: The WAL corruption test (`test_wal.py:44`) verifies that replay returns fewer records after corruption but never asserts that the surviving sequence numbers are consecutive.

corruption-test-expects-single-record-re.text: The WAL corruption test verifies that `replay()` returns exactly one record after corrupting the tail, proving reads stop at the corruption boundary.

corruption-test-exploits-tail-position.text: Test strategy detail, not an architectural invariant — describes how `test_corruption` works rather than a property the codebase must maintain

corruption-test-overwrites-tail-payload.text: `test_corruption` overwrites the last 5 bytes of the WAL file with `0xFF`, targeting the second record's payload or trailing bytes and guaranteeing a CRC mismatch while leaving the first record intact.

count-is-barrier.text: `Count` stage materializes its entire input into a `defaultdict` before yielding any output, making it a pipeline barrier that forces all upstream stages to complete first

count-sort-are-materialization-barriers.text: Count part duplicates existing belief `count-is-barrier`; Sort's barrier nature is implicit in `sort-external-merge`

counting-bloom-4bit-default.text: Already captured in existing belief `cbf-saturated-counters-never-decrement` which states "default 15 for 4-bit counters"

counting-bloom-4bit-safe-at-capacity.text: At designed capacity (n ≤ expected_items), the expected number of saturated 4-bit counters is effectively zero because the per-position load follows Poisson(ln 2 ≈ 0.693), making P(count ≥ 15) ≈ 10⁻¹⁵

counting-bloom-add-silently-ignores-satu.text: CountingBloomFilter.add increments a counter only while it is below `_max_val`, silently ignoring further additions that hash to a saturated position.

counting-bloom-count-can-go-negative.text: `CountingBloomFilter.__len__` (via `_count`) can go negative if `remove` is called more times than `add` for an item that passes the zero-check due to hash collisions.

counting-bloom-counter-saturation-breaks.text: Duplicates existing belief `cbf-saturated-counters-never-decrement` which already captures that saturated counters are never decremented during removal.

counting-bloom-counters-saturate-at-15.text: `CountingBloomFilter` uses saturating 4-bit counters that max out at 15; after saturation, `remove()` becomes a no-op for that position to avoid false negatives.

counting-bloom-filter-reference-counted.text: `CountingBloomFilter` uses reference-counting semantics: an item added N times requires N `remove()` calls before it tests as absent via `__contains__`

counting-bloom-lacks-union-support.text: `CountingBloomFilter` does not support union, while the standard `BloomFilter` has a `union()` method.

counting-bloom-no-thread-safety.text: `CountingBloomFilter` has no thread safety; concurrent `add`/`remove` calls can race on counter reads and writes.

counting-bloom-overload-threshold.text: At 10× overload (10× expected_items inserted), roughly 0.5% of CountingBloomFilter counters saturate; at 20× overload, approximately half saturate, effectively degrading the filter to a non-counting Bloom filter

counting-bloom-remove-decrements-count-d.text: CountingBloomFilter.remove decrements `_count` even when saturated counters are not decremented, so `len()` can underreport the filter's active item count.

counting-bloom-remove-needs-drop-trackin.text: Using `CountingBloomFilter.remove()` during compaction would require `merge_sstables` to report which keys were discarded, which the current implementation does not do — duplicates and tombstones are silently skipped in the merge loop

counting-bloom-saturated-counters-not-de.text: CountingBloomFilter.remove leaves saturated counters fixed instead of decrementing them to avoid underflow corruption.

counting-bloom-saturation-silent.text: Counter saturation in `CountingBloomFilter` is handled silently with no warning when a counter reaches `_max_val`.

counting-bloom-shares-sizing-with-bloom.text: `CountingBloomFilter` uses the same optimal Bloom filter formulas as `BloomFilter` for sizing `m` and `k`.

counting-bloom-supports-deletion.text: `CountingBloomFilter` uses saturating 4-bit counters so entries can be removed via `remove()`, which standard `BloomFilter` cannot do — relevant for maintaining filters over mutable data structures

counting-bloom-trades-correctness-for-un.text: The counting Bloom filter pays 8x memory overhead and introduces false negatives through its removal operation for a capability (element deletion) that the primary use case — immutable SSTables — never needs, since SSTables are write-once and discarded whole during compaction.

justifications.label: Counting bloom filter trades memory and correctness for deletion support SSTables don't require

counting-bloom-useful-for-memtable.text: `CountingBloomFilter.remove()` is architecturally suited for maintaining filters over mutable in-memory structures (memtables) where keys can be overwritten without rescanning, not for SSTable compaction where the entire file is rewritten

counting-bloom-uses-byte-per-counter.text: CountingBloomFilter allocates one full byte per counter position (`bytearray(self._m)` at line 112) despite `counter_bits` defaulting to 4, using 8x the space of a standard BloomFilter's bit array rather than the expected 4x.

crash-between-data-sync-and-truncate-saf.text: If a crash occurs after the data file is synced but before the WAL is truncated, recovery replays already-applied operations; this is safe as long as WAL replay is idempotent.

crash-failure-paths-systematically-untes.text: Crash and failure recovery paths are systematically excluded from the test suite: the WAL has no tests for truncated records or CRC mismatches, LSM crash testing covers only WAL replay and ignores compaction crashes entirely, and SSI write-skew tests exist only in standalone tester files outside the default pytest runner — the most critical correctness scenarios have the least test coverage.

justifications.label: Three independent test gaps all exclude the crash and failure recovery paths

crash-recovery-both-broken-and-unverifie.text: Crash recovery is simultaneously broken and unverified: no storage engine has a safe crash recovery path (non-atomic compaction, batch-blind replay, metadata-excluding CRC), and crash/failure paths are systematically excluded from the test suite — recovery bugs will persist indefinitely because neither the broken mechanisms nor their absence is tested.

justifications.label: A depth-2 conclusion (recovery is unsafe) combined with a depth-1 conclusion (testing excludes crash paths) creates a self-reinforcing deficiency: the bugs exist and the tests cannot find them

crash-safe-file-creation-requires-temp-r.text: The crash-safe file creation pattern requires writing to a temp path, fsyncing the file, renaming it to the final path, and fsyncing the parent directory.

crash-safe-truncation-three-step.text: Describes a proposed fix pattern, not the current codebase behavior; the code does not implement write-to-temp + fsync + rename

crc-detects-not-prevents-data-loss.text: CRC32 checksums in the WAL and Bitcask detect partial writes after a crash but cannot recover the lost data — they convert silent corruption into detected data loss, not into a recoverable state

crc-integrity-only-in-log-structured-var.text: Already captured by `bitcask-no-checksum-validation` (hash-index-storage has no CRC) and `bitcask-crc-covers-payload-only` (log-structured variant does).

crc-mask-is-python2-artifact.text: The `& 0xFFFFFFFF` mask applied after `zlib.crc32` in all modules is a Python 2 compatibility artifact; Python 3's `zlib.crc32` already returns an unsigned 32-bit integer, making the mask harmless but unnecessary.

crc-no-cross-file-atomicity.text: The CRC32 integrity checks in `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py` detect corrupt records within a segment but provide no protection against the cross-file atomicity problem during compaction.

crc-polynomial-change-breaks-wire-format.text: Switching from ISO 3309 (`zlib.crc32`) to Castagnoli (CRC-32C) is a backward-incompatible wire format change; existing data files would fail CRC verification without a format version mechanism in the file header.

crc-polynomial-switch-touches-five-files.text: Switching the codebase from `zlib.crc32` to CRC-32C touches 5 files across 13 call sites.

crc-validates-op-key-value-not-header.text: Largely duplicate of already-accepted `wal-crc-does-not-cover-seqnum`; the positive framing (what IS covered) is the complement of the existing negative framing

crc32-covers-op-key-value-only.text: Duplicate of existing belief `wal-crc-does-not-cover-seqnum` (same fact stated from the opposite direction)

crc32-covers-records-not-files.text: CRC32 is computed per individual record or page (typically hundreds of bytes to a few KB), not per file; file-level corruption is detected only indirectly by failing to decode a record, not by any file-wide checksum

crc32-detects-all-single-double-bit-and-.text: CRC32 polynomial properties catch all single-bit errors, all double-bit errors, and all burst errors up to 32 bits.

crc32-is-linear-and-forgeable.text: CRC32 is a linear function, so an attacker with write access can alter a record and recompute a matching CRC without knowing the original data.

crc32-undetected-corruption-probability-.text: For random corruption, CRC32's probability of an undetected error is approximately 1 in 4.3 billion per record (2^32).

crc32c-hardware-instruction-implements-c.text: Intel SSE4.2 CRC32 and ARMv8 CRC32 instructions implement the Castagnoli polynomial specifically, not the ISO 3309 polynomial.

crdt-convergence-practically-sustainable.text: CRDT merge convergence is both algebraically correct and practically sustainable in production with bounded resource consumption.

justifications.label: Algebraic convergence holds but without causal context ORSet tombstones grow monotonically without bound, making long-lived production deployments unsustainable

crdt-eq-compares-semantic-state.text: All four CRDT types implement `__eq__` to compare semantic state (not object identity), enabling `CRDTReplicaGroup.all_converged()` and the semilattice property tests to verify convergence via equality checks.

crdt-merge-algebra-satisfies-convergence.text: All four CRDT types satisfy the algebraic properties required for strong eventual convergence: merge is idempotent (re-merging produces no change), equality compares semantic state rather than object identity (enabling correct convergence checks), and ORSet tombstones grow monotonically (preventing element resurrection after removal).

justifications.label: idempotent merge + semantic equality + monotonic tombstones = algebraic convergence guarantees hold

crdt-merge-is-idempotent.text: All four CRDT `merge` methods (`GCounter`, `PNCounter`, `LWWRegister`, `ORSet`) are idempotent: merging the same state twice produces the same result as merging once

metadata.example:
def merge(self, other):  # GCounter
    for rid, count in other.counts.items():
        self.counts[rid] = max(self.counts.get(rid, 0), count)
    return self  # max is idempotent

crdt-merge-is-idempotent-and-convergence.text: All four CRDT types demonstrate idempotent merge (re-merging produces no change), semantic equality comparison, and monotonic ORSet tombstones. The sync_all test confirms convergence after two rounds, consistent with merge being commutative and associative, though these properties are exercised by tests rather than proven by the antecedents alone.

crdt-merge-returns-self.text: `merge()` mutates and returns `self` (enabling chaining like `deepcopy(a).merge(b)`) rather than returning a new instance, which means callers must deepcopy before merging if they need to preserve the original state.

crdt-merge-tests-use-deepcopy-isolation.text: CRDT merge tests use copy.deepcopy on operands before merging to verify that merge does not mutate or corrupt the source state.

crdt-module-implements-four-types.text: The CRDT module in `crdts.py` implements four types: `GCounter`, `PNCounter`, `LWWRegister`, and `ORSet`.

crdt-mutation-api-is-non-defensive.text: CRDT mutation APIs lack defensive programming patterns at the boundaries: merge mutates the receiver in place and returns self (requiring callers to defensively copy before merging to prevent aliasing), and remove operations on absent elements silently return False rather than raising errors, making accidental no-ops invisible.

justifications.label: In-place mutation and silent no-ops create aliasing and observability hazards

crdt-state-returns-plain-dicts.text: state() returns plain inspectable dictionaries for all four CRDT types, with GCounter using a counts dict and PNCounter nesting p and n sub-counters.

crdt-sync-deepcopies-source.text: `CRDTReplicaGroup.sync` uses `deepcopy` on the source replica before merging to prevent aliasing between replicas.

crdt-tests-cover-20-scenarios.text: Test count is an unstable implementation detail that changes as tests are added or removed; not a durable architectural claim.

crdts-are-self-resolving.text: Each CRDT type in `crdts.py` (GCounter, PNCounter, LWWRegister, ORSet) encodes conflict resolution in its own `merge()` method, requiring no external strategy enum or callback

crdts-are-state-based-cvrdts.text: All four CRDT types (GCounter, PNCounter, LWWRegister, ORSet) use state-based replication via a `merge()` method that implements a join-semilattice; no operation log or causal delivery is used

critical-wal-operations-always-force-fsy.text: Checkpoints, batch commits, and segment rotations all bypass the configured sync mode by calling fsync unconditionally, creating a two-tier durability model where structural WAL operations are always durable even when individual record writes are not.

justifications.label: Four beliefs establish that force=True fsync is consistently applied at WAL state-transition boundaries but not at individual write boundaries

cuckoo-filter-duplicate-inserts-capped-a.text: Most cuckoo filter implementations cap duplicate inserts at 2 times the bucket size (2kb).

cuckoo-filter-insertion-can-fail-at-high.text: Cuckoo filter insertion may require a chain of relocations and can fail if the table is more than 95% full.

cuckoo-filter-insertion-relocates-existi.text: Cuckoo filter insertion handles collisions by evicting existing fingerprints to their alternate bucket, allowing high occupancy (~95%).

cuckoo-filter-space-overhead-1-05-to-1-2.text: Cuckoo filters use approximately 1.05-1.2x the space of a standard Bloom filter at similar false positive rates.

cuckoo-filter-stores-fingerprints-in-two.text: A cuckoo filter stores small fingerprints (typically 8-12 bits) in a hash table with two candidate buckets per item, using cuckoo hashing for placement.
A cuckoo filter stores a small fingerprint of each item in a hash table with two candidate bucket positions and deletes by removing the fingerprint.

current-file-stores-active-manifest-file.text: LevelDB's CURRENT file contains a single line with the filename of the active MANIFEST, and recovery reads CURRENT first then replays the MANIFEST to reconstruct the file set.

custom-merge-accepts-callback-with-five-.text: The `CUSTOM_MERGE` strategy in `multi_leader.py` invokes a user-provided `merge_fn` callback with `(key, local_val, remote_val, local_ts, remote_ts)` arguments.

custom-merge-replaces-lww.text: Overlaps with existing belief `multi-leader-custom-merge-new-timestamp` which already covers the custom merge strategy behavior.

custom-merge-synthetic-timestamp-max-plu.text: `CUSTOM_MERGE` conflict resolution creates a synthetic timestamp equal to `max(local_ts, remote_ts) + 1` and a canonical origin equal to `max(local_origin, remote_node)`.

data-distribution-and-processing-hit-ind.text: Data distribution and processing both hit fundamental scalability ceilings: neither partitioning strategy provides both reliable routing and ordered access (hash destroys order, range depends on unverified parallel-array invariants), while query and aggregation operations hide unbounded memory barriers behind uniform tuple interfaces, meaning neither the data layout nor the query path scales gracefully under load.

justifications.label: Partitioning limitations at the distribution layer and materialization barriers at the processing layer are independent scalability ceilings that prevent graceful degradation under load.

data-file-dir-entry-same-gap-as-hint.text: Derivable from existing `no-directory-fsync-anywhere` (the gap is universal) combined with `hint-files-are-optimization-only` (hints are safe to lose, data files are not).

data-file-dir-fsync-gap-worse-than-hint.text: The directory-fsync gap for data files causes data-loss consequences (unreachable data, index/disk mismatch, duplicate records) while the same gap for hint files is only a performance concern.

data-scan-skips-value-bytes.text: `_scan_data_file` in the hash-index Bitcask reads each record's header and key but seeks past value bytes; it is still O(data_size) because headers must be parsed sequentially to locate record boundaries

ddia-belief-network-contains-1405-belief.text: The ddia belief network contains 1,405 beliefs: 1,224 premises and 181 derived beliefs across 37 DDIA reference implementations.

ddia-config-via-constructor-params.text: All 37 modules configure behavior entirely through constructor parameters (e.g., `max_file_size`, `sync_mode`, `page_size`) — there are no config files, environment variables, or settings modules.

ddia-conftest-grep-matches-only-topics-j.text: The only matches for the string `conftest` in the ddia-implementations repo are 11 occurrences in `.code-expert/topics.json`.

ddia-module-directories-have-147-entries.text: The 147 directory entries across all ddia-implementations module directories show a consistent per-module structure of an implementation file, a `test_*.py` file, and sometimes a `tester_test_*.py` file.

ddia-modules-self-contained.text: Each top-level directory is a self-contained module with no cross-module imports; implementations are intentionally standalone so each concept can be understood in isolation.

ddia-partitioning-modules-map-to-chapter.text: The `consistent-hashing`, `range-partitioning`, and `secondary-index-partitioning` modules map to DDIA Chapter 6.

ddia-pure-python-stdlib.text: All implementations are Python; the storage engine modules use only stdlib except for `sortedcontainers` in the LSM tree — no frameworks or production infrastructure.

ddia-replication-consensus-modules-map-t.text: The replication and consensus modules (`leader-follower-replication`, `multi-leader-replication`, `leaderless-replication`, `read-repair`, `hinted-handoff`, `leader-election`, `raft-consensus`, `two-phase-commit`, `total-order-broadcast`) map to DDIA Chapters 5 and 9.

ddia-repo-lacks-leveldb-cpp-source.text: The ddia-implementations repository contains no LevelDB C++ source; table/merger.cc, FindSmallest, FindLargest, and direction enums are absent from the codebase.

ddia-root-has-37-module-directories-plus.text: The ddia-implementations repo root contains 37 module directories plus a .gitignore.

ddia-storage-modules-map-to-chapter-3.text: The `hash-index-storage`, `log-structured-hash-table`, `sstable-and-compaction`, `log-structured-merge-tree`, `b-tree-storage-engine`, `write-ahead-log`, and `bloom-filter` modules map to DDIA Chapter 3.

ddia-stream-batch-modules-map-to-chapter.text: The stream and batch modules (`mapreduce-framework`, `batch-word-count`, `map-side-join`, `change-data-capture`, `event-sourcing-store`, `stream-join-processor`, `partitioned-log`) map to DDIA Chapters 10 and 11.

ddia-tester-files-stdout-validation.text: The `tester_test_*.py` files are designed as standalone scripts that print `"test_name PASSED"` / `"test_name FAILED"` to stdout and include `if __name__ == "__main__"` blocks, enabling automated verification without pytest.

ddia-three-file-pattern.text: Most modules follow a consistent three-file pattern: one implementation file, one test file, and a `tester_test_*.py` file (likely a meta-test or test harness validator).

debezium-reads-source-transaction-log-pa.text: Debezium reads the database's own transaction log, such as PostgreSQL WAL or MySQL binlog, rather than participating in the write path.

decode-with-id-no-format-validation.text: `decode_with_id` does not validate the message format before parsing; any 4+ byte input will be interpreted as schema-ID-prefixed data, producing a confusing KeyError on invalid input rather than a clear format error

deepcopy-prevents-snapshot-corruption.text: `save_snapshot()` uses `copy.deepcopy` on the projection state dict to create an independent copy, ensuring subsequent event processing during `catch_up()` does not mutate the saved snapshot

default-pytest-collection-applies.text: Redundant with `no-pytest-config-exists` — the default collection behavior is a direct consequence of the absence of configuration

deferred-cleanup-is-production-pattern.text: Design principle generalization, not a testable fact about this codebase; better suited to a DDIA reading note than a code belief

degradation-is-irreversible.text: System degradation is irreversible: the system degrades monotonically at every abstraction level with no self-healing (leaked pages, growing tree height, accumulating divergence), and no subsystem at any architectural tier has a viable recovery strategy to arrest the erosion — recovery infrastructure is either vestigial, paradoxically over-engineered, or fundamentally missing.

justifications.label: Monotonic degradation with no recovery mechanism at any tier means the system only gets worse

delete-before-rename-ordering.text: Both Bitcask implementations delete old segment files (`os.remove`) before renaming the compacted replacement, creating a crash window where neither old nor properly-named new data is on disk

delete-before-rename-retraction-collapse.text: Retracting the delete-before-rename-ordering gating belief caused 31 derived beliefs to go OUT, including the depth-7 system-converges-on-permanent-dark-failure belief.

delete-semantics-fragmented-from-storage.text: Delete propagation is fragmented end-to-end: tombstone representations differ at every storage layer (ambiguous empty-bytes sentinel, premature compaction purging, replication-dependent lifetime), and derived systems require explicit flush plus old-value CDC events that inconsistent tombstones cannot reliably provide.

justifications.label: per-layer tombstone inconsistency undermines the old-value requirement for correct derived-system updates

deletion-visibility-is-symmetric.text: The same three-condition visibility rule (committed, not in active_at_start, lower tx_id) is applied independently to both the creating and deleting transaction of a version — `_is_visible` runs the same logic in two phases.

derived-system-consistency-requires-flus.text: Derived systems (secondary indexes, materialized views) require two independent conditions for consistency: explicit flush to make mutations visible, and CDC old-value capture to remove stale index entries — either condition failing silently produces stale reads.

justifications.label: Two mandatory conditions for derived-system correctness create a fragile AND-contract where violating either one causes silent data inconsistency

derived-system-interface-requires-proces.text: The `DerivedSystem` contract requires `process_event()`, `rebuild()`, and a `position` attribute.

derived-systems-are-position-tracked.text: Every `DerivedSystem` in the unbundled database tracks a `position` cursor indicating how far through the CDC log it has consumed, enabling independent catch-up and ensuring consumers can resume from where they left off

derived-systems-depend-on-unreliable-eve.text: The derived-system pattern (secondary indexes, materialized views, projections) depends on event infrastructure that is unreliable at its foundation: event sourcing has no durable recovery mechanism and conflates two ID spaces, while derived systems require explicit flush calls and old-value CDC events for consistency — the consumer-side correctness requirements depend on producer-side guarantees that do not hold.

justifications.label: Combines a depth-3 conclusion about event sourcing unreliability with a depth-1 conclusion about derived system requirements, exposing that the consumer pattern demands properties the producer cannot provide

derived-systems-independently-position-t.text: Each `DerivedSystem` tracks its own LSN `position` independently, allowing consumers to fall behind or catch up at different rates without coordinator state or blocking

derived-systems-maintain-consistency-whe.text: Derived systems (secondary indexes, materialized views, projections) can maintain consistency with their source through position-tracked CDC replay: every derived system tracks how far through the CDC log it has processed, and any derived system can be rebuilt from scratch via full event replay producing identical state to incremental processing.

justifications.label: Rebuild-from-replay equivalence plus position tracking enables consistent derived state, gated on the CDC consumer position being volatile (in-memory only, lost on restart)

derived-systems-rebuildable-from-cdc.text: Every `DerivedSystem` implements `rebuild(events)` that clears state and replays from scratch, guaranteeing eventual convergence with the CDC event log regardless of prior state

deserialize-internal-pure-function.text: Too trivial — a deserialization function having no side effects is expected, not an invariant that would break things if violated

deterministic-serialization-enables-inde.text: `json.dumps(sort_keys=True)` ensures all honest PBFT nodes produce identical SHA-256 digests for identical requests without inter-node coordination, transforming trust verification into a deterministic computation

dev-suite-longer-but-not-superset.text: Duplicate: the length claim is already captured by `pytest-files-have-broader-coverage`, and the non-superset claim is captured by the proposed `tester-dev-suites-overlap-not-hierarchical`

dev-tests-longer-than-tester-files.text: Developer `test_*.py` files are consistently longer than tester files, for example 207 vs 125 lines for bloom-filter and roughly 300 vs 200 lines for b-tree.

digest-binds-view-sequence-to-request.text: The `accepted_preprepare` dict enforces a one-to-one mapping from `(view, sequence)` to digest, preventing a Byzantine primary from assigning two different requests to the same protocol slot

digest-recomputed-on-preprepare.text: Backup replicas independently recompute the SHA-256 digest from the request payload in every PRE_PREPARE message; they never trust the primary's claimed digest value

directory-scan-recovery-unsafe-during-co.text: `_load_existing_sstables` using `os.listdir` cannot distinguish pre-compaction from post-compaction file sets after a crash — if the crash occurs after creating the merged SSTable but before deleting the inputs, recovery sees duplicates; the inverse loses data.

distributed-cluster-lacks-reliable-infra.text: The distributed cluster has no reliable foundational infrastructure: membership detection is unreliable in both accuracy (no adaptive thresholds) and propagation (asymmetric convergence rates between membership and data), and ordering infrastructure is broken at every layer (vestigial WAL sequence numbers, conflated event sourcing ID spaces, volatile CDC consumer positions), meaning neither who is in the cluster nor what order things happened can be answered reliably.

justifications.label: Both foundational questions for distributed systems — membership and ordering — are independently broken

distributed-correctness-doubly-unachieva.text: Distributed correctness is doubly unachievable under network partitions: protocols require storage-layer guarantees (crash-safe compaction, CRC-protected metadata) that aren't met, AND partitions amplify the resulting gaps through disrupted gossip-based failure detection and stale leader writes — the prerequisites for correctness are absent even before partitions introduce additional failure modes.

justifications.label: Unmet storage prerequisites plus partition amplification makes correctness doubly unachievable

distributed-correctness-undermined-at-bo.text: Distributed system correctness is undermined at both the storage and protocol layers: storage engines silently assume single-threaded access (no locks, no assertions, no documentation), while the quorum protocol weakens its own semantic guarantees (counting hint storage as successful writes, allowing sub-quorum configurations without error).

justifications.label: Concurrency unsafety in storage compounds with weakened quorum semantics in the distributed layer

distributed-divergence-accumulates-witho.text: Replica divergence accumulates without bound: write operations have compounding correctness gaps (sloppy quorums count hints, sub-quorum configs accepted, conflict resolution split across modules), and the repair mechanism (Merkle-based anti-entropy) cannot fully reconcile because tombstone semantics differ at every layer.

justifications.label: write-path gaps produce divergence faster than the repair path can resolve it

distributed-layer-has-three-incompatible.text: The distributed layer uses three fundamentally incompatible convergence and resolution models with no unifying bridge: CRDTs encode resolution algebraically in merge semantics, the strategy pattern selects between LWW and custom resolution at runtime, AND consensus and membership use irreconcilable strong-leader (Raft) vs. eventual-consistency (gossip) models — composing correct end-to-end behavior requires manually bridging paradigms designed in isolation.

justifications.label: Three isolated convergence paradigms with no composition strategy or bridging mechanism

distributed-layer-incoherent-and-unachie.text: The distributed layer is both internally incoherent and externally unachievable: convergence and ordering models are mutually incompatible across modules (CRDTs encode algebraic resolution, LWW uses wall-clock tiebreaking, gossip uses epidemic thresholds) AND correctness is doubly unachievable under network partitions (storage-layer guarantees are unmet, write correctness gaps are amplified by partition-induced failure detection breakdowns).

justifications.label: Internal model incompatibility and external correctness impossibility are independent failures that together mean the distributed layer cannot converge correctly regardless of network conditions.

distributed-models-incompatible-at-conve.text: The distributed layer has mutually incompatible models at two independent levels: convergence mechanisms (CRDTs encode algebraic resolution, LWW uses timestamp comparison, Raft requires strong leader authority, gossip relies on epidemic propagation) have no unifying bridge, AND ordering models (Lamport clocks provide total order via node-ID tiebreaking, vector clocks provide partial order with incomparable states, hash indexes use non-monotonic wall-clock time) are fundamentally incompatible across modules.

justifications.label: Three incompatible convergence models combined with three incompatible ordering models means the distributed layer has no coherent foundation for either agreeing on state or sequencing events

distributed-protocols-rest-on-unverifiab.text: Distributed protocols rest on doubly invalid foundations: end-to-end correctness requires storage-layer guarantees (crash-safe compaction, CRC-protected metadata) that no storage engine provides, and protocol safety claims are unfalsifiable under the current testing methodology (synchronous simulation, no crash path tests) — the protocols assume both correct storage and correct testing, and have neither.

justifications.label: Two depth-3 conclusions identify independent invalidity: unmet storage assumptions (the guarantees don't exist) and unfalsifiable testing (the test suite can't check them), creating a self-reinforcing correctness void

distributed-protocols-simulate-synchrono.text: All distributed protocol implementations use synchronous message delivery: PBFT runs the full three-phase protocol in a single deterministic call, bully elections resolve cascading responses within one tick, and Lamport clocks deliver messages in the same call stack — none model the network asynchrony that is the core difficulty of distributed systems.

justifications.label: three independent protocol modules share the same synchronous-delivery simplification

distributed-tombstone-gc-requires-downti.text: Any tombstone garbage collection strategy must define a maximum tolerated node downtime; tombstones removed before a down node receives them cause data resurrection via read repair or anti-entropy.

distributed-tombstone-removal-needs-repl.text: In the multi-leader replication module, tombstones cannot be safely removed until all replicas have received the delete, adding a replication-convergence constraint beyond the local compaction-coverage constraint

distributed-writes-have-compounding-corr.text: Distributed write correctness has compounding weaknesses: quorum semantics are weakened by sloppy quorum and permissive configuration, and the conflict resolution that should catch remaining inconsistencies is split between two disconnected mechanisms (self-resolving CRDTs and an incomplete strategy enum).

justifications.label: Weakened quorum guarantees rely on conflict resolution as a safety net, but that net is itself fragmented

do-sync-force-bypasses-sync-mode.text: `_do_sync(force=True)` always calls fsync regardless of the configured `sync_mode`, ensuring durability-critical operations like segment rotation and WAL close are never silently skipped

doc-partitioned-get-delete-touch-one.text: DocumentPartitionedDB.get and delete each touch exactly one partition because the primary key hashes to a single document partition.

doc-partitioned-query-touches-all.text: `DocumentPartitionedDB.query_by_field` always iterates every partition regardless of result count, touching exactly `num_partitions` partitions (scatter/gather with no short-circuit).

doc-partitioned-write-touches-one.text: `DocumentPartitionedDB.put()` always touches exactly 1 partition regardless of how many fields are indexed, because the secondary index is co-located with the document on its home partition.

document-partitioned-query-touches-all-p.text: A document-partitioned query_by_field must query all partitions via scatter/gather, unlike term-partitioned query_by_field which touches at most one partition.

durability-bugs-invisible-to-testing.text: Durability bugs are permanently invisible: the write-to-verify durability pipeline is broken at both ends (fsync policy gaps prevent data from reaching stable storage, and incomplete integrity checks cannot verify it arrived), while crash/failure recovery paths are systematically excluded from testing — the system cannot detect its own durability failures through any available mechanism.

justifications.label: A depth-3 conclusion (durability pipeline broken) combined with depth-1 (testing gaps) produces a depth-4 epistemic impossibility: durability bugs exist and no mechanism — operational or test — can surface them

durability-pipeline-broken-at-both-ends.text: The write-to-verify durability pipeline is broken at both ends: fsync policy inconsistencies across critical paths mean data may never durably reach disk (B-tree skips fsync for structural metadata while paying double for data), and incomplete CRC coverage means corrupted data that does reach disk passes integrity checks undetected (payload-only CRC leaves routing metadata unprotected).

justifications.label: Inconsistent fsync leaves data unwritten; incomplete CRC leaves corruption undetected — neither end of the pipeline is reliable

durable-rename-requires-parent-dir-fsync.text: The correct pattern for durable rename on Linux requires fsyncing the parent directory after `os.rename()`.

dynamo-anti-entropy-unions-all-keys.text: Duplicates existing belief `anti-entropy-unions-all-keys` which already captures that `anti_entropy_repair()` collects keys via set union across all available nodes.

dynamo-cluster-hints-after-quorum.text: `DynamoCluster.put` only stores hints after the write quorum is already met on real nodes, unlike `HintedHandoffStore` which counts hints toward the quorum — making DynamoCluster a strict-quorum-with-opportunistic-hints design, not a true sloppy quorum

dynamo-conflict-detection-same-version-d.text: When multiple replicas hold different values at the same max version number, `ReadResult.is_conflict` is `True` and `value` is a list of all conflicting values rather than a single resolved value

dynamo-deliver-hints-requeues-undelivera.text: When `deliver_hints()` cannot deliver a hint because the target node is still down, it re-queues the hint on the same node.

dynamo-failed-write-rolls-back-version.text: When `put()` fails to meet write quorum, it decrements the version counter to prevent version gaps, then raises `QuorumNotMet`

dynamo-get-reads-all-available-nodes.text: `DynamoCluster.get()` fans out reads to all nodes and collects `VersionedValue` responses from available ones, not just R nodes.

dynamo-hints-single-homed.text: Hinted handoffs for all unavailable nodes are stored on `available_nodes[0]` only, creating a single point of responsibility for hint delivery and a potential hotspot

dynamo-missing-key-read-returns-none-ver.text: Reading a nonexistent key in `DynamoCluster.get()` returns `None` with version 0 and `is_conflict=False`.

dynamo-no-delete-support.text: The leaderless replication implementation (`dynamo.py`) has no delete or tombstone mechanism; adding deletes without tombstones would cause resurrection via read repair or anti-entropy

dynamo-per-key-versioning.text: Version counters in `DynamoCluster._version_counters` are scoped per key, not global across the cluster; independent keys maintain independent version sequences

dynamo-quorum-not-met-only-exception.text: `QuorumNotMet` is the only exception type raised by `DynamoCluster.put()` and `DynamoCluster.get()`.

dynamo-read-repair-ensures-replica-consi.text: Eager all-node read repair after every quorum read ensures all replicas converge to the latest version, because repair propagates to all reachable nodes (not just quorum participants) and per-key versioning prevents false cross-key conflicts.

justifications.label: Read repair converges replicas for existing keys but without delete or tombstone support, deleted keys are resurrected from stale replicas during repair

dynamo-read-repair-is-all-node.text: `DynamoCluster.get()` repairs all available nodes after every read, not just the quorum participants, trading higher per-read write fan-out for faster convergence compared to `ReadRepairStore`.

dynamo-read-repair-is-eager.text: `DynamoCluster.get()` repairs all stale replicas reachable during the read, not just enough to satisfy the quorum — every replica with a version below the max is updated

dynamo-read-repair-on-get.text: Overlaps with accepted `dynamo-read-repair-is-eager` which covers the same behavior with a stronger claim

dynamo-sloppy-quorum-opt-in.text: Hinted handoff only occurs when `DynamoCluster` is constructed with `sloppy_quorum=True`; without it, `deliver_hints()` returns 0 and offline nodes receive no data until anti-entropy runs

dynamo-tester-injects-conflicts-directly.text: `test_dynamo_tester.py` injects conflict scenarios by directly writing divergent `VersionedValue` entries into each node's `_store` rather than orchestrating concurrent writes.

dynamo-tester-lacks-partial-read-quorum-.text: `test_dynamo_tester.py` has no test for partial read quorum failure where R=2 but only one node responds.

dynamo-unavailable-nodes-return-false-no.text: Unavailable `ReplicaNode` write and read operations return `False` and `None` respectively rather than raising exceptions.

dynamo-version-counter-is-global.text: Version assignment uses a single coordinator-level counter per key (`_version_counters`), not per-replica counters, which prevents version conflicts but requires a centralized coordinator

dynamo-version-rollback-on-failed-write.text: Duplicates `dynamo-failed-write-rolls-back-version` accepted from the dynamo.py file entry

dynamo-write-fans-to-all.text: `DynamoCluster.put()` sends writes to every available node, not just W of them; the quorum check gates on acknowledgment count, not send count, maximizing replica consistency

empty-input-produces-empty-output.text: A pipeline with no input lines returns an empty list `[]` rather than raising an error.

empty-predicate-match-still-locks.text: A predicate that matches zero keys still appends a predicate lock to `tx._predicate_locks`, enabling phantom detection if a concurrent transaction later inserts a key that would match

empty-sstable-overlap-edge-case.text: Edge case trivia about empty SSTables defaulting to `min_key=""` — compaction never feeds empty SSTables so this never triggers in practice, making it untestable in the actual codebase.

empty-string-tombstone-bug.text: Duplicate of existing `bitcask-tombstone-is-empty-string` and `bitcask-tombstone-semantics` which already capture the empty-string sentinel and its implications.

encode-with-id-no-magic-byte.text: `SchemaRegistry.encode_with_id` uses a raw 4-byte big-endian schema ID prefix with no magic byte, unlike Confluent's 5-byte header (0x00 + 4-byte ID), so there is no format versioning for future wire format changes

end-to-end-correctness-requires-unmet-st.text: End-to-end distributed correctness is unachievable: protocol-layer weaknesses (sloppy quorums, single-threaded assumptions) depend on storage-layer guarantees (atomic recovery, batch integrity, metadata checksums) that no implementation provides.

justifications.label: distributed protocols assume storage invariants that the crash-recovery analysis proves are violated

entry-count-header-never-verified.text: The entry count stored in the SSTable header by `SSTableWriter.finish()` is trusted by `SSTableReader` but never validated against the actual number of entries read from the data section

equivocating-mode-expands-message-count.text: In `EQUIVOCATING` mode, each broadcast message is replaced by N-1 targeted messages with per-peer distinct digests computed via `compute_digest`, meaning the output list can be larger than the input

erlang-bitcask-defers-segment-deletion-v.text: In Erlang Bitcask, old segment files stay on disk until the last reader's reference count drops to zero, and compaction swaps the keydir atomically.

es-event-ids-are-stream-scoped.text: Event IDs are sequential integers per-stream starting at 1, not globally unique identifiers; `global_position` is the separate cross-stream counter.

es-global-position-tracks-all-streams.text: `global_position` increments monotonically across all streams and equals the total number of events ever appended to the store.

es-live-projection-auto-updates.text: `LiveProjection` automatically applies new events on each `append()` after the initial `catch_up()` call — no subsequent explicit `catch_up()` required.

metadata.example:
for sub in self._subscribers:
    sub(event)  # LiveProjection registered as subscriber

es-optimistic-concurrency-via-expected-v.text: `append(..., expected_version=V)` succeeds only if the current stream version equals V; a stale version raises `ConcurrencyConflict`.

es-persistence-uses-jsonl.text: EventStore disk persistence uses JSONL (newline-delimited JSON) format, loaded in full on construction to rebuild the in-memory state.

es-projection-catch-up-is-incremental.text: `Projection.catch_up()` only processes events after its current `position`, returning the count of newly processed events; a second call with no new events processes zero.

es-projection-position-tracks-global-off.text: Duplicates existing belief `es-global-position-tracks-all-streams` which already covers that projection position is a global offset across all streams

es-snapshot-saves-state-and-position.text: `Projection.save_snapshot()` persists both the projection state and its current position; `load_snapshot()` restores both so that `catch_up()` resumes from the snapshot point.

es-snapshots-are-in-memory-dicts.text: Event sourcing snapshots on `store._snapshots` are plain Python dicts monkey-patched onto the store instance with no serialization; `getattr(self._store, '_snapshots', {})` defensively handles their absence

es-snapshots-incomplete-for-production-u.text: Event sourcing snapshots are triply limited: stored as ephemeral in-memory dicts (lost on restart), excluding subscriber callbacks (requiring re-registration), and ignored by `reconstruct_state` (which always replays from the beginning).

justifications.label: Three independent limitations compound to make snapshots a partial optimization rather than a complete recovery mechanism

es-temporal-query-via-up-to.text: `reconstruct_state(handlers, events, up_to=N)` replays exactly the first N events to rebuild past state at that point in time.

es-verify-is-script-not-pytest.text: `test_verify.py` runs as a standalone Python script with inline assertions and a final print statement, not through a test framework like pytest

ets-enables-concurrent-keydir-writes.text: Describes Erlang ETS internals, not this Python codebase

ets-insert-is-per-key-atomic.text: Erlang ETS implementation detail, not a claim about this Python codebase

ets-is-builtin-concurrent-hash-table.text: ETS is a shared-memory concurrent hash table built into the BEAM VM.

ets-is-zero-copy-across-processes.text: General Erlang/BEAM VM fact, not a testable claim about this codebase

ets-named-lookup-enables-shared-keydir.text: Any process on a BEAM node can find a named ETS table by name via ets:lookup/2, allowing Riak vnodes to share one in-memory keydir.

event-graph-acyclicity-by-construction.text: `_reaches` assumes the event graph is a DAG with no cycle detection; this is safe because `Node` methods only ever link to previously-created events via `_parent` and `_cause`.

event-graph-correctness-via-dual-invaria.text: The event causality graph maintains correctness through two complementary invariants: acyclicity by construction (preventing infinite traversal in reachability checks) and identity-based comparison (preventing conflation of structurally-equal but distinct events).

justifications.label: Either invariant alone is insufficient — cycles would break traversal even with identity checks, and equality-based matching would conflate events even in a DAG

event-ids-are-1-based-sequential.text: `event_id` is a global sequence number assigned as `len(self._events) + 1`, starting at 1 and incrementing by 1 for each appended event with no gaps within a process lifetime

event-infrastructure-unreliable-in-conte.text: Derived systems depend on event infrastructure that is independently unreliable in both content and ordering: events may be lost, duplicated, or mis-addressed due to unreliable persistence and addressing, AND their ordering is broken at every layer — WAL sequence numbers are vestigial, event IDs conflate two spaces, and CDC consumer positions are volatile.

justifications.label: Content unreliability (persistence gaps, addressing errors) combined with ordering unreliability (vestigial seq nums, conflated IDs, volatile positions) means derived systems can trust neither what events say nor what order they arrived in

event-log-persists-but-snapshots-do-not.text: Redundant given `snapshots-are-in-memory-only` (proposed above) combined with existing belief `es-persistence-uses-jsonl`

event-sourcing-and-cdc-converge-on-proje.text: Both `Projection.catch_up` and `DerivedSystem.process_event` track a position cursor, pull/receive ordered events, and apply type-dispatched handlers — the same structural pattern solving "derived data" from different starting points

event-sourcing-conflates-two-id-spaces.text: Event sourcing read operations conflate two ID spaces: projections assume contiguous stream-scoped IDs for catch-up arithmetic, while state reconstruction filters on global event_id, and sequence numbers survive compaction without renumbering — creating potential mismatches when events are removed or compacted.

justifications.label: Stream-local and global ID spaces are used interchangeably across different read paths with no translation layer

event-sourcing-lacks-any-durable-recover.text: Event sourcing has no durable recovery mechanism: appends update in-memory state before persisting to disk with no rollback on failure, snapshots are ephemeral in-memory dicts lost on restart, and state reconstruction must always replay from the beginning with no incremental checkpoint support.

justifications.label: crash-inconsistent appends + non-persistent snapshots = no safe recovery at any level

event-sourcing-projection-catch-up-uses-.text: The event sourcing `Projection` uses snapshots to periodically capture state so that `catch_up()` doesn't have to replay the entire log from the beginning.

event-sourcing-state-is-fully-reconstruc.text: Event sourcing state can be fully reconstructed from the event log: projections are stateless replay functions (cache, not source of truth), and snapshots use deep copy to isolate stored state from mutations.

justifications.label: reconstruction mechanism is correct but the underlying log may be incomplete due to missing fsync

event-sourcing-unreliable-in-persistence.text: Event sourcing is fundamentally unreliable at two independent levels: it has no durable recovery mechanism (in-memory state updated before disk, no crash-consistent append, ephemeral snapshots), and its core addressing abstraction conflates stream-scoped and global ID spaces across read paths, meaning even successfully persisted events may be incorrectly reconstructed.

justifications.label: Non-durable persistence combined with inconsistent event addressing undermines both storage and retrieval

event-store-accepts-arbitrary-event-data.text: `EventStore.append` and `append_batch` do not validate event data; any dict is accepted.

event-store-append-batch-returns-event-o.text: `append_batch` writes three events atomically and returns the event objects.

event-store-append-batch-updates-events-.text: EventStore.append_batch updates both the _events and _streams in-memory structures atomically from a single-threaded perspective.

event-store-append-is-not-crash-consiste.text: Event store appends update in-memory state before persisting to disk with no rollback on failure, batch appends can leave partial writes, and the per-call file open/close pattern adds overhead without providing atomicity guarantees.

justifications.label: Memory-first writes with no rollback plus non-atomic batch persistence equals inconsistency after any crash

event-store-append-notifies-after-persis.text: EventStore.append() persists the event before dispatching it to all subscribers in _subscribers.

event-store-enforces-expected-version-co.text: The `EventStore.append()` and `append_batch()` methods accept an `expected_version` parameter to enforce optimistic concurrency on the write side.

event-store-has-no-update-or-delete-oper.text: The `EventStore` exposes no update or delete operation on events; it is append-only.

event-store-lacks-wal-truncate-compactio.text: The event store has no equivalent to WAL truncate for garbage-collecting old records after checkpoint.

event-store-load-ignores-partial-batches.text: `EventStore._load_from_file` replays every NDJSON line on startup with no mechanism to detect or discard incomplete batches left by a mid-batch crash, unlike the WAL which uses `OP_COMMIT` records as transaction boundaries.

event-store-loads-ndjson-on-init.text: On initialization with an existing persist file, `EventStore` replays the NDJSON file to rebuild `_events` and `_streams`.

event-store-memory-ahead-of-disk.text: Event store appends events to the in-memory `_events` list before calling `_persist_event`, with no rollback on write failure — a crash or I/O error leaves the in-memory state ahead of disk with no mechanism to reconcile.

event-store-ndjson-could-resync-but-does.text: The event store uses newline-delimited JSON where per-line resync is architecturally possible, but `_load_from_file` halts on the first `json.JSONDecodeError` rather than skipping the bad line

event-store-no-explicit-durability.text: `event-sourcing-store/event_store.py:_persist_event` relies solely on Python's context manager `close()` for implicit `flush()` with no explicit `flush()` or `fsync()`, providing no durability guarantee against either process crash or power loss.

event-store-optimistic-concurrency.text: `EventStore.append()` accepts an `expected_version` parameter and rejects appends when the stream's current version doesn't match, implementing optimistic concurrency control for event streams

event-store-optimistic-concurrency-via-e.text: `EventStore.append` takes an `expected_version` parameter for optimistic concurrency on stream appends, rejecting writes when the stream has advanced past the caller's version

event-store-persist-event-fsyncs-json-wr.text: In event-sourcing-store/event_store.py, _persist_event() calls flush() and os.fsync() on the file descriptor after writing the event JSON.

event-store-persist-no-durability.text: `EventStore._persist_event()` in `event-sourcing-store/event_store.py` opens the file in a `with` block, writes JSON, and relies on implicit `close()` — no explicit `flush()` or `os.fsync()`, making persisted events vulnerable to loss on OS crash

event-store-persist-no-flush-no-fsync.text: `EventStore._persist_event` opens the NDJSON file in append mode, writes one JSON line, and closes it without calling `flush()` or `os.fsync()`; written data may remain in OS buffers or Python buffers at crash time.

event-store-persist-no-fsync.text: Subsumed by the more specific `event-store-persist-no-flush-no-fsync` proposed above.

event-store-persist-path-gates-persisten.text: EventStore.append_batch calls _persist_event only when self._persist_path is set; otherwise events are not written to NDJSON.

event-store-persist-pattern.text: `EventStore` in `event-sourcing-store/event_store.py` is the repo's existing model for optional disk persistence: accept `persist_path` in constructor, call `_load_from_file` on init if the file exists, call `_persist_event` on every mutation

event-store-persist-separate-open-close.text: `EventStore._persist_event` performs a separate `open()`/`write()`/`close()` cycle for each individual event, so `append_batch` with N events results in N independent file operations rather than a single buffered write.

event-store-persistence-is-optional.text: `EventStore` persistence is optional; if `persist_path` is not provided, events are stored only in memory.

event-store-projection-registers-handler.text: `make_projection` creates a `Projection`, registers all three handlers via `.when()`, and returns the projection.

event-store-read-all-filters-by-position.text: `read_all(from_position=N)` returns the global event log filtered by position.

event-store-read-all-returns-insertion-o.text: `read_all()` returns events in insertion order across all streams.

event-store-single-threaded-assumption.text: `EventStore` assumes single-threaded access: `event_id = len(self._events) + 1` is a race condition under concurrency, and no locking protects `_events`, `_streams`, or subscriber notification.

event-store-single-writer-assumption.text: The event store's `expected_version` check-then-act pattern in `append` and `append_batch` has no locking, making the optimistic concurrency guard safe only under a single-writer concurrency model — concurrent writers create a TOCTOU race

event-store-uses-stdlib-only-dependencie.text: `event_store.py` imports only Python standard-library modules: `copy`, `json`, `os`, `dataclasses`, `datetime`, and `typing`.

expiration-cutoff-is-one-sided-despite-s.text: `_expire_events` uses `watermark - duration` as a one-sided cutoff for buffer cleanup, while `contains()` is symmetric; this is correct because future events can only arrive at or after the watermark

ext4-auto-da-alloc-limits-to-rename-repl.text: ext4's auto_da_alloc feature mitigates missing directory fsync for replace-via-rename patterns but does not help for new file creation.

ext4-auto-da-alloc-protects-only-replace.text: ext4's `auto_da_alloc` mount option, enabled by default since ~2.6.30, forces new file data allocations to flush before `rename()` completes only for replace-via-rename patterns where the destination already exists.

ext4-data-ordered-protects-consistency-n.text: ext4 `data=ordered` protects filesystem consistency after a crash but does not guarantee durability of recent directory-entry operations, which may sit in the journal commit queue for up to the commit interval.

ext4-data-writeback-can-expose-stale-fil.text: In ext4 `data=writeback` mode, a directory entry for a new file can reach the journal before the file's data blocks are written, so after a crash the file may exist with stale or garbage contents.

ext4-default-journal-commit-interval-5s.text: On ext4 with default mount options, the journal commit interval is typically 5 seconds, providing only probabilistic directory-entry durability.

ext4-file-fsync-does-not-fsync-directory.text: On ext4, `fsync()` on a file does not guarantee the directory entry is durable, so creating a new file requires `fsync()` on the parent directory as well.

ext4-no-ordering-across-file-pages.text: ext4 in `data=ordered` mode writes file data before committing metadata to the journal, but provides no ordering guarantee across pages within a single file's data.

ext4-requires-directory-fsync-for-rename.text: On ext4 with default `data=ordered`, a rename is not guaranteed durable without an explicit `fsync()` on the directory; `auto_da_alloc` only covers the narrow `open(O_TRUNC)+write+close+rename` pattern.

external-sort-is-transparent.text: `Sort` with `memory_limit` produces the same output ordering as an in-memory sort — the external merge-sort is a pure implementation optimization with no semantic difference.

fan-2000-four-bit-counters-sufficient.text: Fan et al. (2000) found that 4-bit counters are sufficient for most practical counting Bloom filter workloads.

fdatasync-benefit-limited-to-linux-files.text: The fdatasync performance benefit applies on Linux filesystems such as ext4, xfs, and btrfs rather than on macOS.

fdatasync-can-be-2-3x-faster-on-ext4.text: On Linux ext4, eliminating the extra metadata barrier with fdatasync can yield 2-3x throughput improvement under heavy write loads.

fdatasync-flushes-data-and-retrieval-met.text: fdatasync flushes file data and only metadata required for subsequent data retrieval, skipping mtime/atime updates.

fdatasync-handles-truncation-size-change.text: fdatasync flushes file-size changes, so truncation paths remain data-safe even though they are usually kept on fsync for conservatism.

fdatasync-minimal-savings-for-append-wor.text: `fdatasync` skips metadata sync only when file size does not change, so for append-only WAL workloads its savings over `fsync` are minimal.

fdatasync-never-used.text: No implementation uses `os.fdatasync()`, missing a safe optimization for append-only WALs where only data (not metadata like mtime) needs to reach disk.

fdatasync-not-available-on-darwin.text: Python's `os.fdatasync` exists only on Linux, not macOS/Darwin; any switch from `os.fsync` requires a platform fallback via `getattr(os, 'fdatasync', os.fsync)` to work on the current development environment

fdatasync-safe-for-all-append-paths.text: Every file opened in append mode (`"ab"`) in this codebase writes sequentially with monotonically increasing file size, making `fdatasync` a safe drop-in replacement for `fsync` on those paths (WAL, Bitcask data files, B-tree WAL)

fdatasync-skips-mtime-and-atime.text: `fdatasync` flushes file data and file-size metadata but skips `mtime` and `atime` updates, unlike `fsync`.

fdatasync-unavailable-on-macos.text: `os.fdatasync` is available on Linux but not on macOS, so the codebase uses `os.fsync` for portability.

fenced-server-rejects-strictly-lower-tok.text: `FencedResourceServer.write` rejects writes where `fencing_token < highest` (strict less-than, not less-than-or-equal), meaning same-token retries succeed — enabling idempotent writes with the same lock acquisition

fenced-server-tracks-highest-token-per-r.text: The `FencedResourceServer` maintains a `_highest_token` dictionary per resource, rejecting writes with tokens strictly lower than the highest seen for that resource.

fencing-moves-safety-to-storage-server.text: Fencing tokens move the safety guarantee from the time-dependent lock to the storage server, which uses a monotonic token comparison that is not time-dependent.

fencing-no-exceptions-on-denial.text: All denial conditions in fencing tokens (lock held, stale token, wrong client) return sentinel values (`None`, `False`, or error dicts) rather than raising exceptions, modeling distributed system responses

fencing-provides-linearizable-writes.text: Fencing tokens provide linearizable write protection at the resource server: stale tokens are permanently rejected (no expiration) and the monotonic token ordering ensures only the most recent lock holder can successfully write.

justifications.label: Server-side fencing is correct but clients retain and use tokens after lock expiry with no invalidation signal

fencing-rejects-stale-writes.text: `FencedResourceServer.write()` rejects any write with a fencing token strictly less than the highest token previously seen for that resource; equal tokens are accepted

fencing-tests-organized-into-five-contra.text: The fencing token test suite is organized into five test classes: `TestLockAcquisition`, `TestLockRenewal`, `TestFencedServer`, `TestScenarios`, and `TestClientEdgeCases`.

fencing-tests-use-plain-methods-no-fixtu.text: The fencing token tests are plain method-based with `pytest` imported but no fixtures or `parametrize` decorators.

fencing-token-client-retains-expired-hel.text: In fencing-tokens/fencing_tokens.py, Client._held_tokens is not cleared when a lock expires, so the client can retain and reuse a token after another client acquires the lock.

fencing-token-counter-is-global.text: The fencing token counter is global across all locks, not per-lock; tokens issued for different locks are comparable and strictly ordered by acquisition time

fencing-token-expiry-inclusive-boundary.text: `FencingToken.is_expired(current_time)` returns true when `current_time >= issued_at + ttl`, making expiry inclusive of the boundary.

fencing-token-monotonic.text: `LockService._counter` starts at 1, increments by 1 on every successful `acquire()`, and is never decremented or reset, guaranteeing strict monotonicity of issued tokens

metadata.example:
token = FencingToken(self._counter, lock_name, client_id, current_time, ttl)
self._counter += 1

fencing-token-tracking-is-per-resource.text: Token high-water marks on `FencedResourceServer` are scoped per resource identifier, so a lower token can succeed on a different resource than the one that saw a higher token

fencing-tokens-do-not-expire-at-resource.text: The `FencedResourceServer` has no TTL or expiration logic for tokens — once a token number is seen, all lower tokens are permanently rejected for that resource

fencing-tokens-use-explicit-current-time.text: All time-dependent fencing token methods take `current_time` as a parameter rather than reading the system clock.

file-content-fsync-consistent.text: The WAL, B-tree PageManager, and Bitcask implementations all fsync file contents after writes, making the directory fsync gap a subtle rather than gross durability defect.

filter-output-satisfies-predicate.text: After a `Filter` stage with predicate `count >= 2`, every output record satisfies the predicate.

find-conflicts-detects-concurrency.text: `find_conflicts` returns `True` if and only if at least two `VersionedValue` entries in the input list have concurrent (mutually non-dominating) vector clocks

find-leaf-bisect-right-consistency.text: _find_leaf, _search, and _insert all use bisect_right (not bisect_left) for child-pointer routing, ensuring all three methods agree on which leaf owns a given key; this is consistent with the split strategy where the separator key equals the first key of the right sibling.

find-leaf-no-type-check.text: _find_leaf does not verify that a page is an internal node before calling _deserialize_internal; a corrupted tree height or misidentified page type produces silently wrong results rather than an error.

find-leaf-range-scan-only.text: _find_leaf is called exclusively by range_scan; point lookups use _search instead, which reads the leaf inline and returns the value rather than the page number.

find-leaf-read-count.text: Covered by existing belief `btree-lookup-reads-bounded-by-height`; _find_leaf has the same height-proportional I/O cost.

first-committer-wins-on-write-conflict.text: When two concurrent transactions write the same key, the first to call `commit()` succeeds and the second is aborted automatically

fixture-usage-is-sparse.text: Only 3 of the `test_*.py` files use `@pytest.fixture` (`test_cdc`, `test_map_side_joins`, `test_bitcask`); most pytest files still use inline setup identical to their tester counterparts

flush-before-fsync-invariant.text: Every `os.fsync()` call in the codebase is immediately preceded by a `.flush()` call, ensuring Python's userspace buffer is drained to the kernel page cache before requesting stable storage persistence.

flush-clears-then-appends.text: `_flush()` both clears `self._memtable` and appends to `self._sstables`, creating a window where data exists in neither location if a concurrent reader checks between the two mutations

flush-creates-sequential-sstables.text: Each `_flush` call creates an SSTable file with a strictly increasing sequence number (zero-padded filename for lexicographic = numeric sort), preserving newest-last ordering in `self._sstables`

metadata.example:
seq = len(self._sstables) + 1
path = os.path.join(self._dir, f"sstable_{seq:06d}.sst")
sst = SSTable.write(path, seq, sorted(frozen.items()))
self._sstables.append(sst)

flush-fsync-pairing-inconsistent.text: Derivable from the combination of existing beliefs `lsm-wal-has-no-fsync` and `wal-fsync-per-entry`.

flush-index-drains-pending.text: `flush_index()` is the sole mechanism that materializes async index updates: it iterates `self._pending`, calls `_apply_index_op()` for each entry, and returns the count of operations applied

flush-moves-data-to-page-cache-only.text: `file.flush()` moves data from Python's internal buffer to the OS page cache but does not force it to physical storage.

flush-only-no-durability.text: General OS/systems principle, not a codebase-specific invariant. Well-known prerequisite knowledge, not a claim about this code that could break if violated.

flush-pushes-to-page-cache-not-disk.text: Python's `.flush()` pushes bytes from the userspace buffer into the OS page cache but does not guarantee they reach physical storage.

flush-skips-immutable-memtable-stage.text: `_flush` writes the frozen memtable directly to an SSTable without staging it in `_immutable_memtables`, creating a brief window where in-flight keys are invisible to `get()` despite `_immutable_memtables` being checked in the read path

flush-survives-process-crash-not-power-l.text: `flush()` moves data from the Python userspace buffer to the OS kernel page cache, which survives a process crash but not a power loss.

flush-without-fsync-leaves-data-in-page-.text: flush() only moves data from a Python buffer into the kernel page cache; without fsync() the data is not guaranteed durable across power failure.

force-true-bypasses-sync-mode.text: Passing `force=True` to `_do_sync()` causes flush+fsync regardless of the configured sync mode, enabling group commit at batch boundaries

force-true-used-at-rotation-and-close.text: The only `_do_sync(force=True)` call sites (lines 165 and 175) correspond to segment rotation and WAL close, both operations where proceeding without a flush would risk data loss or file corruption

format-and-structure-prevent-all-repair.text: The system can neither self-heal during operation nor be evolved to add self-healing capabilities: runtime degradation is permanent (leaked pages accumulate, tree height only grows, no rebalancing occurs, crash recovery has no safe path), AND the rigid binary formats across the entire storage stack prevent adding recovery mechanisms such as resync points, version negotiation, or structural checksums.

justifications.label: Self-healing absent at runtime combined with format rigidity preventing evolutionary repair creates a double bind — the system is stuck with degradation it cannot fix and formats it cannot extend

format-rigidity-prevents-evolutionary-re.text: The system cannot evolve its way out of known corruption vulnerabilities: the rigid binary format design across the entire storage stack prevents forward evolution and post-corruption recovery (no block alignment, no version fields, no extensibility), and the system simultaneously lacks defense-in-depth against the corruption these formats cannot recover from (no input validation, no resync capability).

justifications.label: Rigid formats prevent evolutionary fixes to the corruption vulnerabilities they enable

fourteen-bugs-fixed-across-nine-implemen.text: Belief-driven analysis was used to fix 14 bugs across 9 implementations.

free-list-head-persisted-in-page-zero.text: The free list head pointer is stored as the fifth field of the metadata page (page 0) in the layout `[root_page:4B][height:4B][total_keys:4B][next_free_page:4B][free_list_head:4B]`, making it durable across restarts.

free-list-is-lifo.text: The page free list is LIFO: `free_page` pushes to the head and `allocate_page` pops from the head, so the most recently freed page is reused first.

free-list-is-lifo-stack.text: The B-tree's free page list is a LIFO stack: `free_page` pushes onto the head and `allocate_page` pops from the head, so pages are reused in reverse order of when they were freed.

free-list-is-singly-linked.text: Duplicates existing belief `btree-free-list-intrusive` (free list threaded through freed pages)

free-list-layout-coupled.text: `allocate_page` and `free_page` share an implicit contract on free-list node layout (3-byte zeroed header + 4-byte big-endian next-pointer); neither validates the other's output, so a format change in one silently breaks the other

free-list-lifo-decorrelates-layout.text: LIFO free-list reuse means delete-then-reinsert cycles progressively decorrelate logical key order from physical page order, defeating sequential I/O readahead for range scans.

free-list-reclaims-empty-leaves.text: Overlaps with proposed `btree-empty-leaf-freed-on-delete` and existing `btree-free-list-intrusive`; the reclamation trigger and the free list mechanism are already covered

free-page-can-free-page-zero.text: `PageManager.free_page` has no guard against `page_num == 0`, so freeing page 0 would overwrite the metadata page with a free-list node.

free-page-does-not-change-next-free.text: `PageManager.free_page` leaves the `next_free` high-water mark unchanged; it only updates the `free_head` pointer in metadata.

free-page-metadata-write-bypasses-pages-.text: `free_page` increments `pages_written` only for its `write_page` call; the metadata write via `_write_meta` bypasses the counter.

free-page-not-atomic-with-meta-update.text: Duplicates `btree-free-page-bypasses-wal` which already captures that `free_page()` writes directly without WAL protection.

free-page-only-called-from-delete.text: `PageManager.free_page` is only invoked by `BTree._delete` when removing an emptied leaf node; no other code path frees pages.

free-page-overwrites-content.text: `PageManager.free_page()` overwrites the freed page's content with a zero header and a free-list pointer, destroying the original leaf/internal node data so freed pages cannot be accidentally read as valid tree nodes.

free-page-stores-only-seven-bytes.text: Each free-list page occupies a full page (default 4096 bytes) but stores only 7 bytes of useful data (3-byte zero header + 4-byte next pointer); the remaining bytes are zero padding from `write_page`.
