free-page-two-non-atomic-writes.text: PageManager.free_page performs two non-atomic direct writes (the freed page's data, then metadata) with no WAL logging and no fsync.

freed-pages-reused-via-free-list.text: PageManager.free_page links freed pages into a singly-linked free list, and allocate_page reclaims from this list before extending the file.

fresh-sstables-always-start-at-level-zer.text: `SSTableWriter.finish()` hardcodes `level=0` (sstable.py:104), matching LevelDB's invariant that flushed memtables always produce L0 files

fsync-does-not-retroactively-atomicize-w.text: `fsync()` makes data durable but does not make the preceding `write()` atomic; a crash during `write()` before `fsync()` can leave a partial write, and a crash during `fsync()` can commit any subset of dirty pages.

fsync-file-does-not-guarantee-parent-dir.text: `fsync()` on a newly created file guarantees the file's own data and metadata but does not guarantee that the parent directory entry pointing to that file is durable.

fsync-flushes-all-file-metadata.text: fsync flushes file data plus all inode metadata such as mtime, atime, permissions, and size to stable storage.

fsync-forces-kernel-page-cache-to-stable.text: `os.fsync()` forces the OS to write kernel page cache data to physical disk, providing durability across power loss.

fsync-guarantees-are-per-file-not-cross-.text: POSIX `fsync()` guarantees durability only for the file descriptor passed to it; cross-file ordering requires an explicit sequence of fsync calls by the caller.

fsync-includes-metadata-fdatasync-skips.text: `os.fsync(fd)` forces both data and metadata to disk, while `os.fdatasync(fd)` skips metadata updates not needed for reading data back.

fsync-is-durability-primitive.text: Too broad — the role of fsync is already documented by multiple specific existing beliefs including `all-fsync-sites-data-integrity-only`, `fsync-used-only-for-appends`, `batch-mode-defers-fsync`, and per-engine fsync beliefs

fsync-policy-inconsistent-across-critica.text: The codebase has a systematic fsync policy inconsistency between components: WAL critical operations (checkpoints, batch commits, segment rotations) always force-fsync regardless of configured mode, but B-tree metadata mutations (which are equally critical for crash recovery) skip fsync entirely despite paying double fsync for user data pages.

justifications.label: WAL forces fsync for structural operations while B-tree skips it for equally critical metadata

fsync-semantics-vary-by-filesystem.text: General OS/filesystem knowledge (ext4 vs XFS vs btrfs behavior), not a testable claim about this codebase's code.

fsync-used-only-for-appends.text: `os.fsync` appears in the WAL append path and Bitcask record writes but never in SSTable creation, compaction output, or hint file writes — durability is applied to the append hot path only

full-data-lifecycle-unsafe-from-write-th.text: The complete data lifecycle is unsafe from storage maintenance through data retrieval: compaction is the highest-risk operation that can permanently lose or resurrect deleted data, and the read path from SSTable through CDC to derived systems is unreliable at every stage, meaning data is at risk whether it is being reorganized for efficiency or being served to consumers.

justifications.label: Write-side compaction and read-side SSTable-through-derived-systems hazards independently compromise the full lifecycle

full-stack-restart-fragility.text: Both the physical storage layer and the logical transaction layer are independently fragile under restart, creating a full-stack restart hazard: the B-tree's durability model protects user data pages but not structural metadata (height, sibling chain, free list), while the transaction system's isolation model depends on monotonic counters and abort-as-status-change semantics that have no persistence backing.

justifications.label: Independent restart fragility at the physical-page and logical-transaction layers means a single process restart can simultaneously corrupt both the storage structure and the isolation guarantees.

gc-assumes-version-list-txid-order.text: The no-active-transactions GC path selects the latest surviving version by iterating the version list forward, assuming versions are appended in transaction-ID order.

gc-deletes-empty-key-entries.text: When garbage_collect() removes all versions for a key, it deletes that key from _versions rather than leaving an empty version list.

gc-grace-seconds-default-10-days.text: Cassandra's `gc_grace_seconds` defaults to 864,000 seconds (10 days), the window during which anti-entropy must propagate a tombstone to all replicas before compaction may drop it.

gc-grace-seconds-is-repair-window.text: Describes Cassandra's external design pattern rather than a testable claim about this codebase; useful context but not a codebase invariant.

gc-grace-shorter-than-downtime-resurrect.text: If a node is offline longer than `gc_grace_seconds`, the tombstone can be purged before that node receives it, and the node's stale live value can resurrect via repair.

gc-is-idempotent.text: garbage_collect() is idempotent: calling it twice with no intervening state changes removes zero versions on the second call.

gc-no-active-keeps-one.text: When no transactions are active, `garbage_collect()` retains at most one version per key — the latest committed non-deleted version — and drops everything else including fully-deleted keys.

gc-not-thread-safe.text: `garbage_collect()` mutates `_versions` (replacing lists and deleting keys) without synchronization, assuming single-threaded execution — concurrent reads or writes during GC would race on the dict and its lists.

gc-preserves-active-snapshots.text: Garbage collection removes only versions unreachable by any active transaction, ensuring long-running read-only transactions see consistent data

gc-unconditionally-purges-aborted.text: `garbage_collect()` removes all versions with `created_by` in `_aborted` as its first step, regardless of active transaction state — aborted versions are invisible to everyone and always safe to drop.

gc-uses-min-txid-horizon.text: With active transactions, `garbage_collect()` uses `min(active tx_ids)` as the GC horizon; only versions superseded by a committed version with `tx_id < min_tx_id` are eligible for removal.

get-pending-drains-atomically.text: `get_pending_changes` returns the current `_pending` list and replaces it with an empty list, ensuring each change is delivered exactly once per replication cycle

get-tombstone-check-limited-to-tombstone.text: The get() empty-string tombstone check only prevents resurrection when the record being read is the tombstone itself.

gil-does-not-cross-process-boundaries.text: General Python runtime fact, not a codebase-specific architectural claim

gil-does-not-guarantee-check-then-act-at.text: The GIL prevents interpreter-level corruption of dict operations but does not make a multi-step check-then-act sequence in application code atomic.

gitignore-applies-repo-wide.text: Obvious from reading the file; unprefixed patterns matching at any depth is default gitignore behavior

gitignore-covers-python-only.text: Low value — easily verified by reading the 3-line `.gitignore` file directly

gitignore-is-minimal.text: Trivial project scaffolding detail; not an architectural invariant a developer needs to know

gitignore-trailing-slash-matches-directo.text: The trailing slash in `__pycache__/` and `.pytest_cache/` means only directories with those names are ignored, not files.

gossip-bandwidth-scales-linearly-per-mes.text: Each gossip round transmits the entire membership list per exchange despite a fanout of only one peer per node, making per-message payload O(N) in cluster size and total per-round bandwidth O(N squared) across the cluster, even though only N point-to-point messages are sent.

justifications.label: Fixed fanout bounds message count but full membership exchange makes each message grow linearly with cluster size

gossip-carries-membership-not-data.text: `GossipNode.receive_gossip` merges heartbeat counters and node status (alive/suspected/dead) only; it never exchanges application key-value data, making it a SWIM-style failure detector rather than a data replication protocol

gossip-cleanup-bounds-membership-growth.text: Dead nodes are removed from the membership list after `t_cleanup` elapsed time (default 20), preventing unbounded growth of the membership table from accumulated failure records

gossip-cleanup-removes-entry-entirely.text: After `t_cleanup` elapses, a dead node's record is fully deleted from membership (not just flagged), which enables clean rejoin with a fresh identity

gossip-cluster-add-node-joins-existing-a.text: `GossipCluster.add_node(node_id)` creates a node and joins it to an existing alive node when one is present.

gossip-cluster-remove-node-simulates-cra.text: `GossipCluster.remove_node(node_id)` simulates a crash by stopping the node's heartbeats without sending a leave message.

gossip-cluster-uses-logical-time.text: The gossip simulation uses explicit logical timestamps passed as parameters (not wall-clock time), with a fixed RNG seed for deterministic gossip partner selection, following the same simulated-time pattern as hinted-handoff

gossip-convergence-bound-is-5-log2-n-plu.text: The test `test_convergence_speed_olog_n` asserts gossip converges within `5 * math.log2(n_nodes) + 5` rounds, empirically validated for N = 8, 16, 32, 64.

gossip-convergence-is-olog-n.text: Full membership convergence occurs within O(log N) gossip rounds, empirically bounded by `5 * log₂(N) + 5` rounds in the test suite

gossip-convergence-test-bound-log2n.text: The gossip protocol test asserts convergence within `5 * log2(N) + 5` rounds for clusters up to 64 nodes.

gossip-dead-node-lifecycle-is-comprehens.text: Dead nodes in the gossip protocol follow a comprehensive, irreversible lifecycle with three independent safeguards: death status cannot be reversed by incoming gossip messages, dead node records are fully removed from the membership list after the cleanup interval (not merely flagged), and incoming gossip about already-dead nodes from other peers is silently filtered to prevent zombie reintroduction through stale state.

justifications.label: Three independent mechanisms at receive, status-transition, and cleanup stages ensure dead nodes can never be accidentally resurrected or leak membership memory.

gossip-dead-nodes-filtered-on-receive.text: When receiving gossip, unknown nodes that arrive with `dead` status are silently dropped to prevent zombie membership entries from propagating through the cluster

gossip-death-is-irreversible-via-gossip.text: Once a node's status is `dead`, receiving a gossip message with `status: alive` for that node will never revert it — the merge logic at line 67 checks `local["status"] != "dead"` before allowing exoneration

gossip-deep-copy-isolation.text: All inter-node data transfer (`send_gossip`, `join`, `get_membership_list`) uses `copy.deepcopy` to prevent shared mutable state between simulated nodes

gossip-detect-failures-is-stateless.text: `detect_failures` makes decisions using only `current_time - timestamp_last_updated`; it consults no historical distribution or sliding window, making it a pure point-in-time comparison rather than a statistical inference.

gossip-failure-detection-gates-replicati.text: `GossipNode.get_alive_members` returns the liveness set that anti-entropy, read-repair, and hinted-handoff all depend on to decide which nodes to contact — gossip provides the membership layer that every data-exchange layer needs

gossip-failure-detection-governs-cluster.text: Gossip-based failure detection is the single correctness bottleneck for the distributed cluster: replication, read repair, and hinted handoff all depend on its timeout-driven liveness set, which is bounded by cleanup to prevent unbounded membership growth.

justifications.label: All distributed data operations flow through the gossip liveness set, making failure detection accuracy a cluster-wide concern

gossip-failure-detection-lacks-adaptive-.text: Gossip failure detection is both the single correctness bottleneck for the cluster AND permanently miscalibrated: it governs all replication, read repair, and hinted handoff decisions, yet stores only the most recent timestamp per peer with no arrival history, making it unable to adapt detection thresholds to actual network conditions as phi-accrual detection would require.

justifications.label: The correctness bottleneck permanently lacks the data needed for adaptive accuracy

gossip-failure-detection-skips-self-entr.text: `GossipNode.detect_failures(current_time)` skips the node's own entry by checking `nid == self.node_id` before applying timeout transitions.

gossip-fanout-is-one.text: Each node selects exactly one random peer per gossip round, with bidirectional exchange producing at most N pairwise syncs per round.

gossip-fixed-three-threshold-fsm.text: Failure detection uses exactly three fixed time thresholds (`t_suspect=5`, `t_dead=10`, `t_cleanup=20`) producing a deterministic state machine with no runtime adaptation to network conditions.

gossip-heartbeat-counter-monotonic.text: A gossip node's heartbeat counter is monotonically increasing and never decreases.

gossip-heartbeat-noop-when-dead.text: `GossipNode.heartbeat(current_time)` increments the node's counter and updates its timestamp, but no-ops if the node's status is already dead.

gossip-join-copies-seed-membership-and-r.text: `GossipNode.join(seed_node)` copies the seed's membership list and registers the joining node with the seed, mutating both nodes.

gossip-lacks-piggyback-dissemination.text: The gossip implementation has no piggyback dissemination, and grep for `piggyback` or `disseminat` returns zero results.

gossip-merge-uses-heartbeat-monotonicity.text: `receive_gossip` only accepts remote state when the remote heartbeat counter strictly exceeds the local counter, except for death notifications at equal counters which are also accepted

gossip-no-arrival-history.text: Each node stores only the most recent `timestamp_last_updated` per peer, discarding all inter-arrival time history that would be needed for probabilistic failure detection (e.g., phi accrual).

gossip-node-status-lifecycle.text: Node status follows `alive → suspected → dead → removed` with configurable timeouts `t_suspect`, `t_dead`, `t_cleanup` governing transitions; a suspected node can return to alive if a higher heartbeat counter arrives

metadata.example:
if elapsed > self.t_dead: info["status"] = "dead"
elif elapsed > self.t_suspect: info["status"] = "suspected"
# alive -> suspected -> dead -> removed (after t_cleanup)

gossip-round-bidirectional-membership-ex.text: `GossipCluster.gossip_round` performs a bidirectional exchange of membership lists between each node and a randomly selected peer.

gossip-round-detects-failures-after-exch.text: After each gossip round, every node runs `detect_failures` to update suspicion states.

gossip-round-four-phase-order.text: `GossipCluster.gossip_round(current_time)` executes leave broadcast, heartbeats, random pairwise exchange, and failure detection in that order.

gossip-round-is-bidirectional-exchange.text: Each gossip round performs a bidirectional exchange in which both nodes send their full membership lists to each other.

gossip-suspicion-is-timeout-based.text: Suspicion in the gossip protocol is triggered by elapsed time exceeding `t_suspect` since the last heartbeat update, not by failed probe responses as in the full SWIM paper's ping/indirect-ping protocol

gossip-test-convergence-five-nodes-ten-r.text: `test_convergence_same_membership` verifies that all five nodes see the same alive set after ten gossip rounds.

gossip-test-crash-transition-assertion-t.text: `test_crash_suspect_dead_cleanup` checks the first failure transition with `in ('suspected', 'dead')` because exact timing depends on gossip propagation.

gossip-test-merge-handcrafted-stale-goss.text: `test_merge_conflicting_info` constructs a `stale_gossip` dict by hand to verify that lower heartbeat counters are rejected during merge.

gossip-test-rejoin-manipulates-failed-no.text: `test_dead_node_rejoin` directly manipulates `GossipCluster.failed_nodes` to allow a cleaned-up node to rejoin with fresh state.

gossip-test-suite-is-leaf-module.text: `test_gossip_protocol.py` is a leaf module that no other file imports; it is run directly by pytest or its `__main__` block.

gossip-topology-is-fully-connected.text: GossipCluster uses unrestricted random peer selection (any node can gossip with any other), making the effective topology a fully-connected graph.

gossip-uniform-thresholds.text: All nodes in a `GossipCluster` receive identical threshold values from the cluster constructor at `__init__` (line 117); individual nodes cannot calibrate sensitivity to their specific network path.

gossip-uses-full-membership-exchange.text: Each gossip round transmits the entire membership list via `deepcopy` rather than deltas or piggybacked updates, making per-exchange bandwidth cost O(N) in cluster size instead of O(1) amortized

gossip-voluntary-leave-broadcasts-to-all.text: A leaving node sends its death status to every active peer (not just a random one) before deactivating, unlike normal gossip which uses random pairwise exchange

metadata.example:
def leave(self):
    self.membership[self.node_id]["status"] = "dead"
    self._leaving = True
# cluster broadcasts to ALL peers before deactivating

handlers-must-mutate-state-in-place.text: Both `reconstruct_state` and `Projection` expect handler functions to mutate the `state` dict in place rather than returning a new value; a handler that returns without mutating silently loses its changes

happens-before-requires-two-reaches-call.text: `happens_before` calls `_reaches` in both directions to distinguish "a before b", "b before a", and "concurrent" — a single call can only confirm or deny one direction.

hash-index-all-keys-in-memory.text: Both Bitcask implementations keep every live key in an in-memory dict (`keydir` / `_index`), meaning the key set must fit in RAM; there is no disk-based fallback for partial index spill.

hash-index-assert-partial-guard.text: Duplicates existing belief `bitcask-no-checksum-validation` which states "the only corruption guard is the `assert read_key == key` in `get()`"

hash-index-bitcask-header-format-no-crc.text: `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py` uses header format `"<dII"` containing timestamp, key_size, and value_size, with no CRC field.

hash-index-bitcask-header-has-no-crc.text: In `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py`, the record header packs timestamp, key_size, and value_size with no CRC field.

hash-index-bitcask-lacks-corruption-erro.text: `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py` defines no dedicated `CorruptionError` exception, unlike the log-structured variant.

hash-index-bitcask-no-checksum.text: The hash-index-storage Bitcask records contain no CRC or checksum field, unlike the log-structured-hash-table implementation; on-disk corruption is undetectable during reads or compaction.

hash-index-bitcask-shared-read-handles.text: `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py` uses a single cached file handle per segment for all reads via `_get_reader()`, making concurrent reads to the same segment unsafe due to shared seek position.

hash-index-compact-rotates-merged-output.text: During hash-index-storage/bitcask.py compaction, merged output rotates to a new data file when the max_file_size limit is reached.

hash-index-compact-updates-keydir-in-pla.text: In hash-index-storage/bitcask.py compact(), after merged live records are written to new data files, the keydir is updated in place to point to the new file and offset locations.

hash-index-compact-uses-keydir-liveness.text: hash-index-storage/bitcask.py compact() determines record liveness by checking whether the keydir still points to the immutable file and offset, rather than comparing timestamps.

hash-index-compaction-fsyncs-data-before.text: In `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py` compaction, live entries are written and the data file contents are fsynced before `os.rename()` renames the old files.

hash-index-compaction-manual-only.text: The `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py` `compact()` must be called explicitly by the caller; there is no auto-compact trigger, threshold tracking, or background compaction unlike the `log-structured-hash-table` variant

hash-index-compaction-pops-zero-length-t.text: During `hash-index-storage` compaction, a record with `val_size == 0` is removed from the `latest` dict while scanning immutable files in ascending ID order.

hash-index-data-scan-detects-tombstones.text: Duplicates existing belief `bitcask-tombstone-is-empty-string` which covers both `_scan_data_file` checking `val_size == 0` and `get` checking `value == ""`

hash-index-delete-writes-empty-string-va.text: In `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py`, `delete(key)` writes an empty-string value via `_write_record`, producing `val_size == 0` on disk.

hash-index-empty-string-is-tombstone.text: Duplicates existing belief `bitcask-tombstone-is-empty-string` which already captures that empty-string values are indistinguishable from deletions

hash-index-empty-string-tombstone-collid.text: hash-index-storage/bitcask.py uses an empty string as the tombstone sentinel, so a legitimately stored empty-string value is indistinguishable from a deleted key and get() returns None.

hash-index-get-returns-none-on-empty-val.text: `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py:get` returns `None` when the read value is an empty string.

hash-index-get-tombstone-guard.text: `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py`'s `get()` checks `if value == "": return None`, providing a defense-in-depth layer against tombstone leaks that `log-structured-hash-table`'s `get()` lacks

hash-index-hint-entries-include-file-id-.text: `hash-index-storage` hint entries include `file_id`, `offset`, `size`, and `timestamp` in a 24-byte header plus key bytes.

hash-index-hint-entry-fixed-size-28-byte.text: Each hash-index hint entry has a 24-byte fixed header plus a 4-byte key length plus the key bytes, totaling 28 fixed bytes plus key length.

hash-index-hint-file-ignores-tombstones.text: Duplicates existing belief `bitcask-tombstone-handling-asymmetry` which states `_load_hint_file` unconditionally inserts entries and relies on compaction having already stripped tombstones

hash-index-hint-format-includes-file-id-.text: `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py` hint format `<IQId` stores file_id, offset, size, and timestamp per entry.

hash-index-hint-key-length-is-separate-p.text: In `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py`, the hint key size is encoded as a separate 4-byte `<I` prefix after the fixed `HINT_FORMAT` header.

hash-index-hint-load-lacks-tombstone-che.text: `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py`'s `_load_hint_file` also unconditionally adds every hint entry to the index, with no tombstone check.

hash-index-hint-self-sufficient.text: The `hash-index-storage` hint file contains all four keydir fields (file_id, offset, size, timestamp), making it sufficient to fully reconstruct the in-memory index without reading data files

hash-index-hint-size-field-is-record-siz.text: `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py` hint format `<IQId` uses `size` as total record size, not value size, so `_load_hint_file` cannot detect tombstones by `value_size == 0`.

hash-index-is-memory-bound-by-design.text: Hash index storage is fundamentally memory-bound: every key must reside in RAM for the single-seek O(1) read path, making dataset size directly constrained by available memory with no spill-to-disk fallback.

justifications.label: The O(1) read guarantee is inseparable from the all-keys-in-memory constraint — one cannot exist without the other

hash-index-keydir-has-four-fields.text: The hash-index-storage Bitcask KeyEntry stores four fields: file_id, offset, size, and timestamp.

hash-index-keyentry-size-is-total-record.text: In hash-index-storage/bitcask.py, KeyEntry.size stores the total record size including header, key, and value, not just the value size.

hash-index-keys-must-fit-in-ram.text: Both Bitcask implementations require every live key to be held in a Python dict in memory; the dataset's key space is bounded by available RAM

hash-index-loads-entire-hint-file-into-m.text: hash-index-storage/bitcask.py _load_hint_file reads the entire hint file into a single bytes object and walks it with a manual cursor.

hash-index-no-crc.text: Duplicates existing belief `bitcask-no-checksum-validation` which already captures the absence of integrity checking in `hash-index-storage`

hash-index-no-crc-by-design.text: `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py` intentionally omits CRC to focus on keydir/append-log/compaction; `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py` provides the integrity-checking variant with `zlib.crc32` and `CorruptionError`

hash-index-no-range-queries.text: Neither hash index implementation (`hash-index-storage/bitcask.py` or `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py`) provides a `scan`, `range`, or ordered-iteration method; only exact-key point lookups are supported.

hash-index-read-is-single-seek.text: A Bitcask `get()` does one dict lookup plus one positioned disk read (O(1)), while an LSM-tree `get()` may search the memtable then multiple SSTables from newest to oldest (O(log N) per level)

hash-index-record-header-is-16-bytes-no-.text: hash-index-storage/bitcask.py uses the record header format <dII (timestamp, key_size, value_size), which is 16 bytes and contains no checksum field.

hash-index-stores-string-values-only.text: hash-index-storage/bitcask.py stores string values rather than arbitrary byte sequences.

hash-index-survives-restart.text: Hash-index storage correctly reconstructs its in-memory index from on-disk segments after restart by scanning in ascending order so newer writes overwrite older entries, with fsync-controlled durability for each write.

justifications.label: Restart recovery is correct for normal operation but a crash during compaction leaves segment state that rebuild cannot handle consistently

hash-index-sync-writes-controls-fsync.text: In hash-index-storage Bitcask, the `sync_writes` flag controls whether each `_write_record` call fsyncs to disk; when `False`, recently written records may be lost on crash.

hash-index-tombstone-costs-zero-value-by.text: In `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py`, a tombstone record sets `value_size` to 0, so it adds no value bytes to the record.

hash-index-tombstone-crc-covers-key-only.text: In `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py`, the CRC for a tombstone record covers the key only because the value length is zero.

hash-index-tombstone-detection-uses-size.text: In `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py`, tombstone detection checks the `value_size` field equal to 0 without reading value bytes.

hash-index-tombstone-is-zero-length.text: Covered by existing belief `bitcask-tombstone-is-empty-string`; zero-length value is the direct encoding of empty string

hash-index-tombstone-is-zero-length-valu.text: Duplicate of existing `bitcask-tombstone-is-empty-string` which already captures that tombstones are zero-length/empty-string values.

hash-index-wall-clock-not-monotonic.text: `_write_record` timestamps use `time.time()`, which is not monotonic — NTP adjustments or manual clock changes can cause a newer write to carry an older timestamp, confusing compaction's latest-wins conflict resolution.

hash-index-write-no-index-mutation.text: `_write_record` in `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py` does not modify `keydir`; the caller (`put` or `delete`) is responsible for updating the in-memory index after the write returns.

hash-mod-destroys-key-order.text: Hash-mod partitioning (`hash(k) % num_reducers`) scatters lexicographically adjacent keys across different partitions, making range queries require a full scatter-gather across all reducers; MapReduce `run()` re-sorts the final results to compensate

hash-mod-partition-count-is-static.text: In `mapreduce.py`, `num_reducers` is fixed at job creation (`num_reducers: int = 2`) and never changes during execution; all partition assignments are determined by `hash(k) % num_reducers` with no dynamic rebalancing

hash-mod-skew-shared-across-modules.text: Three modules use the same `hash(k) % num_partitions` pattern with fixed partition counts and no hot-key mitigation: `mapreduce.py:109`, `secondary_index_partitioning.py:56`, and `partitioned_log.py:149` — all share the straggler vulnerability where a single hot key overwhelms one partition

hashlib-reserved-for-crypto-distribution.text: The codebase consistently uses `zlib.crc32` for corruption detection in storage engines and `hashlib` (SHA-256) for content addressing (Merkle trees), uniform distribution (consistent hashing, bloom filters), and cryptographic integrity (BFT) — the two hash families never cross purposes

header-corruption-derails-sequential-sca.text: A corrupted `key_size` or `val_size` in `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py` causes `_scan_data_file` to read wrong byte boundaries, potentially misinterpreting all subsequent records in that file

header-flag-zero-value-collision.text: Design recommendation rather than a testable factual claim about the code — "neither implementation uses X" is better expressed through the existing per-implementation beliefs about their actual tombstone encoding

heap-tiebreak-uses-source-index.text: The merge heap tuple includes a `source_index` field solely to prevent Python from comparing `SSTableEntry` objects when `(key, -timestamp)` ties, which would raise `TypeError`.

heap-tuple-ordering-for-dedup.text: Overlaps with existing `sstable-merge-dedup-newest-timestamp` (newest timestamp wins) and `heap-tiebreak-uses-source-index` (source index as tiebreaker); the negation trick is an implementation detail, not an invariant.

hint-corrupt-worse-than-missing.text: A corrupted hint file silently loads bad offsets into the index with no validation; a missing hint file triggers a CRC-checked full scan via `_scan_segment`, making hint corruption strictly worse than hint absence.

hint-corruption-detected-only-at-read-ti.text: In `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py`, a subtly corrupted hint file produces no startup error; CRC mismatch is detected only when a later `get()` reads a poisoned entry and raises `CorruptionError`.

hint-empty-entries-creates-zero-length-f.text: Passing an empty `entries` list to `_write_hint_file` creates a valid zero-length hint file.

hint-entry-fixed-header-is-20-bytes.text: Each hint entry in `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py` has a 20-byte fixed header plus 4 bytes for key length and the key bytes.

hint-entry-format-u32-pair-plus-key.text: Each hint entry is written as `struct.pack("!II", key_size, offset)` followed by the raw key bytes, with no value bytes or checksum.

hint-entry-header-fields-are-file-id-off.text: Each hint entry begins with a 24-byte header packing `file_id` as uint32, `offset` as uint64, `size` as uint32, and `timestamp` as float64.

hint-expiry-bounds-durability.text: Hints in `HintedHandoffStore` have a TTL; if `trigger_handoff` doesn't run before `created_at + hint_ttl`, `expire_hints` silently drops the hint, permanently losing that replica's copy of the data

hint-file-compaction-resurrection.text: Covered by the combination of existing beliefs `bitcask-tombstone-handling-asymmetry` (hint files don't check tombstones), `bitcask-hint-files-exclude-tombstones` (hint-based recovery can't distinguish deleted from never-existed), and `tombstone-removal-requires-full-key-coverage` (incomplete compaction can resurrect deleted keys)

hint-file-format-repeated-key-size-offse.text: A hint file is a repeated sequence of entries formatted as [key_size: u32, offset: u32, key_bytes: var], with no value bytes or checksums.

hint-file-loss-is-safe.text: Covered by existing `hint-files-are-optimization-only` which establishes that hints carry no unique data.

hint-file-no-fsync.text: Hint files are written without `fsync`; they are a best-effort startup optimization that can be lost on crash without data loss, since the data file remains authoritative.

hint-file-no-integrity-check.text: Neither the hint file writer nor reader performs checksum validation; a truncated or corrupted hint file causes a `struct.error` or `IndexError` on startup rather than a graceful fallback to data file scanning.

hint-file-orphan-crash-risk.text: In `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py`, a crash between deleting a data file and its hint file leaves an orphaned hint that directs reads to a nonexistent data file, causing hard failures on `get()`.

hint-file-write-not-atomic.text: Hint files are written directly to the final path (not via temp-file-and-rename), so a crash mid-generation leaves a partial hint file; `_load_hint_file` handles this by stopping at the first short read

hint-files-are-embarrassingly-parallel.text: Describes Erlang/Riak's optimization strategy, not a testable property of this Python codebase

hint-files-are-optimization-only.text: Hint files accelerate index rebuild during recovery but carry no crash-consistency guarantees; they are not consulted to determine which data files constitute the valid current state

hint-files-cannot-represent-deletes.text: Covered by existing beliefs `lsht-hint-no-tombstone-flag` and `bitcask-hint-files-exclude-tombstones`, which describe this limitation for both implementations

hint-files-do-not-reduce-segment-open-co.text: Hint files in both Bitcask variants reduce bytes read during index rebuild but do not reduce the number of files that must be opened, because there is one hint file per data segment.

hint-files-have-no-inter-file-dependenci.text: Each Bitcask hint file is self-contained and describes exactly one data file's keys, so hint file reads have no inter-file dependencies during the loading phase.

hint-files-only-canonical-entries.text: A hint entry is written only when `self._index[key]` confirms the key's canonical location is the current segment and offset, filtering out entries superseded by later writes or compaction

hint-format-diverges-between-implementat.text: Hash-index hint uses a 24-byte fixed header per entry (`file_id:u32, offset:u64, size:u32, timestamp:f64`) while log-structured hint uses only an 8-byte header (`key_size:u32, offset:u32`), omitting file_id, timestamp, and record size

hint-format-symmetry.text: `_write_hint_file` and `_load_hint_file` must use identical binary layouts: `[HINT_FORMAT header (24 bytes)][key_len uint32 (4 bytes)][key_bytes (variable)]` per entry; any change to one without the other breaks backward compatibility.

hint-format-variable-length.text: Each hint record is `HINT_HEADER_SIZE (24 bytes) + 4 (key_size uint32) + key_length` bytes; the `HINT_FORMAT` constant covers only the fixed 24-byte portion, not the full record.

hint-generation-breaks-on-partial-segmen.text: During hint generation, a short header or payload read causes the scan loop to break, treating the segment tail as truncated rather than raising an error.

hint-generation-no-crc-validation.text: `create_hint_files` does not verify CRC checksums on the segment records it reads (unlike `_scan_segment`), so corrupted data can be silently indexed via hint files

hint-generation-overwrites-existing-hint.text: `create_hint_files` opens a new hint file with overwrite for each frozen segment, replacing any existing hint file for that segment.

hint-generation-propagates-errors-unhand.text: `create_hint_files` has no error handling; `FileNotFoundError`, `struct.error`, and `UnicodeDecodeError` propagate to callers.

hint-generation-skips-active-segment.text: `create_hint_files` never generates a hint file for the active segment, only for frozen (immutable) segments, since a hint for the active segment would be immediately stale

hint-key-length-is-utf8-byte-length.text: The hint file stores key length as the UTF-8 byte length of the key, not its character count.

hint-load-bulk-reads-file.text: `_load_hint_file` reads the entire hint file into memory as one `bytes` object before parsing records.

hint-load-does-not-open-segment-file.text: `_load_hint_file` never opens the segment file; it only stores the provided `seg_path` as the index value paired with the hint entry's offset.

hint-load-last-entry-wins.text: `_load_hint_file` silently overwrites existing `keydir` entries when duplicate keys appear, so the last hint record wins.

hint-load-no-bounds-check-key-size.text: `_load_hint_file` does not bounds-check the `key_size` field; a malformed hint file with an absurdly large `key_size` can cause a large allocation and potentially raise `OverflowError` or `MemoryError`.

hint-load-no-cached-reader.text: `_load_hint_file` does not cache a read handle in `self.file_handles`; hint files are opened and closed once during startup.

hint-load-opens-own-file-handle.text: `_load_hint_file` opens and closes its own file handle, while `_scan_data_file` uses the shared `_get_reader`.

hint-load-overwrites-existing-index-entr.text: `_load_hint_file` unconditionally inserts each hint entry into `self._index`, overwriting any prior index entry for the same key and relying on the caller to process segments oldest-to-newest.

hint-load-requires-valid-utf8-keys.text: `_load_hint_file` decodes key bytes as UTF-8 and will raise `UnicodeDecodeError` on malformed data, which is its only failure mode that is not silently swallowed.

hint-load-uses-embedded-fid.text: `_load_hint_file` uses the `fid` embedded in each hint record rather than the `file_id` parameter when creating `KeyEntry` objects.

hint-load-utf8-keys-only.text: `_load_hint_file` decodes hint-file keys as UTF-8 with no fallback, so invalid UTF-8 raises `UnicodeDecodeError`.

hint-offset-is-segment-offset.text: The `offset` value stored in a hint entry is a byte position in the corresponding `.dat` segment file, not a position within the hint file itself; `get()` uses this offset to seek directly into the segment.

hint-record-fields-fid-offset-size-times.text: Each hint record's fixed header stores `fid` (uint32), `offset` (uint64), `size` (uint32), and `timestamp` (double).

hint-structural-corruption-crashes-on-st.text: A structurally corrupted hint file causes `struct.unpack` to read a bogus `key_size`, slice past the buffer, and raise an uncaught exception during startup.

hint-write-does-not-mutate-in-memory-sta.text: `_write_hint_file` does not modify `keydir`, `file_handles`, or any other instance state.

hint-write-requires-data-file-flushed.text: A precondition of `_write_hint_file` is that the corresponding `.data` file is already fully written and flushed.

hint-written-only-during-compaction.text: `_write_hint_file` is called exclusively from `compact()`, never during normal `put`/`delete` operations; hint files only exist for compacted (merged) data files.

hinted-handoff-ensures-write-availabilit.text: Hinted handoff maintains write availability during replica failures by routing writes to substitute nodes that forward data when the original replica recovers.

justifications.label: Availability is undermined because all hints for all unavailable nodes concentrate on a single substitute, creating a single point of failure that defeats the redundancy goal

hinted-handoff-get-returns-highest-versi.text: `get(key)` queries available preferred replicas and returns the value with the highest version among the responses.

hinted-handoff-hint-cleanup-all-or-nothi.text: `remove_hints_for()` purges all hints for a recovered target node regardless of whether individual hints were successfully delivered or had expired; after `trigger_handoff`, no hints for that node remain on any other node.

hinted-handoff-hint-loss-is-silent-data-.text: If a hint node crashes and its hints are lost before handoff, the target node never receives the data and no error is raised — requiring anti-entropy repair (e.g., Merkle trees) to detect and fix.

hinted-handoff-hint-ttl-exclusive-bounda.text: Hint expiration uses exclusive comparison: a hint created at time `t` with TTL `d` survives at `t + d - 1` but is expired at `t + d`.

hinted-handoff-hints-cleared-after-deliv.text: Duplicate of existing `hinted-handoff-hint-cleanup-all-or-nothing` which already covers post-handoff hint removal.

hinted-handoff-no-exceptions.text: Write failures are signaled via `success: False` in the return dict; the hinted handoff module never raises exceptions in normal operation.

hinted-handoff-node-stores-hints-for-oth.text: A `Node`'s hint log stores `Hint` objects for other nodes; a node does not store hints for itself.

hinted-handoff-one-hint-per-target-per-w.text: Each unavailable preferred replica gets at most one hint stored on one non-preferred node per write operation, preventing hint explosion.

hinted-handoff-reads-skip-non-preferred.text: `get()` only queries preferred replicas, so data existing only as hints on non-preferred nodes is invisible to reads until handoff delivers it.

metadata.example:
preferred = self.get_preferred_nodes(key)
for nid in preferred:  # only read from preferred replicas
    if node.is_available():
        results.append(node.get(key))

hinted-handoff-replica-placement-hash-mo.text: `get_preferred_nodes(key)` selects replicas by computing `hash(key) % N` over a sorted node list and returning `replication_factor` node IDs walking the ring.

hinted-handoff-result-dict-protocol.text: Hinted handoff `put()` and `get()` return plain result dictionaries with fields including `success`, `sloppy`, `hints_stored`, `replicas_written`, `value`, and `version`.

hinted-handoff-sloppy-quorum-counts-hint.text: When `sloppy_quorum=True` (the default), stored hints count toward `write_quorum` the same as direct replica writes, trading consistency for write availability.

metadata.example:
total_acks = len(replicas_written) + len(hints_stored)
success = total_acks >= self.write_quorum

hinted-handoff-sloppy-quorum-writes-to-n.text: When sloppy quorum is enabled and preferred replicas are down, writes succeed by routing to non-preferred substitute nodes that store hints for later delivery.

hinted-handoff-strict-quorum-rejects-ins.text: With `sloppy_quorum=False`, a write fails if fewer than `write_quorum` preferred nodes are available, even if non-preferred nodes could serve.

hinted-handoff-test-default-cluster-five.text: The `make_store()` helper in the hinted handoff tests defaults to 5 nodes labeled A through E, replication factor 3, read/write quorum 2, hint TTL 50, and sloppy quorum enabled.

hinted-handoff-tests-discover-preferred-.text: The hinted handoff tests call `get_preferred_nodes(key)` to discover which nodes own a key before selectively disabling those nodes.

hinted-handoff-time-is-parameter.text: All time-dependent operations (`put`, `trigger_handoff`, `expire_all_hints`) take `current_time` as an explicit argument rather than calling `time.time()`, making the implementation fully deterministic and testable.

metadata.example:
def put(self, key, value, current_time):
    # time passed explicitly, not read from system clock

hinted-handoff-trigger-handoff-replays-n.text: `trigger_handoff(recovered_node_id, current_time)` scans every other node for hints targeting the recovered node and replays each non-expired hint via `put()`.

hinted-handoff-trigger-replays-buffered-.text: `hinted-handoff.trigger_handoff` replays stored `Hint` objects when a node recovers and gossip marks it alive again.

hinted-handoff-ttl-bounds-hint-lifetime.text: Hints expire after `created_at + ttl` (checked via `Hint.is_expired`); a node that stays down longer than the TTL window will not receive those hinted writes and must rely on anti-entropy for convergence.

hinted-handoff-version-monotonic-per-key.text: The coordinator assigns strictly increasing versions per key via a centralized counter, so stale hint replays are absorbed harmlessly by `Node.put()`'s `version >= existing_version` check.

metadata.example:
version = self.versions.get(key, 0) + 1
self.versions[key] = version

his-corruption-can-crash-recovery-on-utf.text: In `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py`, corruption that causes value bytes to be parsed as a record header can crash recovery when `key_bytes.decode("utf-8")` encounters invalid UTF-8.

his-no-integrity-check-on-read.text: Duplicates existing beliefs `hash-index-no-crc-by-design` and `silent-corruption-returns-garbage` which together capture that hash-index-storage performs no integrity verification on read.

his-scanner-treats-zero-val-size-as-tomb.text: In `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py`, `_scan_data_file` treats any record with `val_size == 0` in the header as a tombstone and removes the key from the index.

his-tombstone-is-zero-val-size.text: Duplicates existing belief `bitcask-tombstone-is-empty-string` which captures that hash-index-storage encodes deletion as an empty value, and `bitcask-tombstone-semantics` which covers the semantics.

his-val-size-corruption-cascades.text: Duplicates existing belief `header-corruption-derails-sequential-scan` which states that corrupted key_size or val_size causes _scan_data_file to misparse all subsequent records.

immutable-memtables-list-never-appended.text: _immutable_memtables is initialized at line 210 but no code path ever appends to it.

in-place-rewrite-open-wb-truncates-befor.text: WAL truncation rewrites surviving records in place using `open(f, 'wb')`, which truncates the file to zero before writing any survivors; a crash after this open but before rewriting loses all surviving records.

index-is-volatile.text: All three storage engines rebuild their in-memory index (`keydir`, `_index`) entirely from on-disk files at startup; inconsistent file state after a crash produces a silently incomplete index with no error

init-meta-unprotected-by-wal.text: During initial file creation, `PageManager.__init__` writes metadata and the root leaf page directly via `_write_meta` without WAL protection; acceptable because no user data exists yet to lose.

innodb-btree-merges-on-underflow.text: InnoDB B+ trees maintain a minimum fill factor and trigger a merge with a sibling when a deletion drops a page below it.

innodb-uses-full-merge-on-underflow-and-.text: InnoDB performs full merge on underflow and uses a change buffer for batching.

innodb-uses-optimistic-lock-coupling.text: InnoDB uses read-write latches on buffer pool pages and optimistic lock coupling, acquiring shared latches on descent and restarting with exclusive latches only when a split is needed.

input-validation-systematically-absent.text: Input validation is systematically absent across configuration and API boundaries: the WAL accepts arbitrary strings as sync mode (silently disabling all durability guarantees), truncate accepts out-of-range sequence numbers (silently deleting all data), compaction strategy selection silently falls through to leveled on any unrecognized string, and Merkle proof direction is never validated — misconfiguration produces incorrect behavior rather than failing fast.

justifications.label: Four independent modules silently accept invalid inputs at critical API boundaries

integrity-checking-is-both-incomplete-an.text: Data integrity checking fails in two complementary ways: CRC checksums exclude routing metadata (sequence numbers, page numbers, headers), so corruption in those fields goes undetected; and every reader halts at the first detected CRC failure with no resync capability — meaning both detectable and undetectable corruption are terminal.

justifications.label: incomplete detection + no recovery = both missed and caught corruption are equally fatal

integrity-degrades-along-storage-pipelin.text: Data integrity verification degrades monotonically along the storage pipeline: WAL records have CRC checksums that exclude routing metadata (partial coverage), SSTables have no checksums at all (zero coverage), and neither layer can recover from detected corruption — data transitions from partially verified to completely unverified as it moves through compaction from WAL to SSTable.

justifications.label: Integrity coverage drops from partial (WAL) to zero (SSTable) along the data lifecycle

internal-deserialize-is-pure-function.text: _deserialize_internal has no I/O, mutation, or side effects.

internal-deserialize-no-type-check.text: Covered by existing `btree-deserialize-no-validation` which already states neither deserializer validates page type

internal-deserialize-preserves-serialize.text: _deserialize_internal returns keys in the same order they were serialized, without sorting.

internal-deserialize-raises-struct-error.text: Passing truncated data to _deserialize_internal raises struct.error from a short unpack.

internal-keys-utf8-assumption.text: Covered by existing `btree-keys-decoded-as-utf8` which already captures that keys are decoded as UTF-8

internal-node-children-invariant.text: _serialize_internal assumes len(children) == len(keys) + 1 but does not assert it; too few children raises IndexError, while extra children beyond keys+1 are silently dropped — a potential data-loss path if the invariant is violated.

internal-node-wire-format-is-header-chil.text: A B-tree internal page is formatted as `header(3B) + child_0(4B) + (key_len(2B) + key + child(4B))...`.

internal-nodes-no-sibling-pointer.text: Internal nodes have no sibling pointer field; their binary layout is `[type:1B][num_keys:2B][child₀:4B]([keylen:2B][key][child:4B])...` with no right-link, and `_deserialize_internal` returns a 2-tuple `(keys, children)` vs. the leaf's 3-tuple `(keys, values, next_sibling)`.

internal-page-binary-layout.text: Internal page wire format is [type:1B][num_keys:2B][child0:4B] followed by repeating [keylen:2B][key:varB][child:4B], all big-endian with no alignment padding; this interleaved layout mirrors the logical separator-pointer structure.

iter-descends-left-spine.text: `__iter__` reaches the leftmost leaf by following `children[0]` at every internal level, then walks the sibling chain to `NO_SIBLING` to enumerate all keys in sorted order

iter-generator-is-lazy-and-supports-earl.text: BTree.__iter__ returns a lazy generator, so callers can stop iteration early without reading remaining leaves.

iter-no-counter-reset.text: Unlike get, put, delete, and range_scan, BTree.__iter__ does not call reset_counters() before running, so I/O page-read stats accumulate on top of any prior count — a gotcha when benchmarking iteration.

iter-read-cost-is-internal-levels-plus-l.text: For a tree with H levels and L leaves, BTree.__iter__ reads H-1 internal pages plus L leaf pages.

iter-yields-pairs-in-ascending-key-order.text: BTree.__iter__ yields (key, value) pairs in ascending key order by walking the leaf sibling chain left-to-right.

iter-yields-sorted-pairs.text: Covered by existing beliefs `btree-leaf-sibling-chain` and `range-scan-follows-sibling-chain`; __iter__ uses the same leaf-chain mechanism.

iterate-delegates-to-read-all-records.text: `iterate` uses `yield from _read_all_records()` to lazily stream records, meaning the actual file scanning and parsing logic resides in `_read_all_records`.

iterate-flushes-without-fsync.text: Before reading, `iterate()` calls `fd.flush()` but not `os.fsync()`, so buffered writes reach the OS page cache but are not guaranteed durable on stable storage.

iterate-not-snapshot-isolated.text: `iterate()` releases the WAL lock after flushing but before reading begins, so concurrent appends may or may not be visible to the iterator depending on timing.

iterate-opens-files-read-only.text: During iteration, each WAL segment file is opened in read-only mode (`"rb"`) by `_read_all_records`.

iterate-read-all-records-moves-to-next-f.text: When `_read_record` returns `None` (EOF or partial read), `_read_all_records` moves to the next WAL file rather than stopping.

iterate-returns-marker-records.text: `iterate()` returns all WAL records including COMMIT and CHECKPOINT markers, while `replay()` filters those markers out.

iterate-returns-walrecord-iterator.text: `iterate` returns an `Iterator[WALRecord]` where each `WALRecord` includes `seq_num`, `op_type`, `key`, `value`, and `checksum`.

iterate-sorted-filename-order.text: `_read_all_records` iterates over `.wal` files in sorted filename order.

iterate-stops-silently-at-corruption.text: When `iterate()` encounters a CRC mismatch, iteration stops with no exception or sentinel value — the caller receives all valid records before the corruption with no indication that more data existed.

iterate-yields-all-op-types.text: `iterate()` yields records of every op type (PUT, DELETE, COMMIT, CHECKPOINT) while `replay()` filters to only PUT and DELETE records.

iterate-yields-all-record-types.text: Duplicate of `wal-iterate-preserves-all-ops` proposed above from the earlier entry

join-determinism-from-event-time.text: The stream join processor's output is fully determined by the sequence of `(stream_name, key, value, timestamp)` inputs and `advance_time` calls, with no dependency on wall-clock time — making it deterministically testable without clock mocking

join-uses-symmetric-interval-not-tumblin.text: `TimeWindow.contains()` uses `abs(t1 - t2) <= duration`, making join matching a symmetric interval check centered on each event, not aligned to any fixed time grid

join-window-and-aggregation-window-are-i.text: The join `TimeWindow` duration controls which event pairs can match, while the `TumblingWindowAggregator` window size controls result grouping; these are independent parameters that can differ without violating any invariant

json-dumps-sort-keys-insufficient-for-fl.text: General Python/JSON fact about float-to-string non-determinism, not a codebase-specific invariant — belongs in documentation, not in the belief registry.

kafka-compaction-runs-asynchronously-on-.text: Kafka log compaction runs as a background broker thread and can remove events that consumers have not yet read.

kafka-connect-offsets-durable-in-consume.text: Kafka Connect stores connector offsets in Kafka's internal `__consumer_offsets` topic or a Connect offset backing store so it can resume from the last acknowledged offset.

key-length-cap-uint16.text: Already exists as an accepted belief.

key-range-merkle-diff-returns-key-names.text: `KeyRangeMerkleTree.diff_keys()` returns the string key names of divergent entries, translating numeric leaf indices back to keys

key-range-merkle-encodes-pairs-as-key-co.text: KeyRangeMerkleTree encodes each key-value pair as "key:value" bytes before hashing it in the Merkle tree.

key-range-merkle-sorts-by-key.text: `KeyRangeMerkleTree` sorts input pairs by key before building, so two trees with identical key-value content always produce the same root hash regardless of insertion order

kforceoptimized-skips-non-shrinking-file.text: RocksDB's `kForceOptimized` mode skips bottommost files that contain no tombstones or overwrites to avoid rewriting data that will not shrink.

lamport-clock-never-decreases.text: A node's Lamport clock never decreases; `tick()` and `send_tick()` always increment, and `receive_tick()` takes `max + 1`.

lamport-clock-tick-increments-counter.text: `LamportClock.tick()` increments the counter and returns the new value.

lamport-happens-before-returns-tristate.text: `happens_before(a, b, events)` returns `True` (a causes b), `False` (b causes a), or `None` (concurrent) — modeling a strict partial order with explicit concurrency detection.

lamport-happens-before-uses-graph-not-ti.text: `happens_before()` determines causality by BFS over `_parent`/`_cause` edges in the event DAG, not by comparing timestamps; the `all_events` parameter is accepted but never used.

lamport-message-carries-sender-timestamp.text: `Message` carries `sender_timestamp` so the receiver can update its clock using the sender's timestamp.

lamport-message-counter-is-module-level.text: `_msg_counter = itertools.count(1)` is module-level state that generates unique message IDs across all nodes.

lamport-mutex-lowest-timestamp-priority.text: `LamportMutex` grants critical section access to the requesting node with the lowest timestamp, with other requesters waiting until the holder releases.

lamport-mutex-provides-mutual-exclusion.text: The Lamport mutex correctly ensures mutual exclusion: the requesting node with the lowest timestamp gets priority, and entry requires acknowledgment from every other node in the system, preventing any two nodes from entering the critical section simultaneously.

justifications.label: Mutex correctness is validated only under synchronous delivery simulation, not real network conditions

lamport-mutex-release-removes-request-an.text: `LamportMutex.release(node)` removes the node's request from the queue and broadcasts RELEASE to all other nodes.

lamport-mutex-request-broadcasts-and-col.text: `LamportMutex.request(node)` ticks the clock, adds `(timestamp, node_id)` to the request queue, broadcasts REQUEST messages to all other nodes, and recipients immediately send ACK back.

lamport-mutex-request-queue-sorted-by-ti.text: The Lamport mutex request queue is sorted by `(timestamp, node_id)`, giving a deterministic total order when timestamps collide.

lamport-mutex-requires-all-acks.text: `can_enter()` returns `True` only when the node's request is at the queue head (lowest `(timestamp, node_id)`) AND acknowledgments have been received from every other node in the system.

metadata.example:
others = set(self._nodes.keys()) - {node.node_id}
return others.issubset(self._acks.get(node.node_id, set()))

lamport-receive-tick-guarantees-causal-o.text: `receive_tick` computes `max(local, received) + 1`, ensuring every receive event has a timestamp strictly greater than the corresponding send event, which is the core Lamport clock invariant.

lamport-receive-tick-max-merge.text: `LamportClock.receive_tick(remote_ts)` computes `max(local, remote_ts) + 1`, ensuring the clock advances past both the local and remote state on every receive.

lamport-send-creates-receive.text: `Node.send_message(target, payload)` has a side effect on the target node: it appends a RECEIVE event to the target's event log and advances the target's clock.

lamport-send-delivers-synchronously.text: `send_message` calls `to_node.receive_message()` directly in the same call stack, making message delivery instantaneous and deterministic with no async queue or network simulation.

lamport-send-tick-is-alias-of-tick.text: `send_tick()` is identical to `tick()` and exists as a separate method for semantic clarity.

lamport-timestamp-order-not-implies-caus.text: `a.timestamp < b.timestamp` does NOT imply a→b; two concurrent events can have ordered timestamps, which is a fundamental limitation of Lamport clocks that vector clocks address.

lamport-total-order-breaks-ties-by-node-.text: `total_order()` sorts by `(timestamp, node_id)`, using lexicographic node ID comparison as a deterministic tiebreaker when timestamps are equal.

metadata.example:
def total_order(events):
    return sorted(events, key=lambda e: (e.timestamp, e.node_id))

lamport-total-order-tiebreak-by-node-id.text: `total_order()` sorts events by `(timestamp, node_id)`, using the node identifier as a deterministic tiebreaker for concurrent events with equal timestamps.

large-batch-crash-leaves-partial-batch.text: If a batch is large enough or the OS flushes page-cache pages selectively, a crash can leave the batch's PUT records on disk without the COMMIT record, causing replay to return partial batch records.

late-event-drop-is-hard-cutoff.text: Events with `timestamp < watermark - allowed_lateness` are unconditionally dropped and counted in `stats.late_events_dropped`; there is no secondary path to recover or re-buffer them

lazy-derived-propagation.text: Duplicates existing belief `unbundled-db-flush-required-for-derived` which captures the same decoupling between writes and derived-system propagation

lcs-assumes-l1-plus-non-overlapping.text: `_lcs_compact` assumes the LCS invariant that SSTables within each L1+ level have non-overlapping key ranges; it does not enforce or validate this precondition.

lcs-compact-one-per-call.text: `_lcs_compact` performs at most one merge operation per invocation and returns immediately; cascading compactions across levels require the caller to loop on `run_compaction()`.

lcs-compaction-triggered-by-l0-count-or-.text: Leveled compaction triggers when Level 0 has at least `l0_trigger` SSTables or when any level exceeds its size budget.

lcs-dedups-overlapping-l1-by-id.text: During L0 compaction, `_lcs_compact` collects overlapping L1 SSTables into a set keyed by `id()` so an L1 SSTable overlapping multiple L0 SSTables appears only once in the merge set.

lcs-default-l0-trigger-four.text: `_lcs_compact` uses a default `_l0_trigger` of 4, meaning L0 to L1 compaction is checked when the L0 count is at least 4.

lcs-io-error-leaves-partial-state.text: If `merge_sstables` raises an I/O error during `_lcs_compact`, `self._sstables` can be left partially modified with some input SSTables removed but no merged SSTable added.

lcs-l0-compacts-all.text: L0 compaction always includes every L0 SSTable in the merge set (not just a subset), which can cause large write spikes when many L0 SSTables accumulate before the trigger fires.

lcs-l0-triggers-on-count-not-size.text: Level 0 in leveled compaction triggers based on SSTable count (`l0_compaction_trigger`), not total size, because L0 SSTables can have overlapping key ranges unlike higher levels which maintain non-overlapping invariants

lcs-l1-can-have-overlapping-ranges.text: Duplicate of existing `lcs-produces-single-output-sstable` which already notes L1+ will have overlapping key ranges

lcs-level-size-caps-exponential-fanout.text: Leveled compaction caps a level's size at `level_base_size * fanout^(level-1)`.

lcs-level-size-exponential.text: Level size budgets grow as `base_size × fanout^(level-1)`, so with defaults of 10MB base and 10× fanout: L1=10MB, L2=100MB, L3=1GB, etc.

lcs-levels-grow-exponentially.text: Leveled compaction sizes each level as `level_base_size * fanout^(level-1)` with a 10MB default base and 7 max levels, so each level is 10x the previous by default

lcs-max-levels-default-seven-exclusive.text: `_lcs_compact` uses `_max_levels = 7` as an exclusive upper bound when iterating level-N compaction from L1 through L6.

lcs-max-overlap-prioritizes-convergence-.text: The teaching leveled-compaction implementation picks the SSTable with the most next-level overlap to resolve the largest cluster of key-range conflicts in a single compaction round, prioritizing convergence speed over write amplification.

lcs-no-old-file-cleanup.text: Duplicates `compaction-manager-never-deletes-old-files` from the CompactionManager entry — same claim about the same class.

lcs-overlap-selection-is-quadratic.text: During level N compaction, `_lcs_compact` calls `_overlapping` once per SSTable in the level to find the one with maximum overlap, then once more for the winner — making SSTable selection O(n*m) in level sizes.

lcs-picks-max-overlap-sstable.text: For level N→N+1 compaction, the SSTable with the most overlapping neighbors in the next level is chosen — the opposite of LevelDB/RocksDB's least-overlap heuristic, increasing write amplification per compaction.

lcs-picks-most-overlap.text: Duplicates `lcs-picks-max-overlap-sstable` from the CompactionManager entry — same claim about the same code path.

lcs-produces-single-output-sstable.text: Leveled compaction merges all inputs into one SSTable rather than splitting output by size, which means levels above L0 will contain overlapping key ranges after compaction — violating the real LCS invariant that each level has non-overlapping SSTables.

lcs-requires-caller-set-sstable-level.text: For leveled compaction, the caller must set each SSTableReader.level correctly before registration; CompactionManager trusts this attribute without validating it.

lcs-write-amplification-via-cascade-rewr.text: Leveled compaction can rewrite SSTables already existing in the next level when a level overflows, causing write amplification through cascading rewrites across levels.

leaf-chain-correct-single-threaded.text: The `next_sibling` leaf chain is correctly maintained through splits because the WAL logs the right page before the left page (ensuring the pointer target is durable before anything references it) and no concurrent reader can observe intermediate states

leaf-chain-enables-range-scan-cost.text: The leaf sibling chain allows a range scan to descend once to the first matching leaf (h page reads) and then walk horizontally, costing O(h + L) page reads for N results spanning L leaves.

leaf-entry-cost-is-variable.text: Each leaf entry costs `4 + len(key_bytes) + len(value_bytes)` bytes (2B key length + key + 2B value length + value), so maximum keys per page depends on actual data sizes, not just a fixed `max_keys` count.

leaf-entry-format-is-key-len-key-val-len.text: In a B-tree leaf page, each entry is serialized as `key_len(2B) + key + val_len(2B) + val`.

leaf-no-sibling-sentinel.text: _serialize_leaf defaults next_sibling to 0xFFFFFFFF, the sentinel meaning no next leaf.

leaf-no-sibling-sentinel-is-0xffffffff.text: The leaf next_sibling sentinel NO_SIBLING is 0xFFFFFFFF and marks the rightmost leaf.

leaf-nodes-store-all-values.text: Values are stored exclusively in leaf nodes; internal nodes contain only routing keys and child page pointers, making this a B+-tree not a B-tree

leaf-serialized-overhead-is-7-bytes.text: Every leaf page has a fixed 7-byte overhead (3B header via `HEADER_FMT = '>BH'` + 4B `next_sibling` pointer) before any key-value entries, setting the usable capacity to `page_size - 7` bytes.

leaf-sibling-not-blink.text: Leaf `next_sibling` pointers serve range scans only, not Lehman & Yao concurrent-split recovery; internal nodes have no right-links, making this a standard B+ tree, not a B-link tree

leaf-sibling-pointer-present.text: Duplicates `leaf-wire-format-is-header-sibling-entries` and `btree-leaf-sibling-chain` which already describe the leaf sibling pointer field and sentinel.

leaf-split-rewire-costs-one-extra-page-w.text: During a leaf split, rewiring sibling pointers costs one extra page write per split.

leaf-split-updates-sibling-pointers.text: When a leaf splits, the new page inherits the old page's `next_sibling` pointer and the old page's `next_sibling` is updated to point to the new page — two field writes during an operation that already rewrites both pages

leaf-wire-format-is-header-sibling-entri.text: Leaf pages are laid out as `[type:1B][num_keys:2B][next_sibling:4B][entries...]` where each entry is `[key_len:2B][key][val_len:2B][val]`, all big-endian

lehman-yao-needs-high-keys-and-internal-.text: The existing leaf `next_sibling` pointer is necessary but insufficient for Lehman-Yao concurrent access; the algorithm also requires right-links on internal nodes and a high key per node, neither of which this implementation has

lehman-yao-solves-concurrent-split-trave.text: The Lehman-Yao paper addresses concurrency, not range scans; its protocol prevents a searcher from being invalidated mid-traversal by a splitter modifying a node the searcher already passed through.

lehman-yao-uses-right-links-for-latch-co.text: Lehman and Yao's B-tree protocol adds right-links to every node so a searcher can follow a link after a split without acquiring a read lock on the parent, reducing locking to at most one node at a time (latch coupling).

leveldb-and-rocksdb-use-heap-based-mergi.text: LevelDB's MergingIterator and RocksDB's MergingIterator use a heap-based k-way merge iterator.

leveldb-block-alignment-contains-torn-wr.text: LevelDB's block alignment guarantees a torn write falls within a single block, so recovery can seek to the last block boundary instead of scanning the whole file.

leveldb-block-checksum-covers-data-and-t.text: LevelDB block checksums cover the block data plus the type byte but exclude the length framing.

leveldb-block-format-enables-skip-past-c.text: LevelDB's fixed 32KB block format lets a reader skip to the next block boundary after detecting corruption and resume reading, losing only records in the corrupted block.

leveldb-block-overhead-is-negligible-at-.text: LevelDB's original design cites about 0.03% overhead for block headers at 32KB.

leveldb-compaction-installs-new-current-.text: LevelDB compaction creates a new Version with updated file lists and installs it as current_, leaving the old Version alive while readers hold references.

leveldb-current-file-points-to-active-ma.text: LevelDB uses a CURRENT file containing a single line that points to the active MANIFEST, enabling atomic switchover during MANIFEST rotation.

leveldb-current-updates-via-temp-rename.text: LevelDB updates CURRENT by writing the new MANIFEST name to a temp file, fsyncing it, and renaming it over CURRENT, making MANIFEST rotation crash-safe.

leveldb-filemetadata-includes-file-numbe.text: LevelDB's FileMetaData record stores per-file metadata including file number, file size, smallest key, and largest key.

leveldb-fragment-crash-safety.text: About LevelDB's design, not about this codebase; beliefs should be testable claims about the code a developer works in.

leveldb-fsyncs-manifest-before-file-dele.text: LevelDB fsyncs a VersionEdit to the MANIFEST before deleting old SSTable files, providing crash-safe version transitions.

leveldb-log-format-uses-32kb-block-align.text: LevelDB's log format divides the file into fixed-size 32KB blocks, with each record carrying its own checksum, length, and type header.

leveldb-log-fragment-gap-loses-only-inco.text: In LevelDB's log format, a crash between fragments of a multi-block record causes only that incomplete record to be lost, because block-aligned seeking lets recovery resume after the gap.

leveldb-log-fragment-has-per-fragment-cr.text: Each LevelDB log fragment has its own CRC in a 7-byte fragment header of CRC, length, and type.

leveldb-log-fragment-types-full-first-mi.text: LevelDB log fragments carry a type byte with values FULL, FIRST, MIDDLE, and LAST to mark record boundaries across blocks.

leveldb-log-fragments-independently-chec.text: Each fragmented LevelDB log record chunk is independently checksummed.

leveldb-log-records-have-full-first-midd.text: LevelDB's log record `type` field is one of `FULL`, `FIRST`, `MIDDLE`, or `LAST`, allowing a single logical record to span multiple blocks.

leveldb-log-resyncs-to-next-block-after-.text: In LevelDB's block-aligned log format, corruption can be handled by skipping to the next 32KB block boundary and resuming scanning, losing at most about 32KB of data.

leveldb-log-type-field-handles-spanning-.text: LevelDB's record type field uses FIRST, MIDDLE, LAST, and FULL values to handle records that span block boundaries.

leveldb-log-uses-32kb-blocks.text: LevelDB divides its log file into fixed 32 KB (32768-byte) blocks.

leveldb-log-uses-fixed-32kb-blocks.text: LevelDB's log format divides the log file into fixed 32 KB blocks of 32,768 bytes.

leveldb-manifest-is-append-only-metadata.text: LevelDB's MANIFEST is an append-only write-ahead log for metadata, where each state transition is recorded as a VersionEdit.

leveldb-manifest-is-metadata-wal.text: LevelDB's MANIFEST is a second write-ahead log that records VersionEdit metadata changes to the live SSTable file set, separate from the user-data WAL.

leveldb-manifest-logs-version-edits.text: LevelDB records SSTable membership changes as VersionEdit entries appended to the MANIFEST.

leveldb-merge-iterator-filters-by-snapsh.text: LevelDB's merge iterator operates within a snapshot context and surfaces only entries visible at the reader's sequence number.

leveldb-merge-seek-seeks-children-and-re.text: LevelDB's MergingIterator::Seek(target) calls Seek(target) on every child iterator and then rebuilds the heap, costing O(k log k) for k children.

leveldb-merger-find-smallest-largest-lin.text: LevelDB's FindSmallest and FindLargest helpers perform O(n) linear scans over child iterators to find the iterator with the smallest or largest key.

leveldb-merger-rebuilds-heap-on-directio.text: When LevelDB's merge direction changes, it repositions each child iterator and rebuilds the heap from scratch using FindSmallest or FindLargest.

leveldb-merger-tracks-direction-state.text: LevelDB's MergingIterator tracks a kForward/kReverse direction state to support bidirectional iteration via Next, Prev, Seek, and SeekToLast.

leveldb-reader-ref-unref-protects-sstabl.text: LevelDB readers call Ref() on the current Version at the start of a read or iterator and Unref() when finished, and the Version and its SSTable files can be deleted only when the count reaches zero.

leveldb-record-header-checksum-length-ty.text: A LevelDB log record header consists of a 4-byte checksum, a 2-byte length, and a 1-byte type field.

leveldb-uses-current-file-to-find-manife.text: LevelDB uses a CURRENT file containing the filename of the active MANIFEST, read at startup to locate the MANIFEST.

leveldb-version-is-immutable-file-list-w.text: In LevelDB, a Version is an immutable list of SSTable files per level and carries a reference count.

leveldb-version-set-replays-manifest-edi.text: LevelDB's VersionSet reconstructs the current file catalog by replaying VersionEdit records from the MANIFEST, which is event sourcing for SSTable metadata.

leveldb-versionedit-is-metadata-delta.text: LevelDB's VersionEdit is a delta record describing metadata changes such as adding a file to a level or deleting a file from a level.

leveldb-versionset-holds-current-pointer.text: A LevelDB VersionSet holds a current_ pointer to the latest Version.

leveled-compaction-non-overlapping-range.text: In leveled compaction, each level except L0 has non-overlapping key ranges, so min/max key bounds can skip an entire level.

leveled-compaction-one-sstable-per-level.text: Contradicts existing belief `lcs-produces-single-output-sstable` which documents that the implementation merges all inputs into one SSTable, violating the non-overlapping invariant at levels above L0

leveled-compaction-promotes-to-l1.text: After leveled compaction runs on L0 SSTables, the output readers have `level == 1` set by the caller.

leveled-compaction-promotes-to-next-leve.text: After leveled compaction, resulting SSTables are assigned `level = max_level + 1` where `max_level` is the highest level among inputs, establishing the level hierarchy (observable in test assertion at `test_sstable.py:119`).

leveled-high-write-low-space-amplificati.text: Leveled compaction has high write amplification and low space amplification because entries are rewritten repeatedly as they propagate through levels while non-overlapping key ranges within each level bound duplicate versions.

leveled-nonoverlap-bounds-missing-key-pr.text: In leveled compaction with non-overlapping ranges within each level, a missing-key lookup checks at most one SSTable per level, making worst-case cost O(L) in the number of levels.

leveled-reads-check-one-sstable-per-leve.text: With leveled compaction, a point lookup needs to check at most one SSTable per level beyond L0 because key ranges within each level are non-overlapping.

leveled-triggers-on-l0-count.text: Leveled compaction triggers when the L0 SSTable count meets the `l0_compaction_trigger` parameter

linearizable-cas-checks-at-delivery-time.text: `LinearizableRegister.compare_and_set` checks `current == expected` at delivery time in the total order, not at submission time.

linearizable-read-requires-consensus.text: `LinearizableRegister.read()` broadcasts through the TOB consensus layer rather than reading local state, because a node cannot distinguish "I have the latest value" from "I'm partitioned and stale" without majority confirmation.

live-projection-auto-snapshots-every-n-e.text: When snapshot_interval is set to N, LiveProjection auto-saves a snapshot after every N events processed and resets its events-since-snapshot counter.

live-projection-constructor-sets-positio.text: LiveProjection's base Projection initialization sets _position to 0 before any events are processed.

live-projection-exactly-once-via-positio.text: Live projections achieve exactly-once processing semantics through three reinforcing mechanisms: position-guarded deduplication prevents double-processing during overlapping catch-up and subscription, position advances even for events with no registered handler (preventing future re-evaluation), and the catch-up-then-subscribe pattern eliminates gaps between historical replay and live events.

justifications.label: Three independent mechanisms collectively enforce exactly-once without distributed coordination

live-projection-full-replay-on-restart.text: A `LiveProjection` must replay all events from position 0 on initialization because there is no snapshot restore path wired into its construction

live-projection-handlers-registered-afte.text: Handlers registered after events have already flowed do not receive those earlier events because LiveProjection has no replay triggered by handler registration.

live-projection-idempotent-by-position.text: `LiveProjection._on_event` guards against double-processing via `event_id <= _position`, making it safe to overlap `catch_up()` and live subscription without duplicate handler invocations.

live-projection-is-synchronous.text: `LiveProjection` processes events synchronously inside the `append()` call path via the `_subscribers` mechanism, meaning the caller blocks until all live projections have updated

live-projection-no-error-boundary.text: Handler exceptions in `LiveProjection._on_event` propagate through `EventStore.append()` to the caller; the projection's `_position` is not updated, leaving it behind but recoverable via `catch_up()`.

live-projection-no-snapshot-interval.text: `LiveProjection` is never constructed with a `snapshot_interval`, so the automatic snapshot path in `catch_up()` never triggers for live projections

live-projection-no-unsubscribe.text: Once constructed, a `LiveProjection` cannot be unsubscribed from its store; the callback reference persists in `_subscribers` indefinitely with no removal mechanism.

live-projection-position-advances-withou.text: Events with no registered handler still advance `LiveProjection._position`, preventing re-evaluation on subsequent `catch_up()` calls — position tracks last *seen* event, not last *handled* event.

live-projection-processes-events-synchro.text: `LiveProjection` subscribes to `EventStore._subscribers` and processes events synchronously inside `append()`, making the read model immediately consistent.

live-projection-subscribes-before-catchu.text: `LiveProjection.__init__` registers the subscriber before the user calls `catch_up()`, making duplicate processing possible but event loss impossible in the current single-threaded design

live-projection-uses-subscriber-list.text: `LiveProjection` receives automatic updates by registering a callback in `EventStore._subscribers` (a list of `Callable[[Event], None]]`), which is invoked synchronously inside `append()` and `append_batch()`

lmdb-uses-dual-meta-pages-for-atomic-roo.text: LMDB maintains two copies of the root meta page and writes the new root to the inactive meta page before fsync, making the root pointer swap atomic.

load-hint-unconditional-keydir-insert.text: Duplicates existing belief `bitcask-tombstone-handling-asymmetry` which explicitly describes `_load_hint_file` unconditionally inserting entries
