local-writes-self-immunize.text: Both `put` and `delete` call `_record_seen` with the local node's ID, ensuring the originating node drops its own changes when they loop back through the ring

lock-coupling-holds-at-most-two-latches.text: Lock coupling (crabbing) traverses a B-tree holding at most the parent and child latches simultaneously, releasing the parent when the child is safe.

lock-expiry-enables-reacquisition-withou.text: `LockService.acquire` checks `is_expired(current_time)` before rejecting a competing acquire, so a crashed or GC-paused client's lock is automatically reclaimable after TTL without requiring explicit release

lock-release-deletes-entry.text: `LockService.release()` deletes the lock entry entirely when called by the current holder.

locks-block-future-transactions.text: A participant in the `"prepared"` state holds key-level locks (`self.locks[key] = tx_id`) that cause any subsequent transaction touching the same keys to abort with a lock conflict during its own `prepare()`.

log-structured-auto-compact-threshold-de.text: `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py` triggers synchronous auto-compaction inside `put()` when frozen segment count reaches `auto_compact_threshold` (default 5).

log-structured-bitcask-handle-cache-only.text: In `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py`, the `_file_handles` cache is only used during startup recovery (`_scan_segment`), not for serving reads.

log-structured-bitcask-header-includes-c.text: `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py` uses header format `"!III"` containing crc32, key_size, and value_size.

log-structured-bitcask-no-fsync.text: `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py` uses only `flush()` without `os.fsync()` on data writes, unlike `hash-index-storage` which calls `os.fsync` per record when `sync_writes` is enabled

log-structured-compact-closes-active-fil.text: In `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py`, compaction closes `_active_file` during its write phase, making all reads and writes to the active segment impossible until the active file is reopened under a new name at the end of compaction

log-structured-compact-does-not-call-cre.text: In log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py, `compact()` does not call `create_hint_files`; callers must invoke hint generation explicitly.

log-structured-compact-updates-index-and.text: In `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py` compaction, the index is updated and old segment files are deleted in the same phase without a barrier, so a concurrent reader could see an old index entry pointing to a deleted file.

log-structured-compaction-pops-sentinel-.text: During `log-structured-hash-table` compaction, records whose value equals the `TOMBSTONE` sentinel are removed from the `live_entries` dict.

log-structured-crc-bypassed-by-hints.text: Duplicates existing beliefs `bitcask-crc-validated-on-read-only` and `hint-corrupt-worse-than-missing`, which together establish that hint loading skips CRC verification

log-structured-crc-detects-torn-writes-n.text: The CRC check in log-structured hash table recovery detects partially-written (torn) records but cannot recover data that was only in volatile memory.

log-structured-hash-table-never-fsyncs.text: In `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py`, `_write_record` calls only `flush()` and never `os.fsync()`, so writes are not power-loss durable.

log-structured-hint-creation-decoupled.text: The log-structured Bitcask exposes `create_hint_files()` as a standalone operation callable independently of compaction, while the hash-index variant only writes hint files inside `compact()`

log-structured-hint-creation-is-manual.text: In `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py`, hint file creation requires an explicit `create_hint_files()` call rather than being produced automatically as a side-effect of compaction

log-structured-hint-entries-store-only-k.text: `log-structured-hash-table` hint entries store `key_size` and `offset` in an 8-byte header plus key bytes, with no timestamp or file ID.

log-structured-hint-format-lacks-value-s.text: Duplicates existing belief `lsht-hint-no-tombstone-flag` which states the `!II` format has no field to distinguish live records from tombstones

log-structured-hint-format-stores-key-si.text: `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py` uses `HINT_ENTRY_FMT = "!II"`, storing only key size and offset in each hint entry.

log-structured-hint-generation-separate-.text: `log-structured-hash-table`'s `compact()` does not call `create_hint_files()`; hint generation is an explicit separate step.

log-structured-hint-offset-32bit-cap.text: Hint entry format uses `!II` (two `u32` network-order integers), capping segment file offsets at 4 GiB regardless of `max_segment_size` configuration.

log-structured-index-omits-size-and-time.text: The `log-structured-hash-table` Bitcask variant stores only `(filepath, offset)` in its index, omitting record size and timestamp, requiring an extra header parse on every `get()` to discover record boundaries

log-structured-sentinel-is-in-band.text: `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py` uses `TOMBSTONE = b"__BITCASK_TOMBSTONE__"` as an in-band sentinel in the value space; storing those exact bytes as a value causes silent data loss on recovery when the record is misinterpreted as a deletion

log-structured-tombstone-is-sentinel-byt.text: Duplicate of existing `log-structured-sentinel-is-in-band` which already captures the sentinel byte tombstone encoding.

longer-convergence-widens-conflict-windo.text: Analytical consequence derivable from convergence round counts, not a directly testable code claim.

lookup-cost-is-logarithmic-in-total-vnod.text: `get_node` performs a single `bisect.bisect` over `_ring_positions`, so key lookup is O(log(N×V)) regardless of cluster size.

lsht-crc-covers-key-and-value.text: Duplicates existing belief `all-three-implementations-use-payload-only-crc` which already states CRC covers data payloads (key+value), excluding header/framing metadata.

lsht-crc-detects-val-size-corruption-via.text: In `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py`, if a record's on-disk `value_size` is corrupted to 0, the scanner reads only the key bytes and computes a CRC that does not match the stored CRC computed over key plus original value.

lsht-get-no-tombstone-guard.text: `BitcaskStore.get()` in `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py` returns raw payload bytes without checking for the `TOMBSTONE` sentinel, so an index entry pointing to a tombstone record surfaces `b"__BITCASK_TOMBSTONE__"` as a value

lsht-header-orders-crc-before-lengths.text: In `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py`, the record header format `!III` places the CRC32 field before `key_size` and `value_size`.

lsht-hint-no-tombstone-flag.text: The `log-structured-hash-table` hint entry format (`!II` = key_size + offset) has no field to distinguish live records from tombstones, making `_load_hint_file` structurally unable to replicate `_scan_segment`'s deletion logic

lsht-hint-path-surfaces-tombstone-bytes.text: If hint files exist for both a put and a later delete of the same key, `_load_hint_file` adds the tombstone offset and `get()` returns the raw tombstone sentinel bytes because it lacks a tombstone check.

lsht-recovery-path-divergence.text: Duplicates existing belief `bitcask-tombstone-handling-asymmetry` which already captures the divergent behavior between hint-based and scan-based recovery paths

lsht-scan-stops-on-first-crc-failure.text: Duplicates existing belief `corruption-terminates-scan` which states that a corrupted record terminates the current segment scan.

lsht-tombstone-costs-20-value-bytes.text: In `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py`, a tombstone record sets `value_size` to 20 (the sentinel length), costing 20 extra bytes per delete before compaction.

lsht-tombstone-crc-covers-sentinel.text: In `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py`, the CRC for a tombstone record covers the key plus the 20-byte tombstone sentinel.

lsht-tombstone-detection-reads-value.text: In `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py`, tombstone detection during `_scan_segment` requires reading and comparing the full value bytes against the sentinel.

lsht-tombstone-is-real-value.text: Covered by existing belief `log-structured-sentinel-is-in-band`; the structural identity with normal records is the defining characteristic of an in-band sentinel

lsht-tombstone-sentinel-is-bitcask-tombs.text: In `log-structured-hash-table/bitcask.py`, `TOMBSTONE` is defined as the byte-string sentinel `b"__BITCASK_TOMBSTONE__"`.

lsm-and-sstable-have-no-checksums.text: Neither `log-structured-merge-tree/lsm.py` nor `sstable-and-compaction/sstable.py` compute or verify any checksums; a single bit-flip in a length-prefix field causes cascading misframing of all subsequent records

lsm-basic-crud-crosses-flush-boundary.text: `test_basic_crud` crosses a flush boundary mid-test when the third `put` reaches the memtable threshold.

lsm-compact-assumes-unique-sstable-seq.text: `compact` assumes each SSTable has a unique sequence number because the `(key, -seq)` sort is nondeterministic for equal keys if two SSTables share a sequence number.

lsm-compact-crash-leaves-duplicate-sstab.text: A crash after writing the new SSTable but before deleting old SSTables leaves both old and new SSTables on disk; on restart `_load_existing_sstables` loads all of them, causing duplicate keys but preserving correctness via newest-wins reads.

lsm-compact-deletes-old-sstables-after-n.text: `compact` writes the new merged SSTable first, then deletes every old SSTable file from disk.

lsm-compact-does-not-touch-wal.text: LSM compaction does not read or write the WAL, active memtable, or immutable memtables.

lsm-compact-no-atomic-rename.text: The LSM tree's `compact()` method does not use `os.rename` or `os.replace`; grep for atomic rename operations returns zero matches in the LSM module, meaning the compaction output is written directly to its final path with no atomic swap.

lsm-compact-no-snapshot-safety.text: Duplicated by existing `compact-no-concurrency-safety` which already captures that compaction has no protection for concurrent operations

lsm-compact-removes-all-tombstones.text: Covered by existing beliefs `lsm-compact-removes-tombstones-safely` and `lsm-compaction-is-full-merge` together

lsm-compact-removes-tombstones.text: LSMTree.compact() merges all SSTables into one and removes tombstones during the merge.

lsm-compact-removes-tombstones-safely.text: The LSM Tree's `compact()` method removes tombstones because it performs a full merge of all SSTables, guaranteeing no surviving SSTable can contain a superseded live value

lsm-compact-requires-two-sstables.text: `LSMTree.compact` returns immediately without doing work if there are fewer than two SSTables.

lsm-compact-returns-none.text: `LSMTree.compact` returns `None`; all of its effects are side effects on `self._sstables`, `self._seq`, and the filesystem.

lsm-compact-temporarily-doubles-disk-usa.text: Full LSM compaction temporarily requires enough disk space for both the new SSTable and all old SSTables before the old files are deleted.

lsm-compact-unconditionally-removes-tomb.text: `LSMTree.compact()` unconditionally strips tombstones during merge, with no policy control to skip space reclamation.

lsm-compaction-auto-trigger-threshold.text: LSMTree triggers compaction automatically when the number of SSTables reaches _compaction_threshold.

lsm-compaction-blocks-callers.text: `LSMTree.compact()` runs synchronously in the caller's thread, meaning a `put()` or `delete()` that triggers the SSTable count threshold will block until the full k-way merge completes.

lsm-compaction-delete-last-ordering.text: The LSM tree's compaction ordering is delete-last: it writes the new merged SSTable first and removes old SSTables afterward.

lsm-compaction-deletes-without-fsync-bar.text: The LSM tree's `compact()` calls `os.remove(sst.path)` without an explicit `fsync` on the new SSTable or its parent directory beforehand, meaning the new file's data may not be durable when the old file is unlinked

lsm-compaction-duplicates-safe.text: A crash during LSM compaction produces duplicate entries (old and merged SSTables both present) rather than data loss, because newer SSTables take read precedence.

lsm-compaction-has-no-wal-backup.text: Because the LSM tree's WAL is truncated after each memtable flush, SSTable data has no WAL backup if a later compaction deletes old SSTables before the new one is durable.

lsm-compaction-is-full-merge.text: `compact()` merges all SSTables into a single new SSTable (size-tiered, single-level), not incremental or leveled — simpler but with higher space amplification.

lsm-compaction-last-writer-wins.text: Both LSM implementations resolve key conflicts during compaction by keeping only the newest value; older values are unconditionally discarded with no user-defined merge logic

lsm-compaction-output-is-correct.text: LSM compaction produces correct merged output: tombstones are properly purged from the output SSTable, and the k-way merge is forward-only preserving sort order.

justifications.label: merge logic is correct but concurrent access during compaction can corrupt shared mutable state

lsm-compaction-replaces-all.text: Duplicates existing belief `lsm-compaction-is-full-merge` which already captures that compact() merges all SSTables into one

lsm-compaction-safely-reduces-read-ampli.text: LSM compaction correctly reduces read amplification by merging all SSTables into a single output with last-writer-wins dedup: the full-merge strategy eliminates all redundant entries and the newest value always wins during conflict resolution, producing a minimal SSTable set.

justifications.label: Full merge with last-writer-wins dedup produces correct compacted output, gated on the absence of concurrency control allowing readers to see inconsistent state mid-compaction

lsm-compaction-test-3-to-1.text: `test_compaction` asserts exactly 3 SSTables exist before compaction and exactly 1 exists after.

lsm-compaction-threshold-default-4.text: The `LSMTree` constructor defaults `compaction_threshold` to 4, and compaction fires inline during writes when `len(self._sstables) >= self._compaction_threshold`.

lsm-crash-recovery-impossible-without-ma.text: LSM crash recovery is structurally impossible: the set of live SSTable files exists only in memory with no persistent manifest, so a crash permanently loses the SSTable list, and the WAL that could help reconstruct state has no integrity checking to validate its own records during replay.

justifications.label: No manifest means the SSTable list is lost on crash and no WAL integrity check means reconstruction from WAL is unreliable

lsm-crash-recovery-test-masks-missing-fs.text: The LSM test_crash_recovery simulates a crash by reopening the tree without close(), but because it runs in-process the kernel page cache still holds flushed data and masks the missing fsync.

lsm-crash-test-ignores-compaction.text: `test_crash_recovery` in `test_lsm.py` only covers WAL replay for unflushed memtable entries; no test exercises crashes during SSTable compaction, leaving the most dangerous data-loss window (mid-compaction file deletion) untested.

lsm-delete-uses-put-path.text: `delete(key)` writes a tombstone through the same `put` path used for normal writes.

lsm-deletes-use-tombstones-not-memtable-.text: The LSM tree marks deletions with tombstone entries rather than removing keys from the active memtable.

lsm-flat-compaction-always-bottommost.text: `LSMTree.compact()` in `lsm.py` merges all SSTables into one without level hierarchy, making every compaction implicitly a bottommost-level operation where tombstone removal is always safe

lsm-flush-called-by-put-delete-close.text: `LSMTree._flush` is called from `put()` and `delete()` when the memtable size reaches its threshold, and unconditionally from `close()`.

lsm-flush-does-not-register-frozen-memta.text: `_flush` assigns `frozen = self._memtable` but never appends it to `self._immutable_memtables`, relying on synchronous execution to avoid a read visibility gap.

lsm-flush-double-gap.text: Derivable from existing `lsm-wal-truncated-after-sstable-write` (ordering) + `no-directory-fsync-anywhere` (neither directory entry durable) + `lsm-wal-truncate-destroys-immediately` (WAL gone immediately).

lsm-flush-double-loss-window.text: The LSM `_flush()` truncates the WAL after writing an SSTable, but since neither the SSTable write nor the truncation is fsynced, a crash can lose both the WAL source data and the SSTable destination simultaneously — making the data irrecoverable

lsm-flush-freezes-memtable-by-pointer-sw.text: `LSMTree._flush` freezes the current memtable by saving a reference to it and replacing `self._memtable` with a new empty `SortedDict`.

lsm-flush-is-checkpoint.text: In the LSM tree, the memtable flush serves as the checkpoint: it freezes the memtable, writes it to an SSTable, and truncates the WAL.

lsm-flush-no-explicit-error-handling.text: `LSMTree._flush` has no explicit exception handling; I/O errors from writing the SSTable or truncating the WAL propagate to the caller.

lsm-flush-skips-empty-memtable.text: `LSMTree._flush` returns immediately without creating an SSTable when the memtable is empty.

lsm-flush-synchronous-invariant.text: Duplicate of existing `single-threaded-masks-immutable-gap` which already captures that single-threaded execution is what makes the flush-without-immutable-memtable pattern safe

lsm-flush-triggers-compaction-at-thresho.text: `_flush()` triggers `compact()` when the number of SSTables reaches `compaction_threshold` after writing the new SSTable.

lsm-flush-writes-memtable-to-sorted-ssta.text: The LSM-tree flushes a full memtable as a sorted on-disk SSTable with lexicographic key order and a sparse index.

lsm-flush-writes-sstable-before-clearing.text: In log-structured-merge-tree/lsm.py, _flush() writes the SSTable first, then truncates the WAL, then clears the memtable.

lsm-forward-only-iteration.text: SSTable iterators (`scan`, `scan_all`) support only forward iteration; there is no `Prev()` or reverse scan capability, preventing `ORDER BY DESC` or backward cursor pagination

lsm-full-compaction-drops-tombstones.text: The full compaction in `log-structured-merge-tree/lsm.py:compact` merges every SSTable into one and permanently drops tombstones, then deletes the old SSTables from disk.

lsm-get-probes-all-sstables-on-miss.text: `LSMTree.get()` iterates through every SSTable in reverse sequence order and returns only after checking all of them when a key is absent; without bloom filters, missing-key lookups are O(N) in SSTable count

lsm-has-no-checksumming.text: Duplicates existing belief `lsm-and-sstable-have-no-checksums` which already states neither module computes or verifies any checksums.

lsm-heapq-imported-unused.text: `heapq` is imported but never referenced in the code; `compact()` uses list sorting (`sort by (key, -seq)`) instead of a heap-based k-way merge.

lsm-lacks-superversion-and-context-manag.text: The LSM module has zero references to `SuperVersion` or `super_version` and no `__enter__`/`__exit__` definitions.

lsm-large-dataset-test-parameters.text: `test_large_dataset` uses 10,000 keys with `memtable_threshold=500` and `compaction_threshold=10`, exercising automatic compaction.

lsm-load-sstables-assumes-filename-forma.text: `_load_existing_sstables()` assumes SSTable filenames follow the `sst_NNNNNN.sst` format and would crash on a malformed filename.

lsm-memtable-delete-writes-tombstone.text: The LSM tree's delete operation writes a `TOMBSTONE` into the mutable memtable.

lsm-memtable-has-no-bloom-filter.text: Duplicated by existing `bloom-filter-not-integrated` which already captures that the bloom filter is not wired into the LSM tree

lsm-memtable-is-sorteddict.text: The LSM-tree uses `SortedDict` from `sortedcontainers` as its in-memory memtable (`log-structured-merge-tree/lsm.py:8`).

lsm-memtable-swap-is-reference-not-copy.text: `_flush` line 307 `frozen = self._memtable` captures a Python reference to the SortedDict, not a deep copy, so concurrent mutation of the dict after the swap would be unsafe without synchronization

lsm-memtable-threshold-triggers-flush.text: When the number of entries in the active memtable reaches `memtable_threshold`, the memtable is automatically frozen and flushed to a new SSTable on disk

lsm-miss-probes-all-due-to-no-bloom-inte.text: The LSM tree scans every SSTable on negative lookups because the Bloom filter module — which is correctly implemented with textbook-optimal sizing — is never wired into the read path.

justifications.label: A correct but unused module creates a concrete performance gap: O(N) SSTable probes on miss instead of the O(1) expected false-positive rate

lsm-newest-first-read-path.text: `get()` searches memtable, then immutable memtables, then SSTables in reverse-seq order (newest first), returning the first match; this guarantees newer writes shadow older ones without scanning all levels.

lsm-newest-write-wins-across-sstables.text: Covered by existing belief `lsm-newest-first-read-path` (for point lookups) combined with proposed `range-scan-last-writer-wins` (for range scans)

lsm-no-concurrency-control.text: The LSM tree in `lsm.py` has no locking, reference counting, or Version snapshots; `compact()` mutates `self._sstables` in place, so concurrent readers could see inconsistent state or reference deleted SSTables

lsm-no-manifest.text: The LSM tree has no persistent metadata log (MANIFEST); the set of live SSTable files exists only in memory (`self._sstables`) and is not crash-recoverable independently of directory scanning

lsm-no-synchronization.text: `LSMTree` in `lsm.py` has zero locking, atomic swaps, or synchronization primitives; all shared state (`_memtable`, `_sstables`) is mutated in-place without protection

lsm-no-write-counters.text: The LSM-tree engine has no built-in byte or operation counters for writes; all write instrumentation (WAL appends, SSTable flushes, compaction output) must be added from scratch

lsm-range-scan-dict-priority-overrides.text: LSMTree.range_scan merges sources into a key-to-(priority,value) dict with increasing priority so newer memtable or SSTable sources override older values for the same key.

lsm-range-scan-half-open.text: Duplicates `range-scan-half-open-interval` proposed from the more detailed range_scan entry

lsm-range-scan-iterates-sstables-forward.text: `LSMTree.range_scan()` iterates `self._sstables` in forward order at line 280.

lsm-range-scan-materializes-all.text: `lsm.py:range_scan` loads all matching entries from every SSTable and memtable into a dict before returning any results, making first-result latency proportional to total result set size

lsm-range-scan-uses-heap-based-merge.text: The LSM-tree's `range_scan` merges results from the memtable and all SSTables using a heap-based merge (`heapq` import at `lsm.py:5`).

lsm-read-path-correct-across-flushes.text: The LSM read path maintains correctness across memtable flushes by searching newest-first (memtable then SSTables in reverse sequence order) using a reference swap rather than deep copy for the frozen memtable.

justifications.label: The newest-first search order is correct but the flush implementation creates a window where data exists in neither memtable nor SSTable list, causing transient read misses

lsm-replay-blindly-reinserts-wal-pairs.text: The LSM tree's `_replay_wal` iterates over WAL replay and re-inserts every key-value pair into the memtable without consulting old values.

lsm-replay-strips-seq-nums.text: The LSM tree's `replay` method (`lsm.py:28`) returns `List[Tuple[str, bytes]]`, discarding WAL sequence numbers and making gap detection impossible at the LSM layer

lsm-requires-wal-hash-does-not.text: The LSM tree uses a separate WAL (`lsm.py:14-64`) for crash recovery because its memtable is volatile; the hash index writes directly to the append-only data file, which serves as its own recovery log and needs no WAL.

lsm-reversed-source-order-not-reverse-it.text: The only reverse usage in lsm.py is reversed(self._sstables) and reversed(self._immutable_memtables), which reverse source priority order rather than iteration direction within SSTables.

lsm-scan-race-window.text: Duplicated by existing `range-scan-no-concurrency-protection` which already documents the lack of concurrency safety for range scans

lsm-sparse-index-default-16.text: The SSTable sparse index samples every 16th key by default; a point lookup binary-searches the sparse index then linear-scans up to 16 entries within the candidate block.

lsm-sstable-flush-has-no-fsync.text: Covered by existing `fsync-used-only-for-appends` (fsync never used for SSTable creation) and `lsm-compaction-deletes-without-fsync-barrier`

lsm-sstable-scan-bounded-by-next-index-o.text: In lsm.py, a block scan is bounded by the next sparse-index offset, or by the footer start when the selected block is the last one.

lsm-sstable-uses-bisect-right-to-select-.text: The lsm.py SSTable point lookup uses bisect.bisect_right(keys, key) - 1 on sparse-index keys to choose the candidate block.

lsm-sstable-write-no-fsync.text: The LSM tree's `SSTable.write()` closes the SSTable file without calling `fsync()`, so the file contents may not be durable.

lsm-sstables-tracked-newest-last-by-seq.text: `self._sstables` tracks SSTables sorted by sequence number so that newer SSTables appear last in the list.

lsm-sstables-unprotected-mutation.text: `LSMTree._sstables` is mutated by both `_flush()` (append) and `compact()` (full replacement) with no synchronization, versioning, or ref counting, making concurrent reads unsafe if threading or async is added

lsm-tests-single-threaded-only.text: The LSM test suite (`test_lsm.py`) runs all operations sequentially with no concurrency, so race conditions between `_flush()`, `compact()`, and `range_scan()` are never exercised

lsm-tests-tune-thresholds-for-control.text: LSM tests set `memtable_threshold` low (2–3) to force predictable flushes and `compaction_threshold` high (100) to suppress automatic compaction.

lsm-tests-use-temp-directories.text: Every LSM test creates its own `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()` via a context manager, giving each test a clean filesystem.

lsm-tombstone-gc-not-applicable-to-crdts.text: Covered by combination of existing beliefs `distributed-tombstone-removal-needs-replication-convergence` and `lsm-compact-removes-tombstones-safely`

lsm-tombstone-is-empty-bytes.text: Deletion is represented as `TOMBSTONE = b""` (empty bytes), which means empty-byte-string values and deleted keys are indistinguishable at the storage layer.

lsm-tree-has-no-level-concept.text: `LSMTree` in lsm.py maintains a flat list of SSTables ordered by sequence number with no level assignment; compaction merges all files into one rather than promoting between levels

lsm-truncate-before-sstable-sync.text: Duplicates existing belief `lsm-flush-double-loss-window` which captures the same crash scenario where both WAL and SSTable data can be lost

lsm-two-merge-strategies.text: Compaction uses `heapq`-based k-way merge with `prev_key` deduplication (lsm.py ~line 323), while `range_scan` uses a dict-based materialize-everything approach (lines 275–298) — two fundamentally different merge strategies in the same codebase

lsm-uses-sortedcontainers.text: The LSM memtable uses `sortedcontainers.SortedDict` — the only external dependency across the four storage engine modules examined so far.

lsm-wal-append-before-memtable-mutation.text: `LSMTree.put` and `LSMTree.delete` call `WAL.append` before modifying the in-memory memtable.

lsm-wal-append-flushes-without-fsync.text: `WAL.append` calls `flush()` after writing each record but never calls `os.fsync()`.

lsm-wal-before-memtable.text: Every `put()` and `delete()` writes to the WAL before inserting into the memtable, ensuring no acknowledged write is lost on crash.

lsm-wal-covers-data-not-metadata.text: Duplicates existing belief `wal-protects-data-not-metadata` and overlaps with `lsm-no-manifest`.

lsm-wal-crash-tolerant-replay.text: LSM WAL `replay()` silently discards any trailing partial record by checking remaining bytes at every parse step, making it tolerant of process crashes during `append()`

lsm-wal-entry-size.text: Each LSM WAL entry is exactly `8 + len(key_utf8) + len(value)` bytes: two 4-byte big-endian length headers plus the raw payloads, with no checksum or operation-type field

lsm-wal-has-no-checksums.text: The LSM tree's WAL (`lsm.py:13-63`) uses length-prefixed records with no CRC, relying solely on short-read detection for crash recovery; distinct from the separate `lsm-wal-has-no-fsync` issue

lsm-wal-has-no-commit-markers.text: The LSM WAL (`lsm.py:13-65`) appends bare key-value pairs with no commit or transaction boundaries, safe only because structural changes (compaction, SSTable creation) use atomic file operations outside the WAL

lsm-wal-has-no-fsync.text: The WAL class in `log-structured-merge-tree/lsm.py` calls `flush()` but never `os.fsync()`, making it strictly weaker than the standalone WAL which offers configurable sync modes

lsm-wal-has-no-integrity-check.text: The WAL in `log-structured-merge-tree/lsm.py` uses only length-prefix framing with no CRC or checksum; a single bit flip in the length field causes silent data corruption or misaligned reads

lsm-wal-lacks-fsync.text: The LSM tree's WAL append calls only self._fd.flush() and never os.fsync(), so it is not crash-safe.

lsm-wal-limits-recovery-to-unflushed-wri.text: Duplicates `lsm-wal-truncated-after-sstable-write` (which implies only unflushed data needs recovery)

lsm-wal-no-checksums.text: The LSM WAL format has no checksums or magic bytes; it can detect truncation (incomplete length-prefixed records) but not corruption of existing bytes

lsm-wal-no-crc.text: The LSM tree's WAL (`lsm.py:14-53`) uses only length-prefixed framing with no checksum, making it unable to distinguish corruption from valid data unless a length field causes an out-of-bounds read

lsm-wal-provides-crash-recovery.text: The LSM WAL replays on construction to recover unflushed memtable state, providing crash recovery for in-flight writes.

justifications.label: WAL replay recovers state only if the WAL content is intact; without any checksum, a single bit flip produces silently corrupted recovery data rather than a detectable error

lsm-wal-record-format-be-uint32-lengths.text: The LSM WAL record format uses a 4-byte big-endian unsigned integer key length, UTF-8 key bytes, a 4-byte big-endian unsigned integer value length, and value bytes.

lsm-wal-records-have-four-byte-crc32-pre.text: The LSM tree WAL adds a 4-byte CRC32 prefix per record, and replay stops on CRC mismatch.

lsm-wal-replay-is-side-effect-free.text: `WAL.replay` does not modify the WAL file or in-memory memtable; it returns entries for the caller to insert.

lsm-wal-replay-loads-entire-file.text: `WAL.replay` reads the entire WAL file into memory as a single bytes object before deserializing entries.

lsm-wal-replay-recovers-only-unflushed-w.text: The LSM-tree's WAL replay only needs to recover entries written since the last memtable flush; data already flushed to SSTables is durable by construction.

lsm-wal-replay-returns-raw-bytes-includi.text: `WAL.replay` returns raw value bytes for every entry, including tombstones represented as an empty byte string, without distinguishing puts from deletes.

lsm-wal-replays-on-reopen.text: Constructing a new `LSMTree` on an existing directory replays the WAL to recover unflushed memtable state; this is validated by the crash recovery test which skips `close()` and reopens

lsm-wal-strictly-weaker-than-standalone-.text: The LSM tree's built-in WAL provides strictly weaker guarantees than the standalone WAL module along two independent axes: it has no CRC or checksum for integrity (vs per-record CRC32 in the standalone WAL), and its truncation zeroes the entire file instantly via wb mode (vs careful record-by-record rewriting), meaning corruption goes undetected and truncation is all-or-nothing rather than surgical.

justifications.label: Point-by-point comparison reveals the LSM WAL is weaker in both integrity checking and truncation safety

lsm-wal-truncate-destroys-immediately.text: The LSM tree's `WAL.truncate()` opens the file with `"wb"` mode which zeroes all content instantly, with no intermediate durable state to recover from if a crash occurs before the file is reopened for appending

lsm-wal-truncate-invoked-without-sequenc.text: The LSM tree calls `self._wal.truncate()` with no sequence argument at line 314, unlike the standalone WAL's `truncate(up_to_seq)` signature.

lsm-wal-truncate-is-full-wipe.text: Duplicated by existing `lsm-wal-truncate-destroys-immediately` and `lsm-wal-truncate-no-arg` which together capture that the LSM WAL truncation unconditionally wipes the file with no arguments

lsm-wal-truncate-no-arg.text: The LSM tree at `lsm.py:314` calls `self._wal.truncate()` with no sequence argument, indicating it uses a different WAL interface than the standalone `write-ahead-log/wal.py` module

lsm-wal-truncate-no-error-recovery.text: If any `open()` or `close()` call within `WAL.truncate()` fails, the exception propagates uncaught and can leave `self._fd` holding a closed handle, breaking subsequent `append()` calls

lsm-wal-truncate-no-fsync-replay-window.text: The LSM tree's WAL `truncate` method truncates the WAL without fsyncing the truncation, creating a window where a crash can replay already-applied entries.

lsm-wal-truncate-nonatomic-handle-swap.text: `WAL.truncate` is not atomic: a crash between opening the file in write-binary mode and reopening it in append-binary mode leaves an empty WAL with no open append handle.

lsm-wal-truncate-not-atomic.text: Covered by `lsm-wal-truncate-destroys-immediately` (wb mode zeroes content with no intermediate durable state) and `lsm-wal-truncate-wb-then-ab` (the two-phase reopen pattern)

lsm-wal-truncate-reopens-append-mode.text: `WAL.truncate()` closes the current descriptor, reopens the file with `"wb"` to truncate it, closes that descriptor, and reopens the file with `"ab"` for future appends.

lsm-wal-truncate-wb-then-ab.text: `WAL.truncate()` uses a two-open sequence — open in `"wb"` mode to truncate the file, then reopen in `"ab"` mode for appending — because `"wb"` positions the cursor at offset 0 which is unsafe for a WAL

lsm-wal-truncated-after-sstable-write.text: The WAL is truncated only after a successful SSTable write; if a crash occurs between SSTable.write and WAL.truncate, replay harmlessly re-inserts into the memtable (idempotent because it's a dict).

lsm-wal-truncation-is-total.text: Covered by existing beliefs `lsm-wal-truncate-no-arg` (takes no argument) and `lsm-wal-truncate-destroys-immediately` (erases immediately), which together establish total truncation semantics.

lsm-wal-uses-bare-length-prefixed-writes.text: The LSM WAL writes records as bare length-prefixed key-value pairs with no tags or type information.

lww-auto-increments-timestamp.text: Sequential `LWWRegister.set()` calls without explicit timestamps produce monotonically increasing timestamps (auto-incremented), so ordering is preserved even without caller-supplied clocks.

lww-register-auto-increments-internal-cl.text: `LWWRegister.set` uses an internal auto-incrementing `_clock` so callers do not need to supply timestamps manually.

lww-register-tiebreaks-on-replica-id.text: When two `LWWRegister` writes have identical timestamps, the one with the lexicographically higher `replica_id` wins, making conflict resolution deterministic but arbitrary

lww-tiebreak-by-replica-id.text: Duplicates existing belief `lww-tiebreak-is-deterministic` which already captures that `LWWRegister.merge` uses `(timestamp, writer_id)` tuple comparison for total ordering.

lww-tiebreak-is-deterministic.text: `LWWRegister.merge` uses `(timestamp, writer_id)` tuple comparison, making conflict resolution a total order with no ambiguity since replica IDs are unique

macos-fsync-incomplete-without-fullfsync.text: On macOS/Darwin, `os.fsync()` does not guarantee flushing the disk write cache to stable storage; only `fcntl(fd, F_FULLFSYNC)` provides that guarantee, meaning all 13 fsync sites in the codebase may provide no power-loss durability on the development platform

macos-fsync-not-durable.text: On the development platform (Darwin/APFS), `os.fsync()` may not flush the disk write cache; true durability requires `fcntl(fd, F_FULLFSYNC)`, which is never used at any of the 13 fsync call sites in the codebase.

macos-fsync-not-durable-without-fullfsyn.text: On macOS (the development platform), `os.fsync()` may not flush the disk's hardware write cache; true power-loss durability requires `fcntl(fd, F_FULLFSYNC)` which is never used in the codebase.

macos-fsync-weaker-than-implied.text: The codebase uses `os.fsync()` exclusively, which on macOS/APFS does not flush the disk write cache; true durability requires `fcntl(fd, F_FULLFSYNC)` which is never used anywhere

manifest-append-is-compaction-commit-poi.text: In LevelDB, appending a checksummed VersionEdit record to the MANIFEST is the durable commit point for a compaction, with earlier work tentative and later work cleanup.

manifest-write-is-atomic-compaction-comm.text: In a crash-safe compaction protocol, atomically writing and fsyncing a manifest after fsyncing new files is the commit point before old files may be deleted.

map-side-join-cartesian-on-duplicates.text: When multiple records share the same join key value, all three strategies produce the cartesian product of the matching left and right groups

map-side-join-conflict-prefix.text: When left and right datasets share a non-key field name, `_merge_records` disambiguates with `left_` and `right_` prefixes; this convention applies in all join types including `None`-fill paths for left joins

map-side-join-key-appears-once-in-output.text: `_merge_records` includes the join key exactly once in merged output by taking the left record's key and excluding both source key fields.

map-side-join-missing-key-skip.text: Records missing the join key are silently dropped and counted in `stats["skipped_records"]` rather than raising exceptions, across all three join strategies

map-side-join-no-real-parallelism.text: Mapper parallelism is simulated via round-robin chunking and `_mapper_id` tagging on output records; no threads or processes are used

map-side-join-test-large-dataset-seeded-.text: `test_large_dataset` seeds `random` with 42 and expects exactly 2000 matches from a 1000-by-2000 join.

map-side-join-tests-cover-edge-case-matr.text: The map-side join test suite includes separate tests for inner and left joins, one-to-many, many-to-many, empty datasets, missing keys, field collisions, and sorted versus unsorted input.

map-side-join-three-strategies.text: The module implements exactly three join strategies (broadcast hash, partitioned hash, sort-merge) that all produce identical inner-join results when verified by `compare_join_strategies`

map-side-joins-track-mapper-id-on-output.text: All three map-side join strategies attach a `_mapper_id` field to each output record, enabling verification that partitions/mappers operated independently

mapreduce-combiner-does-not-eliminate-ho.text: The MapReduce combiner reduces data volume before shuffle but does not eliminate the single-reducer bottleneck for a hot key.

mapreduce-combiner-same-signature-as-red.text: The optional combiner in MapReduceJob has the same signature as the reducer.

mapreduce-combiner-transparent.text: Applying a combiner never changes final results; it only reduces intermediate record volume — the combiner must be semantically invisible

mapreduce-input-split-depends-on-num-map.text: MapReduce input splitting in `_split_input` depends on `num_mappers`, so changing worker count changes which records land together.

mapreduce-input-split-preserves-record-c.text: `_split_input` uses integer division with remainder distribution so the sum of chunk lengths equals the input length.

mapreduce-mapper-contract.text: MapReduceJob mapper has contract `(key, value) -> list[(key, value)]`, taking one input record and emitting zero or more intermediate key-value pairs.

mapreduce-materializes-at-phase-boundari.text: MapReduce in `mapreduce.py` writes intermediate data to JSON partition files between map and reduce phases, creating a full materialization barrier that prevents streaming from mapper to reducer

mapreduce-pipeline-feeds-stage-output-to.text: `MapReducePipeline.run()` feeds the output of stage N into the input of stage N+1 and collects each stage's `JobStats` in `_stage_stats`.

mapreduce-reducer-contract.text: MapReduceJob reducer has contract `(key, list[values]) -> list[(key, value)]`, taking a key and all values for that key.

mapreduce-results-deterministic.text: `MapReduceJob.run()` produces identical output regardless of `num_mappers`/`num_reducers` configuration for the same input data — the shuffle/partition step is deterministic

mapreduce-run-accepts-filepath.text: `MapReduceJob.run()` accepts either a list of `(key, value)` tuples or a file path string as input, with the file path handled transparently

mapreduce-stats-tracks-records.text: `job.stats` tracks `map_input_records`, `map_output_records`, `reduce_output_records`, worker counts, and elapsed time after each run

mapreduce-strict-mode-default.text: `MapReduceJob` defaults to strict mode where mapper/reducer exceptions propagate to the caller; `fault_tolerant=True` must be explicitly set to enable silent error skipping

mapreduce-string-input-keyed-by-line-num.text: When `input_data` is a string, `MapReduceJob.run()` treats it as a file path and keys each line by its 1-indexed line number.

mapreduce-temp-directory-cleaned-in-fina.text: `MapReduceJob.run()` removes the temp directory in a `finally` block even when mapper or reducer exceptions occur.

mapreduce-test-file-input-unlinks-in-fin.text: `test_file_input` uses `tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False)` and explicitly calls `os.unlink` in a `finally` block for cleanup.

mapreduce-test-multi-worker-loops-four-c.text: `test_multi_worker_consistency` manually loops over four different `(num_mappers, num_reducers)` configurations.

mapreduce-test-statistics-hardcodes-corp.text: `test_statistics` hardcodes expected counts of 3 input records, 11 intermediate records, and 8 output records for the fox/dog corpus.

mapreduce-tests-are-fixture-free.text: Each test in the MapReduce test module constructs its own `MapReduceJob` using inline mapper/reducer functions, with no shared state between tests.

mapreduce-tests-use-manual-runner.text: The test module's `if __name__ == '__main__'` block implements a minimal runner that iterates over test functions, prints PASS/FAIL, and exits with status.

materialization-barriers-span-storage-an.text: Unbounded in-memory materialization is a cross-cutting concern from storage through batch processing: storage operations (LSM range scans, compaction, SSTable index rebuilds) materialize entire datasets, and pipeline stages (Count) silently accumulate all input before producing output, meaning the materialization problem exists at every layer of the data processing stack.

justifications.label: Both storage reads and batch processing stages have unbounded materialization points

materialized-view-refresh-advances-posit.text: `MaterializedView.refresh()` reads events, applies them, and advances `self._position` at the end.

max-belief-network-depth-reduced-from-7-.text: After two rounds of belief-driven fixes, the maximum belief network depth was reduced from 7 to 4.

max-key-or-value-size-is-65535-bytes.text: Key side covered by existing belief `key-length-cap-uint16`; value side uses the same uint16 length prefix but page size is the practical limit.

max-keys-prevents-overflow.text: The `max_keys_per_page` parameter bounds entries per node so that serialized output fits within `page_size`, with splits triggered before the limit is exceeded

maybe-rotate-assumes-append-mode.text: `_maybe_rotate` assumes `self._fd` is opened in append-binary mode, because `tell()` only reflects true file size under that mode.

maybe-rotate-noops-when-fd-none.text: `_maybe_rotate` returns without action if `self._fd` is `None`, such as after `close()` or during `truncate()`.

maybe-rotate-propagates-errors.text: `_maybe_rotate` has no explicit error handling; exceptions from `tell()` or `_rotate()` propagate to the caller.

maybe-rotate-requires-lock.text: `_maybe_rotate` must be called under `self._lock` but does not acquire or assert the lock itself; all three call sites (`append`, `append_batch`, `checkpoint`) satisfy this obligation.

membership-correctness-masks-hint-data-l.text: The gossip membership lifecycle correctly detects and removes crashed hint-holding nodes, but this membership-layer correctness masks data-layer failure: hints stored on the crashed node are permanently lost with no recovery mechanism or error indication, and the cluster reports the failure as handled because the membership event was processed successfully.

justifications.label: Correct membership lifecycle handling creates false confidence that the failure was fully handled when data was silently lost

membership-detection-unreliable-in-accur.text: The membership subsystem is unreliable at two independent levels that interact destructively: failure detection is both the single correctness bottleneck AND permanently miscalibrated (no arrival-rate history for adaptive thresholds), while membership and data convergence operate at fundamentally different rates (O(log N) membership gossip vs O(N) data propagation in ring topology), meaning incorrect liveness decisions propagate through membership faster than data can adjust to them.

justifications.label: Miscalibrated detection decisions propagate at O(log N) while data convergence lags at O(N), so the system acts on stale liveness information with compounding effect.

memtable-threshold-bounds-recovery.text: The `memtable_threshold` parameter (`lsm.py:202`) directly caps the maximum number of WAL entries that must be replayed on crash recovery, because the WAL is truncated on every flush.

merge-does-not-delete-inputs.text: `merge_sstables` never deletes or modifies input SSTable files; cleanup is the caller's responsibility, and the current `CompactionManager` callers also do not delete old files from disk.

merge-empty-inputs-produce-empty-output.text: If `readers` is empty, `merge_sstables` produces an empty output SSTable.

merge-heap-maintains-one-entry-per-sourc.text: During `merge_sstables`, the min-heap contains at most one entry per source SSTable.

merge-mutates-self-and-returns-self.text: Every CRDT `merge()` method mutates the receiver in place and returns `self`, enabling chaining but meaning callers must `deepcopy()` before merging if the original state must be preserved

merge-no-atomic-write.text: `merge_sstables` writes directly to `output_path` with no temp-file-and-rename pattern, so a crash mid-merge leaves a corrupt partial file at the target path.

merge-output-sorted-by-key.text: The merged output SSTable contains exactly one entry per unique key and is sorted by key.

merge-preserves-tombstones-by-default.text: `merge_sstables` writes tombstones (`value=None`) to the output unless `remove_tombstones=True` is explicitly passed, and no current call site in `CompactionManager` enables removal.

merge-produces-single-file.text: Duplicate of existing `lcs-produces-single-output-sstable` which already states merge produces one SSTable without size-based splitting

merge-returns-reader-on-output.text: `merge_sstables` returns an `SSTableReader` opened on the newly written output SSTable.

merge-sstables-accepts-remove-tombstones.text: `merge_sstables` accepts a `remove_tombstones` boolean parameter that optionally drops tombstone entries during merge.

merge-sstables-has-no-max-file-size-para.text: `merge_sstables` has no `max_file_size` parameter or callback for splitting output into multiple files.

merge-sstables-tombstone-flag-is-caller-.text: `merge_sstables()` accepts a `remove_tombstones` boolean from the caller rather than computing safety from level metadata, so correctness depends entirely on the caller passing the right value

merge-sstables-tombstone-removal-optiona.text: `merge_sstables()` strips tombstones only when called with `remove_tombstones=True`; by default tombstones survive the merge.

merge-sstables-uses-heap-k-way-merge.text: The `merge_sstables` function uses a heap to pick the entry with the smallest key during k-way merge.

merge-sstables-uses-min-heap-negative-ti.text: `merge_sstables` uses a min-heap keyed by `(key, -timestamp, source_index, entry, iterator)` so the newest entry for a duplicate key is popped first.

merge-time-complexity-n-log-k.text: `merge_sstables` performs a k-way merge in O(N log K) time, where N is total entries and K is the number of input SSTables.

merge-tombstone-removal-only-safe-withou.text: Passing `remove_tombstones=True` is only safe when no older SSTables reference the same keys; otherwise dropping a tombstone can resurrect deleted data.

merkle-diff-asymmetric-leaf-counts.text: Two trees with different `_leaf_count` but the same `_padded_size` can be diffed; positions where one tree has data and the other has `EMPTY_HASH` padding are reported as diffs

merkle-diff-enables-efficient-sync.text: `MerkleTree.diff` compares two trees in O(log n) by short-circuiting at matching subtree hashes, providing the divergence-detection layer that would feed `_receive_replica` with only changed keys rather than a full key scan

merkle-diff-enables-targeted-key-range-r.text: Merkle tree diffs produce sorted leaf indices that map directly to key ranges when the tree is built with key-sorted input, enabling anti-entropy repair that transfers only divergent key ranges rather than full dataset comparisons.

justifications.label: Sorted key input + sorted index output = direct mapping from diff results to key ranges needing repair

merkle-diff-filters-padding.text: `diff()` excludes padding indices beyond `max(self._leaf_count, other._leaf_count)`, using `max` (not `min`) so positions where one tree has data and the other has `EMPTY_HASH` padding are still reported as diffs

merkle-diff-is-pure.text: `diff()` and `_diff_recursive` are read-only — they mutate neither tree, allocate only a local result list, and produce no side effects

merkle-diff-leaf-result-index-is-relativ.text: In `_diff_recursive`, a differing leaf appends `idx - leaf_start` to the result, mapping the array index back to the original data index.

merkle-diff-order-is-ascending.text: Differing leaf indices returned by `diff()` are in ascending order as a consequence of left-to-right DFS traversal in `_diff_recursive`

merkle-diff-prunes-matching-subtrees.text: `MerkleTree._diff_recursive()` returns immediately when subtree hashes match, making the diff cost proportional to the number of divergent keys rather than total tree size — the logarithmic efficiency that makes anti-entropy practical.

merkle-diff-requires-same-padded-size.text: `MerkleTree.diff` raises `ValueError` if the two trees have different `_padded_size`, so both trees must round to the same power of 2.

merkle-diff-returns-leaf-indices.text: `MerkleTree.diff()` returns a list of integer leaf indices where the two trees diverge, not subtree nodes or hash pairs

merkle-diff-returns-leaf-indices-not-dat.text: `MerkleTree.diff` returns a list of leaf indices where the trees disagree, not the differing data values.

merkle-empty-tree-has-zero-leaf-count.text: Constructing MerkleTree() with no data blocks produces a tree with leaf_count == 0.

merkle-get-proof-negative-index-rejected.text: `MerkleTree.get_proof` explicitly rejects negative indices rather than using Python-style negative indexing.

merkle-get-proof-rejects-padding-indices.text: `get_proof` bounds-checks against `_leaf_count` (real leaves), not `_padded_size`, so proofs cannot be generated for padding slots even though they have valid hashes in the backing array

merkle-hashes-over-hex-not-bytes.text: Internal node hashes are computed over concatenated 64-char hex digest strings (128 ASCII bytes) rather than raw 32-byte SHA-256 digests, resulting in 4x more data per hash input.

merkle-internal-nodes-hash-hex-concatena.text: Duplicate of existing `merkle-hashes-over-hex-not-bytes` which already captures that internal nodes hash concatenated hex digest strings rather than raw bytes

merkle-proof-direction-is-sibling-positi.text: The `direction` field in each proof sibling tuple indicates where the **sibling** sits (left or right), not the current node — this controls hash concatenation order during verification

merkle-proof-four-leaf-sibling-count-two.text: In a 4-leaf Merkle tree, a proof for a leaf contains exactly 2 sibling hashes.

merkle-proof-is-snapshot.text: Merkle proofs are point-in-time snapshots; a proof generated before `update_leaf` will fail verification against the new root hash, and nothing invalidates the stale proof in-place

merkle-proof-length-equals-height.text: A proof for a tree with `_padded_size = 2^h` contains exactly `h` sibling entries, one per tree level excluding the root

merkle-proof-requires-collision-resistan.text: Merkle inclusion proofs are only secure if the hash function is collision-resistant, because a collision would let a modified data block produce the same proof hash.

merkle-proof-sibling-count-is-log-n.text: Duplicate of `merkle-proof-length-equals-height` — same claim expressed differently (log₂(n) siblings vs h sibling entries); the height-based framing is more precise for non-power-of-2 cases

merkle-proof-sibling-order-bottom-up.text: `get_proof` returns siblings ordered from leaf level to root level (bottom-up), and `verify_proof` consumes them in that same order

merkle-proof-size-is-log-n.text: A Merkle proof contains exactly `height` sibling hashes where height = log2(next_power_of_2(leaf_count)), making both proof size and verification cost O(log N).

merkle-tree-array-indexing.text: The tree uses 0-indexed implicit array layout where children of node `i` are at `2i+1` and `2i+2`, and leaves start at index `padded_size - 1`

merkle-tree-hashes-raw-bytes.text: The Merkle tree implementation avoids serialization canonicalization entirely by accepting caller-provided `bytes` and hashing them directly via `hashlib.sha256(data)`, making it immune to the JSON encoding ambiguity that affects the PBFT digest.

merkle-tree-height-formula.text: A `MerkleTree` with 4 leaves has `height == 2`, indicating height counts internal levels (log₂ of padded leaf count)

merkle-tree-supports-non-power-of-two.text: The implementation handles non-power-of-2 leaf counts (tested with 1 and 3 leaves) via internal padding to the next power of 2 using `EMPTY_HASH`

merkle-tree-uses-sha256-for-cross-replic.text: The Merkle tree uses SHA-256 (`merkle_tree.py:11`) for tamper-evident cross-replica verification via `verify_proof`, while all storage engines use CRC32 — reflecting the split between accidental-corruption detection on trusted local disk and adversarial-integrity across trust boundaries

merkle-update-leaf-is-logarithmic.text: MerkleTree.update_leaf(index, new_data) mutates one leaf and walks up to the root recomputing hashes in O(log N) time.

merkle-update-leaf-rehashes-path-to-root.text: MerkleTree.update_leaf() rehashes from the changed leaf up to the root, costing O(log N) per update to keep the tree current.

merkle-verification-hashes-data-to-leaf-.text: `verify_proof` first hashes the raw data with SHA-256 and rejects the proof if the result does not equal `proof.leaf_hash`.

merkle-verify-proof-is-iterative.text: `verify_proof` recomputes the root by iterating over the proof siblings and hashing upward, with no recursion or tree search.

merkle-verify-proof-is-static-method.text: `verify_proof` is a static method that takes raw data and a `MerkleProof` and requires no `MerkleTree` instance.

meta-page-fixed-20-byte-payload.text: The metadata payload is exactly 20 bytes (5 big-endian uint32s packed as `'>5I'`), zero-padded to `page_size`; the format requires `page_size >= 20` but this is not enforced.

meta-page-is-page-zero.text: The B-tree metadata (root, height, total_keys, next_free, free_head) is always stored at file offset 0 in page 0, which is reserved as the superblock and occupies exactly `page_size` bytes.

miss-emission-requires-watermark-expirat.text: Outer-join miss results are emitted only by _expire_events after the watermark advances past the window boundary; unmatched events remain buffered until expiration.

missing-hint-safe-fallback.text: Duplicates existing beliefs `bitcask-hint-files-skip-scan` and `hint-corrupt-worse-than-missing` (which explicitly states a missing hint triggers a CRC-checked full scan)

mmap-returns-page-aligned-by-definition.text: General OS-level invariant, not specific to this codebase

more-vnodes-monotonically-improves-balan.text: The test `test_vnode_count_affects_balance` asserts that imbalance at 500 vnodes is strictly less than at 1 vnode, and the statistical model (variance ∝ 1/V) guarantees monotonic improvement.

mr-combiner-is-map-side-only.text: The combiner runs inside `_run_mapper` on each mapper's output for a single partition independently; it never sees data from other mappers or other partitions.

mr-fault-tolerant-silently-drops.text: When `fault_tolerant=True`, mapper and reducer exceptions are caught and silently skipped with no logging or error reporting, producing partial results without any indication of data loss.

mr-groupby-requires-presort.text: `_run_reducer` sorts all intermediate pairs by key before calling `itertools.groupby`, which is required because `groupby` only groups consecutive elements with the same key.

mr-hash-partitions-keys.text: MapReduceJob assigns intermediate keys to reducer partitions using `hash(key) % num_reducers`, ensuring all values for a given key reach the same reducer.

metadata.example:
partition = hash(key) % num_reducers
partitions[partition].append((key, value))

mr-intermediate-data-uses-json-files.text: Intermediate shuffle data is serialized as JSON files in a temp directory with naming convention `map-{mapper_id}-part-{partition}.json`.

multi-leader-all-converged-requires-iden.text: MultiLeaderCluster.all_converged() returns true only when every node has the same key set and matching (value, timestamp, is_tombstone) tuples for every key.

multi-leader-cluster-constructor-options.text: MultiLeaderCluster accepts a list of node IDs plus optional topology, strategy, and merge_fn parameters, with topology defaulting to fully connected.

multi-leader-conflict-log-records-strate.text: Conflicts are recorded in `conflict_log` with metadata including the key and the `ConflictStrategy` enum value that resolved them.

multi-leader-conflict-record-captures-bo.text: `ConflictRecord` stores both `local_value` and `remote_value` along with the key and resolution strategy, providing a complete audit trail for every conflict resolution.

multi-leader-convergence-reliable-across.text: Multi-leader replication achieves reliable eventual convergence regardless of network topology: sync uses a safe collect-then-distribute pattern with idempotent merge and monotonically advancing timestamps, and topology choice affects only the duration of observable divergence (linear in node count for ring, single round for all-to-all), not the final converged state.

justifications.label: A depth-1 convergence safety conclusion combined with a depth-2 topology-independence conclusion form a strong positive claim, gated on the silent acceptance of merge_fn=None that crashes at resolution time

multi-leader-convergence-skips-origin.text: `all_converged()` compares `(value, timestamp, is_tombstone)` but intentionally ignores `origin_node_id` (tuple index 2), since different arrival orders can record different origins for the same resolved state

multi-leader-custom-merge-accepts-none-m.text: MultiLeaderCluster accepts strategy CUSTOM_MERGE with merge_fn=None at construction time, deferring the error until the first conflict occurs.

multi-leader-custom-merge-idempotent-acr.text: Custom merge functions are applied once per conflict; repeated sync rounds on already-converged values must not re-trigger the merge, preventing bugs like counters doubling on every sync cycle.

multi-leader-custom-merge-new-timestamp.text: Custom merge resolution creates a new timestamp (`max(local_ts, remote_ts) + 1`) and canonical origin so the merged result supersedes both conflicting inputs in any future LWW comparison

metadata.example:
merged = merge_fn(key, display_local, display_remote, local_ts, remote_ts)
new_ts = max(local_ts, remote_ts) + 1
canonical_origin = max(local_origin, remote_node)
self._store[key] = (merged, new_ts, canonical_origin, False)

multi-leader-custom-merge-requires-merge.text: Constructing a cluster with `CUSTOM_MERGE` strategy and `merge_fn=None` is accepted silently, but raises `TypeError` at the first actual conflict during `sync()`

multi-leader-delete-propagates-tombstone.text: A ReplicaNode.delete() creates a tombstone that, once synced, causes get() to return None on all nodes in the cluster.

multi-leader-idempotent-apply.text: Each `(key, timestamp, origin_node)` triple is applied at most once per node, tracked by the `_seen` set, preventing duplicate application in ring topologies where changes propagate through multiple hops

metadata.example:
if key in self._seen and (remote_ts, remote_node) in self._seen[key]:
    return None  # already applied

multi-leader-lamport-monotonic.text: Successive `put()` calls on the same `ReplicaNode` yield strictly increasing Lamport timestamps.

multi-leader-lww-deterministic-tiebreak.text: LWW conflict resolution compares `(timestamp, node_id)` tuples using Python's lexicographic tuple comparison, guaranteeing all nodes independently reach the same winner without coordination

metadata.example:
if (remote_ts, remote_node) > (local_ts, local_origin):
    self._store[key] = (remote_val, remote_ts, remote_node, is_tombstone)

multi-leader-no-tombstone-gc.text: Multi-leader replication stores tombstones indefinitely with no compaction or garbage collection method, which is safe but accumulates dead entries without bound

multi-leader-ring-convergence-rounds.text: RING topology requires at least N−1 `sync()` rounds to fully propagate a single-source change across N nodes, because each round advances the change by exactly one hop

multi-leader-ring-needs-multiple-rounds.text: Ring topology requires at least 2 sync rounds to propagate a write across 3+ nodes, unlike all-to-all topology which converges in a single round; `sync_until_converged()` loops to handle this.

multi-leader-sync-collects-then-distribu.text: `sync()` drains all pending queues from every node before distributing any changes, preventing intra-round cascading where one node's change would trigger further propagation within the same sync round

multi-leader-sync-count-includes-noops.text: The count returned by `sync()` includes idempotent no-op deliveries (changes already in the target's `_seen` set), so it reflects replication attempts, not accepted changes

multi-leader-sync-designed-for-safe-conv.text: Multi-leader sync is designed for safe convergence: the two-phase collect-then-distribute pattern prevents intra-round cascading, custom merge functions are required to be idempotent across repeated syncs, and merged results receive fresh timestamps ensuring they supersede both inputs.

justifications.label: Three complementary design choices ensure that sync rounds converge monotonically without re-triggering conflicts

multi-leader-sync-is-discrete.text: Replication occurs only when `sync()` is explicitly called; there is no background replication thread or event-driven propagation, giving tests full control over replication timing.

multi-leader-sync-snapshot-isolation.text: Duplicate of existing `multi-leader-sync-collects-then-distributes` which already captures that sync() drains all pending queues before distributing, preventing intra-round cascading

multi-leader-sync-until-converged-raises.text: MultiLeaderCluster.sync_until_converged() raises RuntimeError if convergence is not reached within max_rounds.

multi-leader-test-file-dual-run-mode.text: multi-leader-replication/test_multi_leader.py can run both as a pytest-compatible suite and as a standalone script via its __main__ block.

multi-leader-tester-basic-no-conflict.text: test_basic_replication_no_conflict verifies that non-conflicting writes across 3 nodes converge after one sync with zero conflict records.

multi-leader-tester-many-keys-converge.text: test_convergence_many_keys verifies that 5 nodes with 20 keys each all converge after sync.

multi-leader-tester-standalone-runner.text: tester_test_multi_leader.py runs standalone via python tester_test_multi_leader.py with a manual __main__ runner that prints PASS/FAIL and exits with code 1 on any failure.

multi-leader-tester-strategy-at-construc.text: In tester_test_multi_leader.py, conflict resolution strategy is passed at MultiLeaderCluster construction time via ConflictStrategy and merge_fn, not per operation.

multi-leader-tests-are-self-contained.text: Each multi-leader test function creates its own MultiLeaderCluster and uses no shared fixtures or setup/teardown.

multi-leader-tests-use-all-converged-ora.text: The multi-leader test suite uses the cluster-level all_converged() predicate as its primary eventual-consistency assertion.

multi-leader-tombstone-carries-timestamp.text: Multi-leader replication stores each tombstone tuple with the value, remote timestamp, remote node, and is_tombstone flag.

multi-leader-tombstone-delete.text: Deletes are implemented as tombstone writes (`_TOMBSTONE` sentinel with `is_tombstone=True`) that replicate like normal mutations; `get()` returns `None` for tombstoned keys

multi-paxos-reduces-round-trips-per-slot.text: Multi-Paxos with a stable leader reduces steady-state consensus cost from two round trips per slot to one round trip per slot.

multiple-core-components-assume-single-t.text: The B-tree, garbage collector, and consistent hash ring all assume single-threaded access without locks, assertions, or documentation — a systematic pattern where concurrency unsafety is implicit rather than enforced.

justifications.label: Three independent modules share the same implicit single-threading assumption, suggesting this is a codebase-wide convention that is never explicitly stated or enforced

mvcc-abort-is-logical-not-physical.text: Duplicates `abort-is-status-change-not-disk-rollback` — already captured that abort marks transaction status without reversing writes, relying on visibility checks to filter.

mvcc-active-set-frozen-at-begin.text: `MVCCDatabase.begin_transaction` captures `active_at_start` as a frozen set of all currently active transaction IDs at that moment; it is never modified after creation and serves as the transaction's immutable snapshot boundary

metadata.example:
tx.active_at_start = {
    tid for tid, t in self._transactions.items() if t.is_active}

mvcc-active-tx-not-recoverable.text: Active (uncommitted) transactions cannot survive a process restart; the safe recovery strategy is to treat them as aborted, which is consistent with `_is_visible`'s existing handling of aborted transaction versions as invisible

mvcc-append-only-versions.text: Writers never modify existing `Version` objects (except self-overwrites); new values are appended to per-key version lists, preserving the immutable snapshot for concurrent readers

metadata.example:
self._versions.setdefault(key, []).append(
    Version(key, value, created_by=tx.tx_id))

mvcc-counters-must-be-monotonic.text: `_next_tx_id` and `_next_timestamp` must never reissue a previously used value; if they reset to 1 on restart, visibility comparisons like `created_by < tx.tx_id` silently produce wrong results by conflating old and new transaction IDs

mvcc-database-uses-rlock-for-reentrant-c.text: The MVCC database uses threading.RLock because _commit() calls _abort() and _scan() calls read() reentrantly while holding the lock.

mvcc-delete-stamps-deleted-by-on-visible.text: A delete operation in MVCCDatabase does not remove data; it sets deleted_by on the existing visible Version.

mvcc-isolation-survives-restart.text: MVCC's three-layer visibility model (append-only versions, own-writes visibility, symmetric deletion) with active sets frozen at transaction begin would provide correct snapshot isolation across process restarts if all state were persisted, since the visibility rules themselves are sound and compose correctly.

justifications.label: The visibility model is correct in all observable respects within a session; only the total absence of persistence prevents the isolation guarantees from surviving a restart.

mvcc-no-persistence.text: `MVCCDatabase` has zero serialization or persistence support; all state (`_versions`, `_transactions`, `_committed`, `_aborted`, counters) lives only in memory with no `to_dict`, `from_dict`, or file I/O of any kind

mvcc-pattern-exists-at-row-level.text: The codebase implements MVCC visibility (`ssi_database.py:_visible_value`, `mvcc_database.py:Version`) at the row/key level but not at the SSTable-file level where LevelDB uses Version reference counting for concurrent reader isolation

mvcc-read-returns-last-visible-version.text: MVCCDatabase.read() iterates through a key's versions and returns the last version that _is_visible accepts.

mvcc-snapshot-read-stable-across-concurr.text: A transaction that has begun reading a key continues to read the same value after another transaction commits a write to that key.

mvcc-state-entirely-volatile.text: Duplicate of `mvcc-no-persistence` proposed above — same claim about MVCCDatabase having no persistence

mvcc-store-contains-mixed-commit-states.text: Because MVCCDatabase writes versions eagerly before commit, its `_versions` store can contain versions from committed, uncommitted, and aborted transactions simultaneously.

mvcc-three-layer-visibility-model.text: MVCC visibility is enforced through three complementary invariants: append-only version storage prevents lost updates, own-writes are always visible regardless of commit state, and deletions follow the same visibility rules as writes — collectively ensuring snapshot consistency.

justifications.label: Three independent visibility guarantees combine into a complete snapshot isolation model where no single invariant is sufficient alone

mvcc-txid-monotonicity-assumed.text: The visibility check `created_by < tx.tx_id` assumes transaction IDs are monotonically increasing to mean "started before us"; non-monotonic or reused IDs would break snapshot correctness.

mvcc-uncommitted-data-memory-only.text: In MVCCDatabase, uncommitted transaction writes exist only as in-memory Version objects in `_versions` and never reach a persistent data store; abort works by adding the tx_id to `_aborted` so visibility checks filter it out

mvcc-version-list-per-key.text: MVCCDatabase stores versions as a _versions dict mapping each key to a list of Version objects.

mvcc-visibility-depends-on-tx-metadata.text: `_is_visible` requires `_committed`, `_aborted`, and each transaction's `active_at_start` set; persisting version chains without this metadata makes them unreadable after restore since visibility cannot be determined

mvcc-visibility-is-logical-superversion.text: This is an analogy between two systems rather than a testable factual claim about the code — it asserts conceptual equivalence rather than observable behavior

mvcc-writes-versions-eagerly.text: MVCCDatabase writes versions immediately into the shared `_versions` dict, tagged with the creating transaction's ID, before the transaction commits.

naming-convention-not-uniform.text: The tester/test split uses at least three naming patterns across directories: `tester_test_*.py`, `test_*_tester.py`, and `test_tester_*.py`

neither-bitcask-supports-expiry.text: Neither Bitcask implementation supports per-key TTL or expiry; `hash-index-storage` stores a timestamp in the header but never checks it for expiration, and `log-structured-hash-table` omits timestamps entirely.

neither-partitioning-strategy-fully-reli.text: Neither partitioning strategy offers both reliable routing and ordered access: range partitioning preserves key ordering but depends on maintaining parallel arrays in lockstep with invariants that are never verified (boundaries/partitions correspondence, adjacency assumptions in merge), while hash partitioning provides deterministic single-lookup routing but permanently destroys lexicographic key order, making range queries impossible.

justifications.label: Range partitioning is ordered but fragile, hash partitioning is robust but unordered — each strategy sacrifices the property the other provides

network-partitions-amplify-write-correct.text: Network partitions create a force multiplier on distributed write correctness gaps: partitions disrupt gossip-based failure detection (the single correctness gate for replication, read repair, and hinted handoff), while writes that do proceed operate under already-weakened quorum semantics (sloppy quorums count hints as successes, sub-quorum configurations accepted with only a warning).

justifications.label: Partitions disable the failure detection that replication depends on, while active writes use weakened quorum guarantees

new-file-durability-requires-parent-dire.text: Making a newly created filename durable requires an fsync on the parent directory file descriptor in addition to fsync on the file, because the directory entry is parent-directory metadata.

newest-sstable-wins-reads.text: Duplicate of existing `lsm-newest-first-read-path` which already captures that get() searches newest-first and the first match is authoritative

next-free-page-is-monotonic.text: The `next_free_page` metadata field only ever increases — it is the high-water mark of file extension, never decremented even when pages are freed; file size never shrinks, only interior pages are recycled via the free list.

no-atomic-file-creation.text: No SSTable writer or compaction routine in any implementation uses the write-temp/fsync/rename pattern; all write directly to the final file path

no-block-size-parameter-exists.text: Trivial API naming fact — the branching factor parameter name is already evident from any test or constructor call.

no-ci-or-runner-for-tester-tests.text: No CI pipeline (no `.github/` directory), Makefile, or orchestration script exists to invoke `tester_test_*.py` files; they are run manually via `python tester_test_*.py`

no-collection-customization.text: Duplicate of existing belief `tester-test-files-not-excluded` which already states no `collect_ignore`, `norecursedirs`, `testpaths`, or `python_files` directives exist

no-compaction-manifest.text: None of the three storage engines (hash-index, log-structured-hash-table, LSM) use a manifest or compaction log to make segment replacement atomic; segment discovery is purely filesystem-based via directory listing.

no-compaction-rate-limiting.text: Neither LSM implementation throttles compaction I/O throughput; a large merge will saturate disk bandwidth without regard to concurrent foreground reads or writes.

no-component-has-full-record-crc.text: Subsumed by existing `all-three-implementations-use-payload-only-crc` combined with the new `lsm-and-sstable-have-no-checksums`

no-component-resyncs-after-corruption.text: Every binary record reader in this codebase (WAL, both Bitcasks, LSM WAL, SSTable, B-tree WAL) stops at the first CRC failure, short read, or parse error; none attempt to scan forward for the next valid record boundary

no-concurrency-primitives.text: The entire B-tree implementation contains zero locking, latching, mutex, or thread-safety constructs; it is strictly single-threaded with no concurrent-access support

no-concurrency-protection-on-base-offset.text: Neither `truncate` nor `compact_partition` holds a lock; concurrent calls on the same partition would race on both `_partitions` and `_base_offsets`, assuming single-threaded execution.

no-conftest-anywhere.text: The ddia-implementations repo contains zero `conftest.py` files at any directory level — confirmed by exhaustive grep across all 37 modules, not just root

no-crc-on-records.text: Subsumed by the more specific `hash-index-bitcask-no-checksum` proposed above.

no-cross-file-fsync-ordering-protocol.text: The standalone WAL module provides no mechanism or documentation for enforcing the required WAL-before-data fsync ordering; callers must implement the `fsync(wal)` → `write(data)` → `fsync(data)` protocol themselves.

no-cuckoo-filter-in-codebase.text: The repository contains no cuckoo filter implementation; the counting Bloom filter is the only deletion-supporting probabilistic filter, leaving the saturation problem unsolved

no-cuckoo-or-xor-filter-in-repo.text: The repository has no cuckoo filter, quotient filter, or xor filter implementation; CountingBloomFilter is the only probabilistic membership structure supporting deletion.

no-data-path-is-trustworthy.text: No data path through the system is trustworthy: the primary storage path through compaction is unsalvageable (crash-unsafe within a broken durability pipeline, no concurrent access protection) while the secondary derived-data path through event infrastructure is unreliable in both content semantics and ordering guarantees, leaving no channel through which data can be read or propagated with confidence.

justifications.label: The primary and secondary data paths fail independently and for different structural reasons, making data trust impossible regardless of which access pattern is used.

no-defense-in-depth-against-corruption.text: The system has no defense-in-depth against data corruption: input validation is systematically absent at API boundaries (malformed data enters freely), and corruption is terminal across all readers with no resync capability (corrupted data can never be recovered) — the system is maximally permeable to corruption entry and maximally fragile to corruption presence.

justifications.label: Two depth-1 conclusions cover opposite ends of the data lifecycle (entry vs detection) and both show total absence of protection, making corruption a one-way ratchet

no-direct-page-writes.text: The BTree class never calls `pm.write_page` directly for data pages; all data page writes are routed through `_wal_write_page` (or `_wal_write_meta` for page 0) to maintain the write-ahead invariant.

no-directory-fsync-anywhere.text: No implementation in the codebase calls `os.fsync()` on a directory file descriptor; all fsync calls target data file descriptors only

no-directory-fsync-in-codebase.text: No module in the codebase fsyncs a directory file descriptor; the pattern os.open(dir, os.O_RDONLY) + os.fsync(dir_fd) appears nowhere.

no-disk-artifact-patterns.text: On-disk files created by storage-engine modules (B-tree pages, WAL segments, SSTable files) are not covered by `.gitignore`, relying on test teardown or manual cleanup

no-double-free-detection.text: Calling `free_page` twice on the same page creates a cycle in the free list, which `allocate_page` cannot detect, leading to silent data corruption through repeated page reuse.
