targets = available[:self.read_quorum]
# repair only among the R replicas queried, not all N
for rid in stale:
    self.replicas[rid].put(key, best_value, best_version)

read-repair-stats-track-repair-rate.text: ReadRepairStore tracks repair_rate as the fraction of reads that trigger write-back repairs; the test observes a 50% repair rate when 1 of 2 reads triggers repair.

read-repair-uses-scalar-integer-versions.text: ReadRepairStore uses scalar incrementing integer versions rather than vector clocks, assuming a single logical writer for version assignment.

read-uses-linear-scan-for-offset-gaps.text: `Topic.read` finds the start position by scanning for `msg.offset >= offset` rather than computing an array index, which is necessary because compaction creates offset holes that break arithmetic indexing.

readlines-accepts-list-or-filepath.text: `ReadLines` accepts either a `list[str]` of in-memory lines or a file path string as its input source, providing two input modes from the same stage.

reads-and-writes-same-consensus-path.text: `LinearizableRegister` routes both reads and writes through the same TOB slot mechanism, giving them positions in the same total order — no read-only fast path exists.

rebuild-index-does-not-reset-active-stat.text: `rebuild_index()` does not reset `_active_file` or `_segment_counter`, unlike `_recover` which sets them.

receive-gossip-adds-unknown-alive-nodes.text: If the remote reports an unknown node as alive, `receive_gossip` deep-copies the entry, stamps it with `current_time`, and adds it to local membership.

receive-gossip-assumes-well-formed-input.text: `receive_gossip` performs no input validation; missing `heartbeat_counter`, `status`, or `timestamp_last_updated` keys raise `KeyError` at runtime.

receive-gossip-death-is-sticky.text: Once a node's local status is `dead`, `receive_gossip` will never change it back to `alive`, even if the remote has a higher heartbeat counter — preventing flapping after failure declaration

receive-gossip-deep-copies-on-insert.text: `receive_gossip` deep-copies remote entries before inserting them into local membership, extending the isolation guarantee beyond the `send_gossip`/`join`/`get_membership_list` paths covered by `gossip-deep-copy-isolation`

receive-gossip-equal-counter-death-accep.text: Duplicates existing belief `gossip-merge-uses-heartbeat-monotonicity` which already captures the equal-counter death exception

receive-gossip-no-self-exclusion.text: Unlike `detect_failures` which skips the node's own ID, `receive_gossip` has no self-exclusion guard — if the remote gossip contains an entry for the receiver, it is merged normally

receive-gossip-updates-timestamp-on-high.text: When a remote heartbeat counter is higher, `receive_gossip` resets the local `timestamp_last_updated` to `current_time`.

receive-replica-drops-dominated-incoming.text: `VersionedKVStore._receive_replica` silently drops an incoming version if that version is dominated by any surviving local version.

receive-replica-is-passive-endpoint.text: `_receive_replica` in `vector-clocks/vector_clock.py` is the receiving side of anti-entropy replication; nothing in the codebase calls it automatically — tests simulate the call manually, and no gossip or sync module invokes it

receive-replica-uses-vector-clock-for-co.text: `_receive_replica` uses the supplied vector clock to decide whether to accept, reject, or flag a conflict for an incoming replica value.

reconcile-dominates-all-siblings.text: After `VersionedKVStore.reconcile`, the returned vector clock dominates every input sibling clock.

reconcile-replaces-all-siblings.text: `reconcile` unconditionally replaces all siblings for a key with a single merged version, regardless of whether the provided contexts cover every existing sibling.

reconstruct-state-empty-handlers-returns.text: If `handlers` is empty, `reconstruct_state` returns an empty dict regardless of what events are in the stream.

reconstruct-state-fetches-entire-stream-.text: `reconstruct_state` calls `read_stream(stream_id)` for the entire stream and only then breaks on `up_to`, rather than passing the cutoff to the read.

reconstruct-state-full-replay.text: reconstruct_state rebuilds state by replaying all events from the start up to a specified event_id.

reconstruct-state-is-pure-read.text: `reconstruct_state` never modifies the `EventStore`; it is a read-only fold over a single stream's events that returns a locally-constructed dict

reconstruct-state-missing-stream-returns.text: If `stream_id` does not exist, `reconstruct_state` returns an empty dict.

reconstruct-state-no-snapshot-support.text: `reconstruct_state` always replays from the beginning of the stream via `read_stream` with default `from_version=0`; it does not leverage snapshots, unlike `Projection`

reconstruct-state-supports-point-in-time.text: `reconstruct_state` replays a stream's events only up to a specified event ID, returning the state as it was at that point in time.

reconstruct-state-up-to-is-global-id.text: The `up_to` parameter in `reconstruct_state` filters on global `event_id`, not stream-local version number, despite operating on a single stream

reconstruct-state-up-to-zero-applies-no-.text: If `up_to` is 0, `reconstruct_state` applies no events because all event IDs are at least 1.

record-format-is-length-prefixed.text: Each WAL record starts with a 4-byte little-endian length prefix (not counting itself), followed by CRC, seq_num, op_type, and length-prefixed key/value pairs — minimum 25 bytes per record for empty key/value

record-format-self-describing.text: Covered by existing `record-format-is-length-prefixed`; the key_size/value_size fields making records self-describing is the direct consequence of length-prefixing

record-length-corruption-cascades-to-crc.text: Corruption of the WAL record_length field cascades into a CRC mismatch because it changes which bytes _read_record consumes, making explicit CRC coverage unnecessary.

record-length-implicitly-validated.text: Corruption of `record_length` causes `_read_record` to consume wrong bytes for the payload, which fails the CRC check indirectly — making explicit CRC coverage of the framing field unnecessary

record-seen-called-on-accepted-remote-ch.text: `_record_seen` is called for accepted remote changes as well as local `put` and `delete`, so each forwarded change is processed at most once per node.

recover-activates-highest-id-segment.text: After recovery, `_recover` opens the segment with the numerically highest ID as the active writable segment.

recover-called-once-from-init.text: `_recover` is called exactly once from `BitcaskStore.__init__` and is not intended for external use.

recover-empty-directory-opens-new-segmen.text: If no segments exist on disk, `_recover` sets the segment counter to 0 and opens a new empty segment.

recover-is-read-only.text: Trivially expected of a recovery scan function; this is not an invariant that could be accidentally violated or that constrains design decisions.

recover-propagates-file-errors.text: `_recover` does not catch `OSError` or `FileNotFoundError`; these exceptions propagate and crash the constructor.

recover-segment-filename-parsing-raises-.text: `_find_existing_segments` parses segment IDs by slicing filenames; any file matching `segment_*.dat` with a non-numeric middle raises `ValueError`.

recover-seq-no-gap-detection.text: `_recover_seq_num` finds the max sequence number but does not detect or report gaps in the sequence space, meaning lost records between rotations or corruption are silently ignored.

recover-seq-num-called-once-in-init.text: `_recover_seq_num` is called exactly once during `WriteAheadLog.__init__`, before any new writes occur.

recover-seq-num-halts-on-early-corruptio.text: `_recover_seq_num` breaks on `ValueError` during file scanning, so corruption in an early WAL file prevents it from discovering higher sequence numbers in later files.

recover-seq-num-is-global-max.text: `_recover_seq_num` returns the maximum sequence number across all WAL files, not just the latest file, ensuring correctness even when records are spread across rotated segments.

recover-seq-num-is-read-only.text: `_recover_seq_num` performs no writes or state mutations; it is a pure filesystem scan returning an integer.

recover-seq-num-propagates-os-errors.text: `_recover_seq_num` does not catch `OSError` from opening or reading WAL files; filesystem errors propagate and abort initialization.

recover-seq-num-zero-means-empty.text: `_recover_seq_num` returns 0 when no valid WAL records exist, so the next appended record receives sequence number 1.

recover-seq-skips-corrupt-files.text: `_recover_seq_num` treats CRC errors as file-local (abandons the corrupted file, continues scanning subsequent files), unlike `_read_all_records` which stops all scanning on corruption.

recovery-destroys-both-durability-and-is.text: A single restart simultaneously destroys both durability and isolation guarantees along independent axes: the WAL's carefully calibrated write-time durability tiers (per-write fsync vs batch-only fsync) become invisible to recovery, and the transaction isolation model's composed invariant layers (MVCC visibility plus SSI conflict detection) break because abort metadata and monotonic counters are non-persistent.

justifications.label: Restart independently breaks the durability contract (WAL tiers lost) and isolation contract (transaction metadata lost)

recovery-requires-participant-availabili.text: `Coordinator.recover()` checks `is_available()` before re-sending decisions and skips unavailable participants, meaning a double failure (coordinator crash + participant crash) leaves locks held until both are up and recovery re-runs.

recovery-scans-all-segments.text: All three storage implementations (WAL, hash-index Bitcask, log-structured Bitcask) scan every segment file on startup to rebuild state, making recovery time proportional to segment count rather than data volume.

recovery-simultaneously-over-and-under-e.text: Recovery is paradoxically both over-engineered and under-implemented: the WAL builds complete sequence number and checkpoint infrastructure that's never consulted during replay, while the actual recovery paths lack batch atomicity and metadata CRC protection — engineering effort was invested in infrastructure that goes unused while the active recovery path remains unsafe.

justifications.label: Vestigial recovery infrastructure coexists with unsafe actual recovery paths

redlock-lacks-fencing-token.text: Redlock provides TTL-based mutual exclusion but does not provide a fencing token or server-side stale-write rejection mechanism.

reduce-side-sort-group-uses-itertools-gr.text: Duplicates existing belief `mr-groupby-requires-presort` which already covers the itertools.groupby dependency on pre-sorted input

reference-implementations-lack-tombstone.text: None of the DDIA reference implementations combine tombstone support with time-bounded garbage collection; the multi-leader module stores tombstones indefinitely and the Dynamo module has no delete support at all.

rename-is-atomic-but-not-durable-without.text: `os.rename()` is atomic at the VFS level but not durable; the directory entry metadata can be lost on crash unless the directory itself is fsynced.

rename-modifies-source-and-destination-d.text: `os.rename()` modifies directory entries in both the source and destination directories.

rename-without-dir-barrier.text: Both Bitcask compaction paths (`hash-index-storage/bitcask.py:297`, `log-structured-merge-tree/bitcask.py:301`) perform `os.rename()` without a subsequent directory fsync, making the rename non-durable on ext4 and XFS

renew-preserves-token-number.text: `LockService.renew()` extends the lock TTL by mutating `issued_at` and `ttl` without changing the `FencingToken.token` value, while re-`acquire()` by the same client issues a new higher token

metadata.example:
def renew(self, lock_name, client_id, current_time, ttl=10):
    existing.issued_at = current_time
    existing.ttl = ttl
    return True  # same token number, extended TTL

replay-after-seq-not-validated.text: `replay` does not validate that `after_seq` is non-negative; passing a negative value effectively returns all records.

replay-comments-document-exclusion.text: The `replay()` implementation comments explicitly state that all PUT/DELETE records are included while COMMIT and CHECKPOINT markers are excluded.

replay-does-not-enforce-batch-atomicity.text: Despite the docstring claiming replay "skips uncommitted batches," the implementation returns all PUT/DELETE records regardless of whether a matching COMMIT record exists — a crash mid-batch will replay partial batch records

replay-filters-by-seq-and-op-type-only.text: replay() applies only a sequence number filter (skip records with seq_num <= after_seq) and an op-type filter (keep only PUT/DELETE records), returning all PUT/DELETE records regardless of whether a matching COMMIT record exists.

replay-flush-before-read.text: `replay` flushes the write file descriptor under `self._lock` before reading, ensuring all prior `append` calls are visible on disk during the read phase

replay-lacks-batch-atomicity-across-impl.text: Both the unbundled WAL and B-tree WAL replay all CRC-valid records without verifying batch completeness, meaning partial batches from mid-write crashes are silently applied as if they were complete transactions.

justifications.label: Two independent WAL implementations share the same replay-safety gap, suggesting a systematic design choice (or oversight) rather than an isolated bug

replay-no-external-file-lock.text: `replay` does not use file-level locking to protect against concurrent external writers modifying WAL files during the read phase.

replay-not-lock-protected-during-read.text: The file read phase of `replay` runs without holding `self._lock`, so concurrent `append` calls during replay could produce a partial read of in-flight writes

replay-records-in-log-order.text: The records returned by `replay` are in log order: file order (sorted filename) and then byte offset within each file.

replay-returns-eager-list.text: `replay` returns an in-memory `List[WALRecord]` snapshot, not a lazy iterator — the full result set is materialized before returning, which can be large if the WAL is large

replay-returns-only-put-delete.text: Duplicates existing `wal-replay-ignores-commit` — both describe filtering out non-data records during replay

replay-stops-at-corruption.text: Duplicates existing `wal-crc-mismatch-halts-all-replay` — same claim that CRC failure terminates replay for all subsequent records

replay-strict-greater-than-filter.text: `replay(after_seq=n)` returns records with `seq_num` strictly greater than `n` (exclusive lower bound), not greater-or-equal — passing 0 replays the entire log

replay-test-returns-six-data-ops-from-ei.text: In the WAL test, 3 individual operations plus a 3-operation batch plus COMMIT and CHECKPOINT produce 8 total records, but `replay()` returns only the 6 data operations.

replay-uses-read-all-records.text: `replay` delegates the actual file scanning and record parsing to `_read_all_records`, the same internal iterator used by `iterate`.

replica-get-accepts-empty-string.text: Replica.get accepts any string key, including the empty string, because it performs no key validation.

replica-get-does-not-check-availability.text: `Replica.get` does not consult `self._available`; filtering unavailable replicas is the caller's responsibility via `ReadRepairStore._available_replicas()`.

replica-get-has-no-side-effects.text: `Replica.get` performs no mutations, availability checks, or I/O — it is a pure dictionary lookup, unlike `ReadRepairStore.get` which triggers read repair on stale replicas.

replica-get-no-version-filtering.text: Replica.get performs no version filtering, tombstone handling, or conflict resolution; those responsibilities live in ReadRepairStore.

replica-get-returns-stored-tuple-without.text: Replica.get returns the stored `(value, version)` tuple directly from `_store` without making a copy.

replica-get-returns-tuple-or-none.text: `Replica.get` returns a `(value, version)` tuple when the key exists, or `None` when it doesn't — callers must guard against `None` before destructuring, as there is no sentinel tuple.

replica-put-does-not-validate-version-ty.text: Replica.put does not validate that `version` is an integer; passing a non-comparable type such as a string would raise a TypeError at the comparison.

replica-put-no-concurrency-safety.text: The version check and store update in `Replica.put` are not atomic (TOCTOU race on lines 22–25); the method is unsafe under concurrent access without external locking.

replica-put-pure-in-memory-mutation.text: Replica.put has no I/O, logging, or callbacks; on success it only mutates `self._store`.

replica-put-rejects-older-versions.text: `Replica.put()` silently rejects writes with a version strictly less than the stored version (returns `False`), enforcing monotonic version advancement; equal versions are accepted as last-writer-wins.

replica-put-success-stores-exact-tuple.text: After a successful Replica.put, `self._store[key]` equals the exact `(value, version)` tuple supplied by the caller.

replica-versions-caller-coordinated.text: `Replica.put` does not generate version numbers; version assignment is the responsibility of `ReadRepairStore.put`, which reads the max version across all replicas (including unavailable ones) before writing.

replica-versions-start-at-one.text: Versions assigned by `ReadRepairStore.put` start at 1 (computed as `max_version + 1` with initial max of 0), so a version of 0 in `ReadRepairStore.get` return values means "key not found," not "initial version."

replication-tombstone-ttl-bounds-removal.text: Distributed systems often retain tombstones for a TTL such as Cassandra's `gc_grace_seconds` so all replicas receive the delete before the tombstone can be removed.

repo-contains-37-ddia-modules.text: The ddia-implementations repository contains 37 standalone Python implementations of DDIA concepts.

repo-modules-are-strictly-isolated.text: Every top-level module in ddia-implementations is an independent implementation with no shared libraries, base classes, or cross-module imports.

repo-modules-follow-three-file-pattern.text: Each ddia-implementations module follows a three-file pattern: `<implementation>.py`, `test_<name>.py`, and `tester_test_<name>.py`.

repo-modules-group-into-six-layers.text: The 37 ddia-implementations modules are grouped into six layers mirroring DDIA's structure: storage engines, replication, consensus, partitioning, transactions, and stream/batch processing.

repo-runtime-uses-stdlib-only.text: All ddia-implementations modules use only the Python standard library at runtime, with pytest used only for testing.

reprepare-merges-by-sequence.text: When the new primary merges prepared sets from VIEW_CHANGE messages, it deduplicates by sequence number using first-writer-wins without verifying that all nodes prepared the same request at that sequence — relying on the PBFT safety proof that at most one request can be prepared per (view, seq).

requeue-without-seen-causes-infinite-loo.text: Without `_seen` idempotency, re-enqueueing accepted remote changes into `_pending` causes an infinite propagation loop in a ring topology.

resolve-record-dead-code.text: `writer_field_map` is constructed but never referenced in `_resolve_record`, making it dead code likely left from a refactor

resolve-record-fields-decoded-with-both-.text: For fields present in both writer and reader schemas, `_resolve_record` decodes values using both the writer and reader field types, enabling type promotion.

resolve-record-name-check-in-decode.text: `_decode` enforces that writer and reader record schemas have matching `name` values before calling `_resolve_record`.

resolve-record-no-cycle-detection.text: `_resolve_record` has no cycle detection for nested records; a recursive record type would recurse infinitely, although the `Schema` parser does not support recursive types.

resolve-record-relies-on-python-dict-ord.text: Result field ordering in `_resolve_record` relies on the Python 3.7+ dict insertion-order guarantee.

resolve-record-shared-defaults.text: Default values in `_resolve_record` are inserted by reference without deep copying, so mutable defaults (lists, dicts) would be shared across all decoded records that use the default

resolve-record-skip-unknown.text: Writer fields not present in the reader schema are fully consumed from the buffer via `_skip()` and discarded, ensuring the byte stream stays correctly positioned for subsequent fields

resolve-record-truncated-buffer-raises-v.text: A truncated record buffer causes `ValueError` from lower-level `read_varint` or `struct.unpack` calls during `_resolve_record`.

resolve-record-two-pass.text: `_resolve_record` uses a two-pass algorithm: pass 1 consumes all writer fields from the buffer in wire order (decoding or skipping each), pass 2 assembles the result dict in reader field order from decoded values and defaults

resolve-record-zero-writer-fields-uses-d.text: If the writer record schema has zero fields, `_resolve_record` builds the result entirely from reader field defaults.

resource-token-tracking-is-independent.text: Each resource in `FencedResourceServer` maintains its own `_highest_token` entry, so a high token on resource A does not cause rejection of a lower token on resource B.

riak-bitcask-fsyncs-hint-before-deleting.text: Production Bitcask (Riak) fsyncs a hint file before deleting the old segments it replaces.

riak-bitcask-hint-entries-have-checksums.text: Production Bitcask (Riak) includes a checksum in each hint entry so partial hint-file writes are detected.

riak-bitcask-hint-files-uses-per-entry-c.text: Production Riak Bitcask hint files include per-entry CRC32 checksums, and a corrupted hint file triggers fallback to a data scan.

riak-bitcask-writes-hint-via-atomic-rena.text: Production Bitcask (Riak) writes hint files to a temporary file, fsyncs, then renames atomically so a hint file is either fully present or absent.

riak-causal-context-compresses-tombstone.text: Riak uses a compact version vector (causal context) to implicitly tombstone tags at or below the vector's sequence entry, compressing an arbitrary number of tombstones into one integer per replica.

riak-delete-modes-three.text: Riak offers three delete modes: `keep` (retain tombstones indefinitely), `timeout` (default 3 seconds), and `immediate` (remove after all vnode acknowledgments).

ring-election-message-complexity-linear.text: Ring-based Chang-Roberts election uses O(n) messages per election because the election message traverses the ring once.

ring-election-requires-ring-repair-on-fa.text: A ring-based election requires ring repair if a node fails mid-election, unlike the Bully implementation where unavailable nodes simply do not respond.

ring-requeues-via-apply-remote-change.text: `apply_remote_change` appends accepted changes to the receiving node's `_pending` list, enabling store-and-forward propagation in ring topology; without this re-enqueue, changes would stop at the first hop.

ring-requires-n-minus-one-rounds.text: `RING` topology advances changes by exactly one hop per `sync()` round due to snapshot-isolated pending queue draining, requiring N-1 rounds for a single-source change to reach all N nodes.

ring-sends-only-to-successor.text: In `Topology.RING`, each node sends its pending changes only to its successor at `(i+1) % len(_node_order)` during a sync round.

ring-topology-convergence-is-linear-in-n.text: Ring topology requires O(N) sync rounds for full convergence because each round advances changes by exactly one hop via store-and-forward requeuing, unlike fully-connected topologies that converge in one round.

justifications.label: Three observations pin convergence delay to the store-and-forward mechanism: apply-remote-change requeues to pending, and pending drains one hop per sync

ring-topology-needs-multiple-sync-rounds.text: A 3-node ring topology requires at least 2 `sync()` rounds to achieve full convergence, unlike a fully-connected topology which converges in 1 round.

rocksdb-bottommost-level-compaction-cont.text: RocksDB's `BottommostLevelCompaction` enum controls when the engine performs expensive compaction of the deepest level for space reclamation.

rocksdb-is-bottommost-level-flag-enables.text: RocksDB's `CompactionJob::is_bottommost_level` flag indicates that a compaction job is at the bottom level and can safely drop tombstones.

rocksdb-merge-writes-deltas-without-read.text: RocksDB's Merge(key, operand) writes a delta without reading the existing value, unlike Put(key, new_value).

rocksdb-mergeoperator-defines-fullmerge-.text: RocksDB's MergeOperator interface defines FullMerge (called with a base value) and PartialMerge (called without a base value).

rocksdb-rate-limiter-throttles-compactio.text: RocksDB's `rate_limiter` throttles compaction I/O to protect foreground latency.

rocksdb-superversion-bundles-memtable-im.text: In RocksDB, a SuperVersion bundles the current MemTable, the immutable MemTables awaiting flush, and the current Version containing the SSTable file set.

rocksdb-superversion-wraps-memtable-and-.text: RocksDB's `SuperVersion` wraps the current memtable, immutable memtables, and current SSTable list into a single versioned snapshot.

rocksdb-versionset-snapshots-file-set.text: RocksDB's VersionSet uses immutable Version snapshots of the live file set so readers can continue reading an old Version while a compaction creates and installs a new Version.

rocksdb-versionset-uses-immutable-versio.text: RocksDB's VersionSet maintains immutable Version snapshots; compaction creates a new Version by applying a VersionEdit rather than mutating the current version.

root-hash-trust-is-external.text: Duplicates existing belief `verify-proof-root-trust`, which already states that `verify_proof` does not authenticate the root and callers must obtain a trusted root independently.

root-split-creates-new-root-with-one-key.text: When the root splits, `put` creates a new root internal node containing one separator key and two children: the old root and the new sibling.

rotate-assumes-fd-open.text: `_rotate` assumes a non-`None` `self._fd` is still open; it does not check `fd.closed` before calling `flush()`.

rotate-assumes-numeric-wal-filenames.text: `_rotate` assumes every `.wal` file in the directory follows the `NNNNNN.wal` naming convention; a file like `notes.wal` causes `int(...)` to raise `ValueError`.

rotate-called-from-open-latest-and-maybe.text: `_rotate` is called from `_open_latest` at startup or when the latest file is at capacity, and from `_maybe_rotate` after writes exceed the size threshold.

rotate-called-from-three-paths.text: Call-graph detail that establishes blast radius but is derivable from `wal-no-directory-fsync` (which already implies all rotation-dependent write paths are affected) and is fragile to refactoring.

rotate-missing-directory-fsync.text: Duplicate of `wal-no-directory-fsync` which already covers all segment creation and deletion

rotate-propagates-errors.text: `_rotate` does not catch exceptions from `os.fsync` or `open`; failures propagate to the caller.

rotation-always-fsyncs.text: The WAL `_rotate()` method unconditionally calls `flush()` and `os.fsync()` before closing the current segment, providing a durability checkpoint even in `none` mode

rotation-preserves-fd-invariant.text: After `_maybe_rotate` returns, `self._fd` is guaranteed non-None and open for writing (assuming it was non-None on entry), because `_rotate()` always opens a new file.

safe-compaction-uses-write-temp-fsync-re.text: The standard safe compaction pattern writes the new SSTable to a temporary file, fsyncs it, atomically renames it over the old file, then deletes the input SSTables.

saturation-boundary-untested.text: No test in `test_bloom_filter.py` exercises the counter saturation boundary (16+ collisions at a single position) to verify deletion correctness under overflow

save-snapshot-deep-copies-state.text: `save_snapshot` uses `copy.deepcopy` to isolate the stored snapshot from subsequent mutations to `_state`

sbt-db-is-riak-default.text: General BEAM VM knowledge about Riak production conventions, not a testable claim about the target codebase. The entry itself notes it "draws on general BEAM VM knowledge rather than code observations in the target repository."

scalable-bloom-lookup-linear-in-slices.text: `ScalableBloomFilter` membership checks scan all slices via `any()`, so lookup cost grows linearly with the number of slices.

scalable-bloom-slice-fp-ratio-is-0-5.text: `ScalableBloomFilter` adds new filter slices with `fp_ratio=0.5` per slice, so each slice targets half the false positive rate of the previous slice.

scalable-bloom-tightens-fpr.text: Each new slice in `ScalableBloomFilter` uses FPR of `p * (ratio ^ slice_index)`, so the aggregate false positive rate stays bounded even as the filter grows unboundedly

scan-range-corrupt-data-silent.text: If `_read_entry` encounters truncated data mid-range, `_scan_range_for_key` silently returns `(False, None)` rather than raising an error, making corruption indistinguishable from a missing key

scan-range-end-exclusive.text: `_scan_range_for_key` treats the `end` byte offset as exclusive and stops scanning before reaching it.

scan-range-file-open-errors-propagate.text: `_scan_range_for_key` has no explicit exception handling for file-open errors; a missing or unreadable SSTable file raises `FileNotFoundError` or `OSError` to the caller.

scan-range-no-state-mutation.text: Trivial — a read method being read-only is expected behavior, not an invariant that would break things if violated

scan-range-opens-file-per-call.text: `_scan_range_for_key` opens `self.path` in binary read mode on each call inside a `with` block.

scan-range-sorted-order-assumption.text: `_scan_range_for_key` assumes entries between `start` and `end` are sorted by key ascending; it breaks early on `k > key`, so unsorted data causes silent false negatives

scan-range-tombstone-transparent.text: Duplicates existing belief `sstable-get-does-not-filter-tombstones` which already captures that tombstone interpretation is the caller's responsibility

scan-segment-is-read-only.text: Too trivial — a scan/recovery function being read-only with respect to disk is expected behavior, not a surprising invariant.

scan-segment-no-path-validation.text: `_scan_segment` performs no validation on `seg_path`; if the file is missing or unreadable, `open()` raises an OS exception such as `FileNotFoundError` that propagates to the caller.

scan-segment-offset-recorded-before-head.text: `_scan_segment` records each record's byte offset with `f.tell()` before reading the 12-byte header, and stores that offset in the index entry.

scan-segment-ordering-invariant.text: `_scan_segment` must be called on segments in ascending segment-ID order for the index to correctly reflect last-write-wins semantics; no runtime check enforces this ordering — it is the caller's responsibility.

scan-segment-returns-none-mutates-index.text: `_scan_segment` returns `None` and communicates results entirely by mutating `self._index`.

scheduler-binding-benefits-ets-writes-mo.text: General systems knowledge about CPU cache behavior, not a claim about code in the target repository.

schema-registry-decode-with-id-fetches-w.text: SchemaRegistry.decode_with_id parses the first four bytes as a big-endian uint32 and uses that ID to retrieve the writer schema from the registry before Avro decoding.

schema-registry-encode-with-id-appends-a.text: SchemaRegistry.encode_with_id returns a 4-byte big-endian schema ID immediately followed by the Avro-encoded payload.

schema-registry-in-memory-only.text: `SchemaRegistry` is a pure in-memory dict with monotonic ID assignment, with no persistence, HTTP API, or subject-based grouping

schema-registry-no-compat-enforcement.text: Schema registration accepts any schema without checking compatibility against previously registered versions under the same subject, unlike Confluent which enforces backward/forward/full compatibility on registration

secondary-index-document-class-unused.text: The `Document` dataclass exists as a domain concept but the DB classes accept `pk` and `fields` separately and never consume `Document` instances.

secondary-index-empty-index-entry-delete.text: When the last primary key is removed from an index entry, both DB classes delete the entry from the index dict rather than leaving an empty set.

secondary-index-invalid-partition-raises.text: `get_partition` in secondary_index_partitioning.py raises IndexError on an invalid partition_id because there is no guard.

secondary-index-no-error-on-missing.text: `get()` on a nonexistent key returns `OperationResult(data=None)` and `query_by_field()` for absent values returns empty results rather than raising exceptions; documents missing indexed fields are stored but not indexed.

secondary-index-partition-assignment-use.text: DocumentPartitionedDB assigns documents by `hash(pk) % num_partitions`, while TermPartitionedDB assigns index terms by `hash(value) % num_partitions`.

secondary-index-stale-entry-cleanup.text: Both `DocumentPartitionedDB` and `TermPartitionedDB` remove stale index entries before writing new ones during `put` and `delete`, preventing phantom results from old field values.

secondary-index-uses-inverted-index-nest.text: Both DocumentPartitionedDB and TermPartitionedDB store secondary indexes as nested dicts of the shape `{field: {value: set(pks)}}`.

sector-write-atomic-within-single-sector.text: Modern disks write in 512-byte or 4096-byte sectors; a write within one sector is typically hardware-atomic, while a write spanning multiple sectors can result in a torn write.

seen-check-precedes-conflict-resolution.text: `apply_remote_change` performs the `_seen` idempotency check before conflict resolution, after extracting the change fields.

seen-set-keyed-by-ts-origin.text: `_seen` maps each key to a set of `(timestamp, origin_node_id)` tuples; a change is skipped if its exact `(ts, origin)` pair is already in the set for that key

segment-rotation-dir-entry-unsynced.text: When a new segment file is created during rotation, its directory entry is never fsynced; a crash after writing records to the new segment but before directory flush leaves records in an orphaned inode.

segment-rotation-limits-corruption-blast.text: Both Bitcask implementations rotate to new segment files at a configurable size threshold, bounding the maximum data loss from stop-at-first-error to the records trailing the corruption within a single segment

segment-rotation-threshold-depends-on-re.text: Test design detail explaining magic numbers, not an architectural invariant

seq-num-corruption-causes-silent-data-lo.text: Duplicates existing belief `seq-num-corruption-is-silent` — the specific truncate/replay failure modes are consequences of the already-documented gap

seq-num-corruption-is-silent.text: A bit flip in a WAL record's `seq_num` passes CRC validation and is silently accepted with the wrong sequence number, potentially corrupting replay filtering, truncation boundaries, and recovery sequence numbering

seq-num-crc-fix-is-zero-cost.text: Adding `seq_num` to the CRC input requires changing two lines (`_encode_record` and `_read_record`) with no measurable runtime overhead, since CRC32 over 9 extra bytes is negligible

seq-num-deflation-causes-truncate-data-l.text: A deflated seq_num can cause truncate to incorrectly discard committed records, silently losing data.

seq-num-is-semantic-not-framing.text: The WAL seq_num field is a semantic field, not a framing field; a corrupted seq_num produces a structurally valid record that passes all integrity checks the WAL performs.

seq-num-zero-means-empty.text: Derivative of existing belief `wal-seq-starts-at-one` — if seq starts at 1, a recovery result of 0 trivially means no records exist.

serialization-has-no-overflow-check.text: `_serialize_leaf` packs all entries into a buffer without comparing its length to `page_size`; overflow prevention is entirely the caller's responsibility

serialize-leaf-is-pure.text: `_serialize_leaf` is a pure function with no side effects; all I/O happens in the caller via `_wal_write_page`

serialize-leaf-length-overflow-raises.text: _serialize_leaf raises struct.error if a key or value length cannot fit in an unsigned 16-bit field (>= 65,536 bytes).

serialize-leaf-preserves-order-no-verifi.text: _serialize_leaf preserves the input order of keys and values and does not sort or verify that keys are sorted.

setup-bottommost-scans-below-output-leve.text: About RocksDB's `Compaction::SetupBottomMostLevel()` internals, not about this codebase; the relevant gap is already captured by `sstable-compaction-manager-lacks-bottommost-detection`.

sha256-preimage-resistance-prevents-netw.text: SHA-256's preimage resistance makes it computationally infeasible for a network adversary to modify a hash and have it match the original data.

shadow-paging-recovery-constant-time.text: Shadow paging recovery is constant-time because it only needs to select the valid root page, whereas WAL recovery time is proportional to log length since the last checkpoint.

sibling-asymmetry-reflects-purpose.text: Duplicates `sibling-field-is-structural-only` which already establishes that sibling pointers serve range scans, not concurrency.

sibling-chain-enables-but-unused-for-reb.text: Redundant — combines `btree-leaf-sibling-chain` (sibling pointers exist) and `btree-no-underflow-rebalancing` (no rebalancing happens) without adding a new testable claim

sibling-direction-matters.text: Proof siblings are tagged "left" or "right" because SHA-256 concatenation is order-dependent — `H(A||B) != H(B||A)` — so swapping sibling position produces a different parent hash and verification fails.

sibling-field-is-structural-only.text: Leaf pages carry a `next_sibling` field in their serialized format (`NO_SIBLING = 0xFFFFFFFF` sentinel), but no tree operation uses sibling pointers for traversal or merging — it is scaffolding, not a live data structure. Note: may refine existing `btree-leaf-sibling-chain`.

sibling-pointers-leaf-only.text: Sibling pointers exist only on leaf nodes (`_serialize_leaf` at line 182); internal nodes have no right-links, making this a B+-tree, not a B-link tree

sibling-preservation-on-concurrent-write.text: `VersionedKVStore.put` never drops an existing version unless the new version's clock dominates it; concurrent versions are preserved as siblings.

sibling-sentinel-convention.text: Trivial implementation detail already partially covered by `sibling-field-is-structural-only` which mentions the `NO_SIBLING = 0xFFFFFFFF` sentinel

silent-corruption-returns-garbage.text: A bit-flip in a value region of `hash-index-storage/bitcask.py` causes `get()` to return corrupted data with no error; the only partial integrity check is the key-equality assertion

silent-data-loss-is-default-operational-.text: Silent data loss is the default operational mode: corruption propagates through every data transformation pipeline without detection (compaction copies without CRC validation, hint generation skips integrity checks), and the testing methodology cannot observe durability failures (no crash tests, no fsync verification), meaning data degrades continuously with no feedback signal to operators.

justifications.label: Undetected corruption propagation plus invisible durability bugs equals continuous silent data loss

silent-mode-drops-all-outbound.text: `SILENT` Byzantine mode returns an empty list for all outbound messages, but the node still processes incoming messages and updates internal state — simulating a crash fault rather than a protocol violation

single-file-design-enables-atomic-sync.text: `PageManager` stores metadata (page 0) and data pages in a single file, so one `os.fsync()` call in `sync()` covers both; splitting into separate files would require multiple fsyncs with ordering constraints in the commit fence

single-kv-size-validated.text: `BTree.put` raises `ValueError` for any single key-value pair that cannot fit in a page, blocking the case where even one entry would overflow

single-threaded-by-design.text: `BTree` has zero synchronization primitives; the sibling chain, split logic, and page allocation are correct only because no concurrent reader or writer can observe intermediate states

single-threaded-cpython-masks-live-proje.text: In single-threaded CPython execution, no `append()` can interleave during `catch_up()` because `read_all()` returns a snapshot and append notifications occur only between calls.

single-threaded-masks-immutable-gap.text: In the synchronous single-threaded LSM execution model, the missing immutable memtable lifecycle step causes no observable data loss because `_flush()` completes atomically within the caller's execution flow

single-write-not-atomic-across-pages.text: General filesystem/OS knowledge, not a testable claim about this codebase

size-tiered-compaction-produces-overlapp.text: Under size-tiered compaction, SSTables at the same tier have overlapping key ranges, so min/max key bounds cannot rule out an SSTable during lookups.

size-tiered-triggers-on-sstable-count.text: Size-tiered compaction triggers when the total SSTable count meets the `min_threshold` parameter

slow-path-parallelism-requires-ordered-m.text: Tombstone ordering during recovery already covered by `bitcask-recovery-order-is-ascending`

smaller-segments-reduce-truncation-rewri.text: Smaller `max_file_size` segments reduce WAL truncation cost because more old segments can be deleted wholesale and the partial segment straddling the truncation boundary is smaller to rewrite.

snapshot-discards-writer-identity.text: _snapshot discards the writer transaction ID returned by _visible_value; causal dependency tracking is handled by callers like read and read_predicate, not by _snapshot itself.

snapshot-empty-for-nonpositive-timestamp.text: If snapshot_ts is 0 or lower than any committed version, _snapshot returns an empty dict.

snapshot-excludes-uncommitted-writes.text: `_snapshot` only includes committed versions (`commit_ts <= snapshot_ts`); all three call sites manually overlay `tx._writes` and `tx._deletes` when they need the transaction-local view

snapshot-keyed-by-projection-name.text: Each projection's snapshot is stored under `self.name` in `_store._snapshots`, so two projections with the same name on the same store will overwrite each other

snapshot-linear-scan-complexity.text: _snapshot has O(K × V) time complexity, where K is the number of distinct keys and V is the average number of versions per key, because _visible_value does a linear scan over all versions for each key.

snapshot-loss-triggers-full-replay.text: When event sourcing snapshots are missing, the system falls back to replaying all events from the log to reconstruct aggregate state — correct but O(n) in total event count

snapshot-returns-detached-copy.text: `SSIDatabase._snapshot` returns a new dict each call; callers in `read_predicate` and `commit` mutate it freely (overlaying writes, removing deletes) without corrupting the MVCC store

snapshot-state-excludes-subscription.text: Snapshot data (`_store._snapshots`) contains only `state` and `position`; subscriber callbacks registered in `EventStore._subscribers` are not captured, so restoring a snapshot does not restore live-update behavior

snapshot-uses-next-timestamp-for-current.text: During commit validation, `_snapshot(self._next_timestamp)` captures all committed versions because `_next_timestamp` is strictly greater than any existing `commit_ts`

snapshots-are-in-memory-only.text: Projection snapshots are stored in `store._snapshots` (an in-memory dict), not persisted to disk, so they are lost on process restart

snapshots-dict-is-monkey-patched.text: The `_snapshots` attribute is not declared on `EventStore`; it is lazily created by `Projection.save_snapshot` via `hasattr`/setattr on the store instance

snapshots-keyed-by-projection-name.text: Projection snapshots are stored in EventStore._snapshots keyed by the projection's name.

sort-dataset-appends-missing-keys-unsort.text: `sort_dataset` returns a sorted list but appends records missing the join key at the end without sorting them.

sort-external-merge.text: `Sort` stage spills sorted chunks to temp JSONL files when the in-memory buffer exceeds `memory_limit`, then uses `heapq.merge` with a `KeyedRecord` wrapper (seq tiebreaker) for stable k-way merge

sort-merge-join-compares-strategy-result.text: `compare_join_strategies()` runs `BroadcastHashJoin`, `PartitionedHashJoin`, and `SortMergeJoin` on the same data and verifies identical results after normalizing away `_mapper_id` tags.

sort-merge-join-detects-presorted-input.text: `SortMergeJoin` inspects whether input is already sorted and reports this via `stats["sorted_input"]`, allowing it to skip the sort step on pre-sorted data

sort-merge-join-linear-time-when-sorted.text: The SortMergeJoin executes a single linear pass (O(n + m) time) when both inputs are pre-sorted by the join key, requiring no hash table.

sparse-index-bisect-narrows-to-interval-.text: Substantially covered by existing belief `sstable-lookup-is-two-phase` which describes the binary-search-then-linear-scan pattern with O(log(N/B) + B) cost

sparse-index-limits-corruption-blast-rad.text: A corrupted data entry in an SSTable only affects lookups within one sparse index segment (between two adjacent index offsets, default 16 entries); keys indexed by other segments remain correctly accessible

sparse-index-sorted-order-invariant.text: Overlaps with `scan-range-sorted-order-assumption` and the general sorted-order invariants already captured across SSTable beliefs

split-brain-called-once-per-tick.text: `_resolve_split_brain` is called exactly once per `tick()`, as the final step after all normal message delivery.

split-brain-current-time-no-validation.text: `_resolve_split_brain` performs no validation on `current_time` and assumes it is a monotonically increasing integer consistent with the simulation.

split-brain-delivers-two-hops.text: Election messages from demoted leaders are delivered one level deep (election message + immediate response), not recursively to convergence; the next `tick()` finishes any remaining propagation.

split-brain-demotes-losers-via-start-ele.text: `_resolve_split_brain` demotes each losing leader by calling `node.start_election(current_time)`, which increments the term, sets state to candidate, clears leader_id, and returns ELECTION messages.

split-brain-ignores-unavailable-nodes.text: Only nodes where `is_available()` is `True` are considered when detecting and resolving split-brain; crashed nodes' stale leader state is ignored.

split-brain-leaves-winner-untouched.text: `_resolve_split_brain` leaves the highest-ID leader completely untouched, keeping its leader state, term, and heartbeat schedule.

split-brain-no-error-handling.text: `_resolve_split_brain` has no explicit error handling; missing receivers are silently dropped via `self.nodes.get(msg.receiver_id)` returning `None` and the `if receiver` guard.

split-brain-not-recorded-in-history.text: Elections triggered by `_resolve_split_brain` do not call `_record_leader`, so leadership changes from split-brain resolution are absent from `election_history`.

split-brain-runs-after-message-drain.text: `_resolve_split_brain` executes only after the tick's `while all_messages` delivery loop has fully drained, never mid-delivery.

split-chain-rewiring-order.text: During a leaf split, the new right page is written with the old leaf's `next_sibling` before the old leaf is rewritten to point to the new page; WAL ordering ensures the pointer target is durable before anything references it

sqlite-btree-rebalances-below-one-third-.text: SQLite's B-tree attempts redistribution with siblings when a page drops below roughly 1/3 full, and merges if redistribution fails.

sqlite-fcntl-sync-abstracts-platform-dif.text: About SQLite's VFS abstraction, not a claim about this codebase

sqlite-fsyncs-directories-after-file-ops.text: About SQLite's internal behavior, not a claim about this codebase

sqlite-fsyncs-new-file-dir-before-journa.text: SQLite ensures a new file's directory entry is fsynced before invalidating the journal or WAL, so the new file is durable before old recovery data is discarded.

sqlite-rollback-journal-copies-original-.text: SQLite's legacy rollback journal copies original pages to the journal before modifying the database file; crash recovery restores the database from those pre-modification pages.

sqlite-uses-full-merge-redistribute-when.text: SQLite performs full merge/redistribute when a page drops below approximately 1/3 full.

sqlite-uses-write-temp-fsync-rename-fsyn.text: SQLite, PostgreSQL, and RocksDB follow a four-step file replacement protocol: write a temporary file, fsync the temporary file, rename it to the final name, then fsync the parent directory.

sqlite-wal-chains-checksums-by-seeding-w.text: SQLite's WAL computes each frame's checksum by feeding the previous frame's checksum as the initial value, forming a hash chain.

sqlite-wal-header-salt-invalidates-frame.text: SQLite WAL mode uses a header salt value to invalidate existing WAL frames without physically removing them, so replay after a crash is idempotent.

ssi-commit-returns-dict-not-exception.text: `SSIDatabase.commit()` returns a structured dict `{"committed": bool, "reason": str|None, "conflicts": list}` rather than raising, letting callers inspect what conflicted for retry logic

ssi-commit-scans-committed-txns.text: The commit method checks for conflicts against committed transactions by scanning the _committed_txns append-only log for transactions that are concurrent with the committing transaction.

ssi-committed-transactions-immutable.text: Once a transaction is appended to _committed_txns, its state is never modified.

ssi-conflict-priority-order.text: When multiple conflict types are present, _conflict_reason reports them in priority order: write-write > phantom > read-write > constraint.

ssi-constraints-checked-at-commit.text: SSIDatabase maintains a _constraints collection of named invariant functions that are checked against a hypothetical post-commit snapshot during commit validation.

ssi-extends-mvcc-with-dependency-trackin.text: `SSIDatabase` adds a `_dependency_graph` and `_predicate_locks` on top of MVCC to detect read-write conflicts (write skew) that basic snapshot isolation permits

metadata.example:
self._dependency_graph = {}  # tx_id -> set of tx_ids
# on read:
if writer_tx_id is not None:
    self._dependency_graph[tx.tx_id].add(writer_tx_id)

ssi-isolation-holds-under-single-thread.text: SSI's composed invariant layers provide correct serializable snapshot isolation: MVCC enforces visibility through append-only versions and symmetric deletion rules, and SSI validation ensures own-writes are checked before store consultation, preventing lost updates.

justifications.label: Garbage collector's lack of thread safety could remove versions that active transactions need for visibility checks, violating MVCC invariants

ssi-own-writes-require-buffer-check.text: `SSIDatabase.read` must check `tx._writes` and `tx._deletes` before consulting `_store`, since a transaction's own writes aren't materialized into the shared store until commit — unlike MVCCDatabase where eager writes make own-writes visible automatically

ssi-pessimistic-mode-aborts-at-read.text: When `_pessimistic` is true, `_check_read_conflict` raises `RuntimeError` and sets `tx._status = "aborted"` at read time rather than waiting for commit — eager detection vs optimistic validation

ssi-phantom-detection-uses-predicate-ree.text: Phantom detection re-evaluates each stored predicate function against current committed state at commit time, comparing both key sets and values to the snapshot-time result

ssi-read-only-skip-validation.text: Read-only transactions (empty write set) bypass all conflict detection in `commit()` and always commit successfully — they cannot cause write skew because they don't write

ssi-serializability-through-layered-inva.text: SSI's commit path relies on three mutually reinforcing properties: read-only transactions skip validation (safe because the store contains only committed data from prior commits), and within a single transaction, writes and deletes for the same key are mutually exclusive, preventing conflicting modifications to that key within the transaction's own write set.

justifications.label: The read-only optimization is only correct BECAUSE the store invariant holds; the three beliefs form a dependency chain, not independent observations

ssi-store-contains-only-committed-data.text: `SSIDatabase._store` only contains versions stamped with commit timestamps; uncommitted writes live in `tx._writes` until commit, so every version in the store is guaranteed to be from a committed transaction

ssi-visibility-is-timestamp-comparison.text: `SSIDatabase._visible_value` determines visibility by a single comparison (`commit_ts <= snapshot_ts`) with no active-set tracking, because the deferred-write model guarantees all stored versions are committed

ssi-write-skew-detection-uses-commit-tim.text: SSIDatabase write skew detection identifies concurrent transactions by checking `commit_timestamp > tx.start_timestamp`.

ssi-writes-deletes-mutually-exclusive.text: `write()` discards any pending `delete()` for the same key and vice versa; a key is in `tx._writes` XOR `tx._deletes`, never both simultaneously

sstable-block-size-is-index-interval.text: `SSTableWriter`'s `block_size` parameter controls the sparse index frequency (one index entry per N records), not a physical byte-aligned block size; records are written contiguously with no padding or alignment to fixed byte boundaries.

sstable-compaction-manager-copies-list.text: `CompactionManager.get_sstables()` returns `list(self._sstables)` (a shallow copy), preventing iterator invalidation from concurrent mutation but not preventing file-deletion races on the underlying SSTable files

sstable-compaction-manager-lacks-bottomm.text: The `CompactionManager` tracks `_max_levels` (default 7) but has no logic to check whether lower levels contain overlapping key ranges before deciding tombstone removal, unlike LevelDB/RocksDB which use `VersionSet` metadata for this

sstable-compaction-never-removes-tombsto.text: The SSTable `merge_sstables` function accepts `remove_tombstones=False` and the `CompactionManager` never sets it to true, so partial compactions retain tombstones.

sstable-corrupted-timestamp-can-select-w.text: A bit-flip in an SSTable timestamp decodes as a valid float with no checksum, which can cause merge_sstables to pick the wrong entry when resolving by highest timestamp.

sstable-crash-leaves-zero-count-header.text: A crash between SSTableWriter creation and `finish()` leaves `entry_count=0` in the file header while data records exist on disk; `SSTableReader` trusts the header count and reads the file as empty, silently losing all written entries.

sstable-empty-table-supported.text: `test_sstable.py` verifies that an SSTable containing zero entries can be written and read.

sstable-entries-carry-timestamp.text: SSTableEntry in sstable-and-compaction/sstable.py has a timestamp field (line 28).

sstable-entry-types-binary.text: The SSTable format supports exactly two entry types (value and tombstone via `TOMBSTONE_MARKER`); there is no third type for merge operands, which would be required for RocksDB-style merge support

sstable-file-layout-header-entries-spars.text: An SSTable file is laid out as `[header][entries...][sparse index][footer]`.

sstable-footer-format-index-offset-index.text: `FOOTER_FMT = ">QI"` encodes an 8-byte index offset and a 4-byte index count, totaling 12 bytes.

sstable-footer-start-past-eof-causes-str.text: In lsm.py load_index(), a corrupted footer_start beyond EOF makes f.seek() succeed, but subsequent reads return empty bytes and struct.unpack raises struct.error.

sstable-format-lacks-integrity-and-effic.text: The SSTable format has no integrity or efficiency safeguards: entries carry no CRC or checksum, range scans bypass the sparse index and scan from file start, and the entry count header is trusted without verification — meaning corruption goes undetected, negative lookups are unnecessarily expensive, and truncated files produce silent data loss.

justifications.label: three independent gaps (integrity, index usage, header validation) leave the format defenseless

sstable-get-bisect-right-minus-one.text: `SSTable.get` uses `bisect.bisect_right(keys, key) - 1` to find the rightmost sparse-index key less than or equal to the target.

sstable-get-clamps-before-first-index-to.text: If the target key is smaller than every sparse-index key, `SSTable.get` clamps the selected index to 0 instead of returning a miss.

sstable-get-does-not-filter-tombstones.text: Already exists in the accepted beliefs registry

sstable-get-miss-returns-none.text: `SSTableReader.get()` returns `None` for keys not found in the table, rather than raising an exception

sstable-get-rebuilds-key-list-every-call.text: `SSTable.get` extracts sparse index keys into a fresh list on every call rather than caching them, making each lookup O(m) in index size before the binary search begins

sstable-get-requires-prior-load-index.text: For SSTables loaded from disk, `load_index()` must be called before `get()` or every lookup silently returns `(False, None)` — the method does not call `load_index()` itself

sstable-get-returns-tombstone-as-found.text: `SSTable.get` does not filter tombstones; a deleted key is returned as found with the tombstone value, leaving interpretation to the caller.

sstable-has-magic-and-version.text: The SSTable format (`sstable.py:10-11`) uses a 4-byte magic `b"SSTB"` and a 2-byte version field, making it the only binary format in the repo with format versioning

sstable-has-no-in-place-mutation-api.text: SSTable and SSTableReader expose no method to delete, update, or remove entries in place; deletes are written as tombstone entries and compaction rewrites whole files.

sstable-has-timestamps-lsm-ignores-them.text: `SSTableEntry` in `sstable.py` carries a `timestamp` field, but `lsm.py`'s merge and conflict resolution uses only structural SSTable ordering (sequence number priority), not per-entry timestamps

sstable-header-format-magic-version-entr.text: `HEADER_FMT = ">4sHI"` encodes the 4-byte magic `SSTB`, a 2-byte version, and a 4-byte entry count, totaling 10 bytes.

sstable-lacks-checksums.text: Covered by accepted `lsm-and-sstable-have-no-checksums` which includes both components

sstable-layer-compounds-integrity-and-pe.text: The SSTable layer has mutually reinforcing integrity and performance deficiencies: no per-entry CRC or checksum means corrupted entries return wrong values silently, and no Bloom filter integration forces every negative lookup to scan all SSTables sequentially, maximizing both the probability and frequency of encountering those silent corruptions.

justifications.label: Missing checksums create silent corruption; missing Bloom filter maximizes scan exposure to that corruption

sstable-load-index-reads-last-12-bytes.text: `SSTable.load_index()` seeks to the last 12 bytes of the file to read `footer_start` (8 bytes) and `index_count` (4 bytes).

sstable-lookup-is-two-phase.text: Point lookups in both SSTable implementations first binary-search the sparse index to identify a block, then linearly scan entries within that block's byte range; total cost is O(log(N/B) + B)

sstable-magic-is-only-integrity-check.text: The 4-byte magic `b"SSTB"` at offset 0 is the only data integrity check in the `sstable-and-compaction` SSTable read path; it gates file-type validation but provides no corruption detection for keys, values, timestamps, or structural offsets

sstable-merge-accepts-reader-objects.text: `merge_sstables()` takes `SSTableReader` instances directly as inputs, using a streaming iterator interface rather than loading entire files into memory

sstable-merge-dedup-newest-timestamp.text: When multiple SSTables contain the same key, `merge_sstables` keeps only the entry with the highest timestamp via heap ordering `(key, -timestamp)`, silently discarding all older versions.

sstable-merge-forward-only.text: The k-way merge in `sstable-and-compaction/sstable.py` is forward-only with no direction tracking or reverse iteration support; there is no direction enum, no `FindLargest`, and no heap rebuild on direction change.

sstable-merge-tombstone-removal-defaults.text: merge_sstables has a remove_tombstones parameter that defaults to False, so tombstone removal is explicitly opt-in.

sstable-metadata-has-level-field.text: `SSTableMetadata` in `sstable-and-compaction/sstable.py` tracks a `level` field, indicating the compaction module is structured for leveled compaction even though `lsm.py` uses flat single-level merges

sstable-metadata-has-level-field-but-no-.text: Duplicates existing belief `sstable-metadata-level-field-unused`, which already captures that the level field exists but has no operational use.

sstable-metadata-has-min-max-keys.text: SSTableMetadata contains min_key and max_key fields that enable range checks before any I/O.

sstable-metadata-level-field-not-persist.text: SSTableMetadata in sstable-and-compaction/sstable.py tracks a level field at line 39, but no metadata log persists it across crashes.

sstable-metadata-level-field-unused.text: `SSTableMetadata.level` in `sstable-and-compaction/sstable.py` exists as a field but has no persistent backing; level assignments would be lost on restart without a MANIFEST equivalent

sstable-metadata-tracks-key-range-and-le.text: Field existence is already implied by `sstable-metadata-level-field-unused`; the key range tracking is a minor structural detail

sstable-no-checksums.text: The SSTable format has no CRC or checksum on entries or blocks; the only validation is a magic-byte assertion (`MAGIC == b"SSTB"`) on file open.

sstable-point-lookup-correct-under-sort-.text: SSTable point lookups return correct results through two-phase search (binary search on sparse index to identify block, then linear scan within block), with clean None returns for keys not present in the table.

justifications.label: Two base beliefs about SSTable read-path correctness form a positive claim gated on the caller's responsibility to maintain sorted key order — violation silently corrupts binary search results with no error, since add() performs no sort validation

sstable-range-scan-end-exclusive.text: `range_scan(start, end)` is inclusive on `start` and exclusive on `end`.

sstable-range-scan-is-sequential-read.text: Because SSTable entries are sorted on disk, a range scan seeks via the sparse index and then reads sequentially.

sstable-range-scan-no-index-skip.text: `SSTableReader.range_scan(start, end)` scans from the beginning of the file rather than using the sparse index to skip ahead, making it O(N) regardless of range position.

sstable-reader-caches-min-max-timestamp-.text: `SSTableReader` caches `_min_key`, `_max_key`, and `_timestamp` by reading the first entry and scanning from the last sparse-index entry to find the final entry.

sstable-reader-reconstructs-metadata-by-.text: SSTableReader reconstructs min_key and max_key on open by reading the first and last entries from the SSTable file rather than loading them from a persistent manifest.

sstable-scan-is-streaming.text: `SSTable.scan()` and `scan_all()` use Python generators (yield), meaning individual SSTables already support streaming — only the cross-SSTable merge layer materializes

sstable-scan-uses-sparse-index-start-key.text: SSTable.scan uses its sparse index and bisect_right to locate a starting key within a single SSTable file.

sstable-short-read-guards-prevent-overru.text: `_read_entry()` in the LSM SSTable checks for short reads on key and value fields, preventing buffer overruns on truncated files but silently skipping all remaining entries in the scan range

sstable-single-entry-min-max-equal.text: For an SSTable with exactly one entry, `min_key` equals `max_key` in the metadata.

sstable-sorted-order-caller-responsibili.text: `SSTableWriter.add()` does not enforce sorted key order; violation silently corrupts binary search in `SSTableReader.get()`.

sstable-sparse-index-bounds-corruption.text: A corrupted SSTable data entry only affects lookups within one sparse index segment; the sparse index provides independent entry points into different file regions, bounding corruption blast radius to ~`block_size` entries

sstable-sparse-index-bounds-per-table-co.text: Composite of existing beliefs `sstable-lookup-is-two-phase` (per-table cost) and `lsm-get-probes-all-sstables-on-miss` (cross-table count)

sstable-sparse-index-every-nth.text: `SSTableReader` loads a sparse index into memory that records every `block_size`-th key and byte offset; point lookups binary-search the index then linearly scan within the block.

sstable-sparse-index-in-footer.text: Both SSTable implementations store the sparse index at the end of the file with a footer pointer, meaning bloom filters could be co-located in the same footer region without changing the file layout

sstable-sparse-index-interval-fixed-per-.text: The sparse index interval is fixed per SSTable at construction time.

sstable-test-is-script-not-framework.text: `test_sstable.py` is a linear script using bare `assert` statements and `print` progress markers, not a pytest/unittest suite — it runs top-to-bottom in a `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory` context.

sstable-test-size-tiered-threshold-2.text: `test_sstable.py` exercises size-tiered compaction with `min_threshold=2` and triggers compaction when two or more SSTables exist.

sstable-tester-covers-empty-single-entry.text: `TestEdgeCases` covers an empty SSTable, a single-entry SSTable, and a merge where all entries are tombstones.

sstable-tester-helper-default-block-size.text: The `make_sstable` test helper defaults to `block_size=4`, so a five-entry SSTable spans at least two blocks and exercises sparse-index lookups.

sstable-tester-input-entries-pre-sorted.text: The tester suite always supplies pre-sorted keys to `make_sstable`; it never tests out-of-order insertion.

sstable-tester-range-scan-exclusive-end.text: `SSTableReader.range_scan(start, end)` uses an inclusive start and exclusive end boundary, as verified by the tester suite.

sstable-tester-tests-happy-path-only.text: Meta-observation about test coverage, not a testable architectural invariant about the codebase itself

sstable-tester-uses-tmp-path-fixture.text: Every test method in `tester_test_sstable.py` uses pytest's `tmp_path` fixture, giving each test an isolated temporary directory with automatic cleanup.

sstable-tombstone-encoding-0xff.text: Tombstones are encoded on disk as a single `0xFF` byte in the value position; this is unambiguous because valid value-length fields are 4 bytes big-endian and cannot start with `0xFF` at realistic value sizes.

metadata.example:
TOMBSTONE_FLAG = 0xFF
# tombstone entries: key present, value = 0xFF marker

sstable-tombstone-is-null-value.text: Tombstones are represented at the API level as `SSTableEntry` objects with `value=None`, not as a separate deletion record type.

sstable-trailer-single-point-of-failure.text: The SSTable's 12-byte trailer (`footer_start` offset + entry `count`) is an unprotected single point of failure; its corruption makes the entire file's sparse index and data entries unreachable with no fallback discovery mechanism

sstable-validates-magic-before-read.text: The SSTable reader validates the 4-byte magic (`b'SSTB'`) before parsing any data.

sstable-wal-truncation-race.text: Subsumed by the more specific `lsm-flush-double-loss-window` above

sstable-write-path-has-dual-fragility.text: The SSTable write path has two independent fragility points: sorted key order is the caller's responsibility with no enforcement (violation silently corrupts binary search), and the file header is written as a placeholder then patched via seek-back after all entries are written (a crash between data write and header patch leaves a structurally invalid file).

justifications.label: Both the invariant contract and the write protocol have independent unguarded failure modes

sstable-writer-append-then-patch.text: `SSTableWriter` writes a placeholder header, appends all entries and the sparse index, then seeks back to byte 0 to patch the final entry count — an unfinished SSTable has `entry_count=0` and appears empty.

sstable-writer-finish-lacks-fsync.text: SSTableWriter.finish() calls close() without any preceding fsync(), so SSTable data may remain in the page cache.

sstable-writer-finish-no-fsync.text: `sstable-and-compaction/sstable.py:SSTableWriter.finish()` closes the file without calling `flush()` or `os.fsync()`, relying on implicit Python close-time buffer flush with no disk durability guarantee.

sstable-writer-is-natural-filter-builder.text: The `SSTableWriter.add()` → `finish()` lifecycle is the natural integration point for per-SSTable bloom filter construction, since keys are already iterated in sorted order during the write pass

sstable-writer-never-fsyncs-data-or-dire.text: `sstable-and-compaction/sstable.py` writes SSTables via `SSTableWriter.finish()` but never calls `os.fsync()` on the file data or the directory; the LSM tree's `SSTable.write()` has the same gap.

sstable-writer-no-fsync-on-close.text: `SSTableWriter.finish()` at `sstable-and-compaction/sstable.py:91` calls `close()` without prior `fsync()`, leaving newly flushed SSTables vulnerable to loss if the OS page cache hasn't been written to disk

sstable-writer-opens-final-path-directly.text: SSTableWriter.__init__ opens the SSTable at its final path with open(filepath, 'wb') rather than using a temporary path.

sstable-writer-single-file-lifecycle.text: `SSTableWriter` binds to one file descriptor at construction with no method to rotate to a new file mid-write, making it structurally incompatible with size-bounded output splitting

sstable-zero-footer-count-causes-all-key.text: When the SSTable trailer's count field decodes to 0, load_index() leaves the sparse index empty and get() returns (False, None) for every key.

stage-timing-subtracts-downstream.text: `Stage._tracked_process` subtracts time spent after each `yield` (downstream processing time) to attribute wall-clock time accurately to each individual stage

standalone-wal-always-pairs-flush-fsync.text: Already in the accepted beliefs list.

standalone-wal-header-packs-length-then-.text: The standalone WAL record header format `<IIQBi` serializes the record length before the CRC field.

standalone-wal-proper-sync.text: Claim that standalone WAL pairs flush+fsync "in all three sync modes" is inaccurate — `"none"` mode intentionally skips fsync, contradicting the entry's own analysis.

standard-bloom-filter-uses-one-bit-per-p.text: BloomFilter stores its bit array in `bytearray((self._m + 7) // 8)`, using one bit per position.

standard-bloom-suffices-for-immutable-ss.text: Standard bloom filters lack deletion support, but SSTables are write-once-then-discarded, so deletion is never needed and the 8x space savings over counting filters is free

stcs-assumes-input-sstables-sorted.text: `_stcs_compact` relies on `merge_sstables` assuming each input SSTable yields entries in key order; `add_sstable()` does not prevent adding an unsorted SSTable.

stcs-compact-does-not-delete-old-files.text: Duplicates `compaction-manager-never-deletes-old-files` — already captured that CompactionManager orphans input files on disk after merging.

stcs-compact-mutates-sstable-list.text: `_stcs_compact` both removes old and appends new entries to `self._sstables` as a side effect; callers must not hold references into the list across a compaction call.

stcs-compaction-threshold-default-4.text: Size-tiered compaction merges a size tier into one SSTable when the tier accumulates `min_threshold` SSTables, with a default of 4.

stcs-duplicate-sstable-remove-raises-val.text: `_stcs_compact` uses `list.remove(sst)` on each compacted input; if an SSTable appears in multiple buckets or was already removed, this raises `ValueError` and is not defended against.

stcs-low-write-high-space-amplification.text: Size-tiered compaction has low write amplification and high space amplification because it merges similarly sized groups and allows multiple SSTables with overlapping key ranges to coexist.

stcs-merges-all-qualifying-buckets-per-c.text: Size-tiered `run_compaction()` processes every bucket that meets `min_threshold` in a single call, while leveled compaction processes at most one level per call.

stcs-merges-within-size-tiers.text: Size-tiered compaction only merges SSTables in the same size tier (determined by `_get_tier()` comparing `file_size` against `_size_thresholds`); it never merges a small SSTable directly with a much larger one.

stcs-min-threshold-controls-merge-trigge.text: In size-tiered compaction, the min_threshold parameter controls how many similarly sized SSTables must accumulate before a merge is triggered; the test uses min_threshold=2.

stcs-min-threshold-default-four.text: A size tier must accumulate at least 4 SSTables (the default `_min_threshold`) before `_stcs_compact` merges them; buckets below this threshold are skipped entirely.

stcs-no-op-returns-empty-when-no-bucket-.text: Calling `_stcs_compact` when no size bucket meets `_min_threshold` is safe and returns an empty list without merging anything.

stcs-output-path-collision-overwrites-ex.text: If `_next_path()` returns a path that already exists, `SSTableWriter` opens it with `wb` and silently overwrites the existing file.

stcs-overlapping-key-ranges.text: Size-tiered compaction allows multiple SSTables at the same tier to contain overlapping key ranges, requiring point lookups to check all SSTables in a tier

storage-crash-recovery-has-no-safe-path.text: No storage engine has a fully safe crash recovery path: compaction lacks atomicity, WAL replay ignores batch boundaries, and CRC checksums leave routing metadata unprotected — corruption can enter via unprotected metadata, persist through non-validating compaction, and survive recovery via batch-unaware replay.

justifications.label: Three independent crash-recovery gaps compound: atomic file operations are absent, batch integrity is unchecked during replay, and metadata sits outside CRC coverage

storage-engines-use-flush-and-fsync-for-.text: The B-Tree PageManager, WAL, Bitcask, and LSM implementations call flush() followed by os.fsync() to force writes to stable storage.

storage-has-no-self-healing-at-any-layer.text: Storage engines degrade monotonically during normal operation (leaked pages, growing height, no rebalancing) and have no safe recovery after crashes (non-atomic compaction, partial batch replay, unchecked metadata) — there is no path from degraded state back to healthy state.

justifications.label: depth-2 degradation + depth-2 crash unsafety combine to show no self-healing exists at any layer

storage-operations-have-unbounded-memory.text: Three core storage operations materialize entire datasets in memory with no streaming, pagination, or backpressure: LSM range scans load all matching entries into a dict before returning, compaction buffers all merged entries into a list before writing, and SSTable lookups rebuild the sparse index key list on every call — creating O(n) memory pressure proportional to total data size rather than result size.

justifications.label: All three operations eagerly materialize full datasets with no memory bound

store-range-scan-passes-global-bounds.text: `RangePartitionedStore.range_scan` passes the same global `start_key`/`end_key` to every overlapping partition rather than clamping to partition boundaries, relying on `bisect_left` to naturally exclude out-of-range keys.

strategy-enum-covers-two-of-three.text: `ConflictStrategy` implements LWW and custom merge but not CRDTs; the CRDT module exists separately in `crdts.py` with no integration into the multi-leader replication strategy dispatch

strategy-selection-is-binary.text: `CompactionManager` compares `strategy` with `==` against `"size_tiered"` — any other string silently selects leveled compaction with no validation or error.

stream-join-bounds-materialization-via-w.text: `StreamJoinProcessor` expires buffered events when they fall below `watermark - window_duration`, bounding memory at the cost of potentially dropping late-arriving matches

stream-join-buffers-bounded-by-window.text: The processor actively expires events so buffer sizes remain proportional to `window_duration × event_rate`, not total events processed; tests confirm buffers stay under 10 per side after 1000 events with a 5-second window.

stream-join-buffers-keyed-by-join-key.text: `StreamJoinProcessor` buffers events in per-side `defaultdict(list)` keyed by join key and probes only the same key in the opposite buffer.

stream-join-correctness-depends-on-windo.text: Stream join correctness depends on consistent alignment across three independent window mechanisms: join and aggregation windows are configured independently with no constraint preventing misalignment, expiration uses a one-sided cutoff that doesn't match the symmetric matching predicate, and buffer size is bounded only by the window duration relative to watermark advancement rate.

justifications.label: Three independently configured window mechanisms must stay semantically aligned without enforcement

stream-join-defers-miss-emission-until-e.text: `StreamJoinProcessor` emits outer-join misses only at expiration (`watermark - window_duration`), not eagerly on arrival.

stream-join-event-timestamp-is-event-tim.text: `StreamEvent.timestamp` represents event time, not processing time.

stream-join-full-outer-emits-both-side-m.text: In a FULL_OUTER join, unmatched left events produce miss results with right_event=None and unmatched right events produce miss results with left_event=None.

stream-join-get-results-destructive.text: `get_results()` swaps out and resets the accumulated results list; callers see only results since the previous drain (pull-based consumption model)
