wal-max-file-size-is-soft-limit.text: `_max_file_size` is a soft cap: the check triggers rotation for the *next* write, it does not prevent the current write from exceeding the limit.

wal-module-has-batch-atomicity-pattern.text: Duplicates existing belief `wal-batch-atomicity-via-commit-record`, which already describes the COMMIT-marker pattern for atomic batch writes.

wal-module-uses-locking-lsm-does-not.text: The WAL module in `write-ahead-log/wal.py` uses `self._lock` for thread safety across its mutation paths, while the LSM tree module has zero locking or concurrency control despite having the same concurrent-access risks

wal-multi-segment-continuity-is-reliable.text: Multi-segment WAL replay provides reliable cross-segment continuity: segment rotation fsyncs the outgoing file before closing it, and EOF within one segment advances to the next rather than terminating replay, ensuring no inter-segment data loss during normal operation.

justifications.label: Reliable under normal operation but missing directory fsync means a crash could lose a newly created segment directory entry

wal-no-begin-marker.text: The WAL protocol has no BEGIN record type, making it impossible during replay to distinguish a standalone PUT from the first record of a multi-record batch — the structural root cause of why COMMIT markers cannot enforce atomicity.

wal-no-begin-marker-prevents-batch-group.text: Substantially overlaps with accepted `wal-no-nested-batches` and existing `replay-does-not-enforce-batch-atomicity`

wal-no-block-fragmentation.text: Duplicates existing `wal-contiguous-no-block-alignment` which already states the WAL uses variable-length records with no fixed block boundaries.

wal-no-commit-method.text: The standalone `WriteAheadLog` class in `write-ahead-log/wal.py` has no `commit` method; sync-then-truncate coordination must be implemented by a higher-level storage engine that composes the WAL with a data file

wal-no-concurrent-group-commit.text: The WAL uses a single `threading.Lock` and a write counter for batch sync rather than a concurrent waiter queue, so it cannot amortize fsync cost across concurrent callers the way PostgreSQL's group commit does.

wal-no-directory-fsync.text: The WAL implementation never fsyncs the parent directory after segment creation or deletion, meaning file metadata changes (including unlinks) are not guaranteed durable on crash on Linux

wal-no-gap-detection.text: Neither the WAL reader nor any visible consumer checks for sequence number gaps after replay, making silent data loss from mid-file corruption undetectable

wal-no-nested-batches.text: The WAL format has no batch-start marker and no nesting support; the lock held during `append_batch` prevents interleaving, making nested or concurrent batches structurally impossible

wal-no-partial-batch-test.text: Close to existing `wal-no-torn-write-tests`; partial batch is a subset of torn write scenarios

wal-no-resync-after-corruption.text: A corrupted `record_length` in the WAL causes `_read_record` to misframe all subsequent records; there is no magic-byte or scan-forward recovery mechanism to re-synchronize

wal-no-rollback-on-io-failure.text: If `write()` or `fsync()` fails mid-batch in `append_batch`, sequence numbers are already incremented with no rollback mechanism, creating a permanent gap in the sequence space.

wal-no-torn-write-tests.text: The WAL module has no tests for truncated records, CRC mismatches, or partial writes; the B-tree module tests CRC corruption explicitly but the WAL does not

wal-no-undo-recovery.text: Duplicates `wal-is-redo-only` — already captured that the WAL implements only redo recovery with no undo phase.

wal-none-sync-mode-is-no-op.text: In WAL sync mode 'none', the _do_sync method performs neither flush() nor fsync().

wal-not-imported-outside-tests.text: No production module imports the standalone `WriteAheadLog`; it is only referenced in `test_wal.py` and `tester_test_wal.py`, meaning crash-safe commit coordination using this module is unimplemented

wal-op-commit-constant-value-3.text: OP_COMMIT is defined as integer value 3 in write-ahead-log/wal.py.

wal-op-type-is-redundantly-crc-protected.text: In `write-ahead-log/wal.py`, `op_type_byte` is included in both the CRC input and the record header, making it the only header field that receives CRC protection.

wal-op-types-are-put-delete-commit-check.text: The WAL op_type byte is one of four values: PUT(1), DELETE(2), COMMIT(3), CHECKPOINT(4).

wal-open-latest-external-delete-crashes.text: If an external process deletes the last WAL file between `_wal_files()` and `os.path.getsize()` in `_open_latest`, `getsize` raises `FileNotFoundError` and crashes the constructor.

wal-open-latest-init-only.text: `_open_latest` is called exclusively from `__init__`, so the TOCTOU window between `_wal_files()` and `os.path.getsize()` cannot be hit by concurrent WAL operations

wal-open-latest-postcondition.text: Substantially overlaps with `rotation-preserves-fd-invariant`; same postcondition pattern for a closely related method.

wal-open-latest-three-step-non-atomic.text: `_open_latest` performs directory listing via `_wal_files()`, then `os.path.getsize()` on the last file, then `open(..., 'ab')`, with no atomicity guarantee across the three steps.

wal-open-latest-two-callers.text: Call site enumeration is unstable and more trivia than invariant; not something that would break if violated.

wal-overshoot-file-rotates-on-reopen.text: _open_latest checks os.path.getsize(last) < max_file_size on startup, so a WAL file overshot by a batch triggers a new file on the next open.

wal-partial-read-is-eof.text: `_read_record` returns `None` on partial/short reads (torn writes), treated as EOF; this is distinct from CRC mismatch which raises `ValueError` — the distinction separates "crash during write" from "data corruption."

wal-partial-truncate-idempotent-replay.text: If the standalone WAL's `truncate()` crashes mid-iteration over files, un-processed files retain old records that will be replayed on recovery; this is safe because PUT and DELETE are idempotent against an already-current store

wal-protects-data-not-metadata.text: The WAL protects user key-value writes but does not record SSTable-level state transitions (flush, compaction, level assignment), leaving metadata changes unprotected across crashes

wal-provides-crash-safety-not-concurrenc.text: The WAL syncs with `os.fsync` for durability guarantees only; it has no role in coordinating concurrent access, consistent with the single-threaded design

wal-read-all-no-lock.text: Covered by existing `replay-not-lock-protected-during-read` which captures the same locking gap

wal-read-all-requires-caller-flush.text: Covered by existing `replay-flush-before-read` (replay flushes before reading) and `iterate-flushes-without-fsync` (iterate flushes without fsync)

wal-read-path-validates-crc.text: _read_record recomputes CRC32 on every record read and raises ValueError on mismatch, so corrupted records are not silently accepted as long as length fields parse.

wal-read-record-advances-by-4-plus-recor.text: On successful read, `_read_record` advances the file position by `4 + record_length` bytes.

wal-read-record-crc-mismatch-raises-valu.text: On CRC mismatch, `_read_record` raises `ValueError` (including the sequence number in the message) rather than returning None.

wal-read-record-invalid-utf8-raises.text: Invalid UTF-8 in key or value causes `_read_record` to raise `UnicodeDecodeError` (unhandled).

wal-read-record-key-offset-17.text: The key bytes are extracted by slicing from offset 17 (after 4-byte CRC, 8-byte seq_num, 1-byte op_type, and 4-byte key_len) within the record body.

wal-read-record-no-length-bounds-check.text: `_read_record` does not validate that `key_len` or `val_len` are within the bounds of the record body; a corrupted length can cause a short slice, which is later caught by the CRC check if the payload doesn't match.

wal-read-record-stateless.text: `_read_record` is a module-level function with no dependency on `WriteAheadLog` instance state, enabling its use during WAL construction/recovery before the object is fully initialized.

wal-read-record-truncation-safe.text: Duplicates `wal-partial-read-is-eof` which already establishes that short reads are treated as EOF.

wal-read-record-unknown-op-maps-to-unkno.text: If the op_type_byte is not in `OP_NAMES`, `_read_record` silently maps it to the string `"UNKNOWN"` via `OP_NAMES.get()`.

wal-record-dataclass-has-no-old-value-fi.text: The `WALRecord` dataclass stores `seq_num`, `op_type`, `key`, `value`, and `checksum`, with no field for the previous value of the key.

wal-record-format-layout.text: The WAL v1 record layout is: 4-byte record_length, 4-byte CRC, 8-byte seq_num, 1-byte op_type, 4-byte key_len, key bytes, 4-byte val_len, and value bytes.

wal-record-format-length-prefixed.text: Each WAL record on disk is prefixed with a 4-byte little-endian uint32 length covering everything after itself, allowing the reader to atomically skip or validate entire records.

wal-record-frame-layout.text: A WAL record frame is laid out as 4-byte record length, 4-byte CRC32, 8-byte sequence number, 1-byte op type, 4-byte key length, key, 4-byte value length, and value.

wal-record-header-contains-record-length.text: `write-ahead-log/wal.py:_encode_record` writes a length-prefixed record with 4-byte record length, 4-byte CRC32, 8-byte seq_num, 1-byte op_type, 4-byte key_len, key, 4-byte value_len, and value.

wal-record-length-excludes-own-prefix.text: The `record_length` field counts 21 + len(key) + len(value) bytes — everything after the 4-byte length prefix itself — so total on-disk size per record is `record_length + 4`.

wal-record-length-prefix-is-4-bytes.text: The WAL record format uses a 4-byte record_length prefix before the CRC, sequence number, operation type, key length, key, value length, and value.

wal-record-length-prefixed.text: Every WAL record is prefixed with a 4-byte little-endian length covering all subsequent fields (CRC through value), enabling the reader to know exactly how many bytes to consume

metadata.example:
record_length = 4 + 8 + 1 + 4 + len(key) + 4 + len(value)
header = struct.pack("<IIQBi", record_length, crc, seq_num, op_type_byte, len(key))
return header + key + struct.pack("<i", len(value)) + value

wal-record-op-type-is-1-byte.text: The WAL record format stores a 1-byte op_type field after the sequence number.

wal-record-sequence-number-is-8-bytes.text: The WAL record format stores an 8-byte sequence number after the 4-byte CRC field.

wal-records-have-no-random-access-index.text: WAL records have no random-access index, so there is no reliable way to find the next valid record boundary after corruption.

wal-recover-breaks-on-short-read.text: During recovery, if the remaining bytes are insufficient for the 12-byte header or the payload plus 4-byte checksum, parsing breaks and treats it as a torn write at the tail.

wal-recover-entry-layout.text: Each WAL entry is laid out as `[seq:4B][page_num:4B][data_len:4B][page_data:data_len B][checksum:4B]`.

wal-recover-io-error-leaves-wal-intact.text: If an I/O error occurs during `write_page` or `sync()` in recovery, the exception propagates and the WAL is left intact for the next startup to re-attempt recovery.

wal-recover-on-every-startup.text: `BTree.__init__` calls `WAL.recover()` unconditionally on every startup; an empty WAL short-circuits after a single read with no further I/O

wal-recover-seq-num-shares-toctou-shape.text: `_recover_seq_num` iterates `_wal_files()` and opens each WAL file during initialization, giving it the same list-then-open TOCTOU shape as `_open_latest`.

wal-recover-seq-vs-read-all-differ.text: `_recover_seq_num` uses `break` on corruption (continues to next file) while `_read_all_records` uses `return` (stops everything) — recovery is lenient to maximize the sequence counter, replay is strict to avoid replaying past corruption

wal-recover-then-truncate.text: WAL recovery fsyncs the data file via `page_manager.sync()` before truncating the WAL, so a crash during recovery itself leaves the WAL intact for re-replay

wal-recovery-contract-is-valid-prefix.text: The WAL's recovery model guarantees a valid-prefix contract: both corruption (CRC mismatch halts replay returning prior valid records) and partial writes (treated as EOF, not error) cause replay to stop cleanly, always returning a consistent prefix of the written log.

justifications.label: Both corruption and torn write handling converge on the same stop-and-return-valid behavior, defining an implicit valid-prefix contract

wal-recovery-depends-on-listdir.text: WAL segment discovery during recovery uses `os.listdir()`, so any segment whose parent directory entry was not fsynced becomes invisible after a crash — connecting the dir-fsync gap to concrete data loss.

wal-recovery-discards-entry-on-checksum-.text: During WAL recovery, a checksum mismatch causes the entry to be silently discarded and replay to stop.

wal-recovery-infrastructure-is-vestigial.text: The WAL carries vestigial recovery-related infrastructure: sequence numbers are monotonically assigned under lock and stored in every record but never consulted for ordering, deduplication, or gap detection during recovery (file position alone determines replay order), and checkpoint records occupy positions in the same sequence space but are neither searched for during recovery scanning nor used as truncation watermarks.

justifications.label: Sequence numbers and checkpoint records form a coherent recovery protocol that was implemented but never wired up

wal-recovery-scans-full-file.text: `_recover_seq_num` in `write-ahead-log/wal.py` reads every record in every WAL file sequentially from byte zero; there is no seek-to-end or block-skip optimization, making recovery O(file-size)

wal-replay-accepts-after-seq-filter.text: The WAL `replay()` method accepts an `after_seq` parameter used to filter records by sequence number.

wal-replay-accepts-standalone-appends-wi.text: Standalone records written by `append()` are included in `replay()` output without requiring a `COMMIT` marker because each append is individually fsynced.

wal-replay-after-seq-is-exclusive.text: `replay(after_seq=n)` returns only WAL records whose sequence number is greater than `n`, making the filter exclusive at the checkpoint boundary.

wal-replay-built-on-iterate.text: `replay()` is implemented by consuming the raw record stream from `iterate()` and filtering or grouping records into committed batches.

wal-replay-filters-commit-and-checkpoint.text: replay() filters out COMMIT and CHECKPOINT control records and returns only PUT/DELETE records.

wal-replay-flushes-without-fsync.text: `WriteAheadLog.replay()` flushes the active file descriptor but does not fsync before scanning WAL files.

wal-replay-ignores-commit.text: `replay()` returns all PUT/DELETE records regardless of whether they are followed by a COMMIT record, meaning uncommitted batches are replayed identically to committed ones.

wal-replay-includes-uncommitted-puts.text: Duplicates `replay-does-not-enforce-batch-atomicity` and `wal-replay-ignores-commit`, which already establish that replay returns all PUT/DELETE records regardless of COMMIT presence.

wal-replay-is-flat.text: Duplicates existing belief `wal-replay-ignores-commit` which already states replay returns all PUT/DELETE records regardless of COMMIT presence

wal-replay-is-read-only.text: Trivial — a replay/recovery method being read-only is expected design, not a breakable invariant

wal-replay-iterates-segments-in-filename.text: WAL replay iterates segment files in sorted filename order, so sequence-number monotonicity across file boundaries is not explicitly verified.

wal-replay-no-atomicity-check.text: `replay()` does not verify that batch operations have a corresponding COMMIT record; partial batches from a mid-write crash would be replayed as if committed, since replay filters only by record type, not by batch completeness

wal-replay-order-matches-append-order.text: Sequential order preservation is inherent to reading a sequential log file; not an invariant that could be violated by a code change

wal-rotate-bypasses-do-sync.text: Overlaps with existing belief `rotation-always-fsyncs`; the counter-reset implication is a second-order effect of the broader issue already captured in `batch-write-count-not-reset-on-forced-sync`.

wal-rotate-does-not-fsync-directory.text: The WAL's `_rotate` method fsyncs the old WAL file but does not fsync the directory entry for the newly created file.

wal-rotate-fsync-before-close.text: `_rotate` always fsyncs the outgoing segment before closing it, ensuring no buffered writes are lost during segment rotation.

wal-rotate-fsyncs-directory-after-new-se.text: In write-ahead-log/wal.py, _rotate() fsyncs the directory after creating a new WAL segment file.

wal-rotate-new-segment-dir-entry-unsynce.text: In `write-ahead-log/wal.py`, `_rotate()` fsyncs the old segment's contents before closing but does not fsync the directory after creating the new segment file; the new WAL segment's directory entry could be lost.

wal-rotate-next-filename-increments-last.text: WAL `_rotate()` computes the next filename by parsing the integer prefix of the last WAL file and adding one.

wal-rotate-no-gap-protection.text: If a segment file is manually deleted from the directory, `_rotate` can produce a filename that reuses a previously-used number, since it derives the next name solely from the current highest filename.

wal-rotate-opens-new-segment-in-ab-mode.text: `_rotate()` creates the new WAL segment by calling `open(self._current_file, "ab")`, which creates the file and modifies the parent directory.

wal-rotate-reachable-from-all-write-path.text: `_rotate()` in `write-ahead-log/wal.py` is reachable from `_open_latest` at startup and via `_maybe_rotate` from `append()`, `append_batch()`, and `checkpoint()`, exposing all WAL write paths to the directory-fsync gap.

wal-rotation-creates-new-files.text: The new-file-creation behavior during rotation is already implied by existing rotation beliefs; the primary significance is about ext4 `auto_da_alloc` interaction, which is filesystem behavior rather than a codebase invariant.

wal-rotation-creates-new-files-not-repla.text: WAL rotation creates new numbered `.wal` files via `open(..., "ab")` rather than replacing an existing file, so ext4 `auto_da_alloc` does not protect the new directory entry.

wal-rotation-creates-numbered-segment-fi.text: WAL segment rotation creates numbered .wal files such as 000001.wal and 000002.wal when a segment exceeds max_file_size.

wal-rotation-creates-unsynced-directory-.text: Already exists as an accepted belief with this exact ID

wal-rotation-follows-sync-step.text: In WAL `append()`, `_maybe_rotate()` is called after `_do_sync()`, so rotation follows the sync step.

wal-rotation-is-post-write.text: Both `append` and `append_batch` call `_maybe_rotate()` after write and sync complete; rotation never interrupts an in-progress write, and the file only rotates on the next operation

wal-rotation-lacks-directory-fsync.text: `write-ahead-log/wal.py:_rotate()` creates a new WAL file without fsyncing the directory, so after a crash the new file might not appear in the directory listing and `_wal_files()` would miss it on recovery.

wal-rotation-monotonicity-untested.text: `test_rotation` asserts record count after rotation but does not verify that sequence numbers are monotonically increasing across file boundaries — the cross-file monotonicity invariant holds by construction but has no regression test.

wal-rotation-on-size.text: The core claim (WAL rotates based on file size) is obvious from the code structure; the more interesting ordering invariant is captured by `wal-rotation-is-post-write`.

wal-rotation-test-uses-max-file-size-100.text: `test_rotation` sets `max_file_size=100` to force multiple `.wal` segment files and verifies all 20 records are readable across segments.

wal-segment-naming-zero-padded.text: WAL segment filenames are zero-padded 6-digit integers (`000001.wal`, `000002.wal`, ...) derived from the highest existing filename plus one, which makes lexicographic sort equal numeric sort.

metadata.example: self._current_file = os.path.join(self._dir, f"{next_num:06d}.wal")

wal-seq-num-drives-truncate-and-replay-f.text: The WAL seq_num drives truncate (keeps records with seq_num > up_to_seq) and replay filtering (skips records with seq_num <= after_seq).

wal-seq-num-global-monotonic.text: `_seq_num` is a single in-memory counter that only increments via `+= 1`; all records across all WAL files share one monotonically increasing sequence space that never resets, even across file rotation.

wal-seq-num-is-monotonic-not-page-lsn.text: WAL `seq_num` increases monotonically across all records but is not stamped onto data pages, so there is no mechanism to detect whether a replayed operation was already applied — making replay non-idempotent against the underlying store.

wal-seq-num-recovered-on-init.text: On construction, `_recover_seq_num()` scans all WAL files to find the maximum surviving sequence number, guaranteeing the monotonic counter never goes backward across crashes

wal-seq-nums-are-vestigial.text: WAL sequence numbers are monotonic and strictly increasing but entirely vestigial: they are computed under lock, stored in every record, and parsed during recovery, yet never consulted for ordering, deduplication, or gap detection — file position alone determines replay order.

justifications.label: Four beliefs establish that sequence numbers are maintained with full rigor but serve no functional purpose

wal-seq-nums-strictly-monotonic.text: Sequence numbers increment under a threading.Lock and are never reused; on recovery, all WAL files are scanned to find the high-water mark so new records continue the sequence.

metadata.example:
with self._lock:
    self._seq_num += 1
    seq = self._seq_num

wal-seq-reset-on-commit.text: The WAL sequence counter resets to 0 on every commit; sequence numbers are only meaningful within a single uncommitted transaction window

wal-seq-starts-at-one.text: Sequence numbers begin at 1 for the first appended record; an empty WAL reports `current_seq_num() == 0`

wal-seq-unused-in-recovery.text: The 4-byte sequence number field in each WAL entry is parsed during `recover()` but never consulted; replay order is determined solely by file offset

wal-sequence-numbers-enable-ordered-reco.text: WAL sequence numbers provide infrastructure for ordered recovery: they are recovered from disk on init, checkpoints consume positions in the same monotonic space, and the total ordering could enable gap detection and ordered replay.

justifications.label: sequence number infrastructure exists and is maintained but replay ignores it entirely

wal-single-writer-fd.text: At most one file descriptor is open for WAL writes at any time; `_rotate` closes the old fd before opening the new one.

metadata.example:
self._fd = open(self._current_file, "ab")
# single file descriptor, all writes go through self._fd

wal-single-writer-thread-level.text: The WAL enforces single-writer via `threading.Lock` but has no inter-process locking mechanism (no flock/PID file), so the single-writer invariant holds only within a single OS process

wal-size-check-uses-disk.text: `_open_latest` checks on-disk file size via `os.path.getsize`, not an in-memory counter, making it correct across crash/restart boundaries.

wal-supports-sync-batch-none-modes.text: WriteAheadLog._do_sync supports per-write fsync ('sync'), batched fsync every N writes ('batch'), and no fsync ('none').

wal-sync-has-three-modes.text: The WAL `_do_sync` method supports three sync modes: sync, batch, and none.

wal-sync-mode-configurable.text: The sync mode configurability is covered by `wal-batch-sync-count-controls-durability-window`; the force-sync behavior of `append_batch` and `checkpoint` is covered by `wal-batch-always-fsyncs` and `wal-checkpoint-forces-sync`.

wal-sync-mode-default-is-sync.text: `WriteAheadLog` defaults to `sync_mode="sync"`, calling `flush()` + `os.fsync()` after every single `append` call — the safest and slowest mode.

wal-sync-mode-none-is-unsafe.text: Durability gap covered by `none-mode-never-syncs-on-append`; testing observation is not a code invariant

wal-sync-mode-none-skips-fsync-without-f.text: When sync_mode is none and force is false, _do_sync performs no fsync.

wal-sync-mode-survives-crash.text: With `sync_mode="sync"`, WAL records are durable immediately after `append` returns — they survive process death even if `close()` is never called.

wal-sync-mode-unvalidated.text: `WriteAheadLog` accepts any string as `sync_mode` without validation; values other than `"sync"` and `"batch"` silently disable all fsync.

wal-sync-modes-test-only-constructs-wal.text: `test_sync_modes` only constructs a WAL in each of the `sync`, `batch`, and `none` modes without error; it does not verify durability behavior for those modes.

wal-sync-modes-three.text: The WAL supports three sync modes: 'sync' (fsync every write), 'batch' (fsync every N writes), and implicit 'none'.

wal-tail-corruption-safe.text: Covered by existing `wal-corruption-returns-valid-prefix` and `wal-partial-read-is-eof` which together establish that partial/torn writes at EOF are handled safely

wal-test-basic-covers-individual-and-bat.text: `test_basic` exercises three individual appends followed by a three-operation batch and asserts replay returns six PUT/DELETE records with COMMIT/CHECKPOINT filtered out.

wal-test-crash-recovery-omits-partial-ba.text: `test_crash_recovery` only verifies standalone PUTs survive a reopen and does not test the partial-batch scenario where PUTs exist on disk without a trailing COMMIT.

wal-test-suite-has-nine-tests.text: `write-ahead-log/test_wal.py` contains 9 test functions covering basic operations, crash recovery, corruption, truncation, rotation, iteration, empty WAL, sync modes, and large values.

wal-test-suite-lacks-partial-batch-crash.text: The WAL test suite does not include a test for a crash during `append_batch` (partial write without a COMMIT record).

wal-tests-omit-filesystem-error-paths.text: The WAL test suites have no explicit tests for a nonexistent directory, disk full, or permission errors.

wal-tests-use-temp-directory-isolation.text: Every test in `write-ahead-log/test_wal.py` uses `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()` as a context manager so WAL files are isolated and cleaned up automatically.

wal-thread-safety-stranded-by-callers.text: The WAL carefully serializes all mutations (append, append_batch, checkpoint, truncate) under a threading.Lock, but both callers that depend on it have no synchronization for their own shared state: the LSM tree mutates _memtable, _sstables, and _immutable_memtables without any locking or atomic swaps, and _sstables specifically is mutated by both flush (append) and compact (full replacement) concurrently — the lock protects the log but not the data structures built from it.

justifications.label: WAL's threading.Lock is the only concurrency protection in the storage stack, but it guards the wrong layer — callers that depend on WAL durability have no protection for their own shared state

wal-three-op-batch-commit-seq-seven.text: A three-operation WAL batch produces a COMMIT record at sequence 7 in the test case.

wal-three-sync-modes.text: Already covered by existing `batch-mode-defers-fsync` and `none-mode-never-syncs-on-append` which document the individual sync mode behaviors

wal-truncate-blocks-all-operations.text: `truncate` holds `self._lock` for its entire duration (close, rewrite, reopen), blocking all concurrent appends, replays, and iterates

wal-truncate-bypasses-do-sync-counter-re.text: truncate calls os.fsync at wal.py:184 outside _do_sync, so _write_count is not reset by truncation.

wal-truncate-closes-active-fd-before-sca.text: WriteAheadLog.truncate() flushes, fsyncs, closes the current file descriptor, and sets _fd to None before scanning segment files.

wal-truncate-closes-write-fd.text: `truncate()` flushes, fsyncs, and closes the current write file descriptor before iterating segments, preventing conflicts with files it may need to delete or rewrite

wal-truncate-current-seq-deletes-all.text: Passing `current_seq_num()` as `up_to_seq` to `truncate` deletes all records because every record has a sequence number at or below the current sequence number.

wal-truncate-deletes-empty-files.text: WAL files where every record has `seq_num <= up_to_seq` are deleted entirely via `os.remove` rather than left as empty files on disk

wal-truncate-deletes-empty-segment-files.text: During WAL truncation, any segment file with no surviving records is deleted entirely rather than rewritten.

wal-truncate-deletes-files-with-no-kept-.text: If no records remain above the truncation sequence number, `WriteAheadLog.truncate()` deletes the WAL file entirely.

wal-truncate-deletes-oldest-first.text: `truncate()` iterates segments via `_wal_files()` in oldest-first order, so a crash mid-truncation leaves a contiguous suffix of segments — preserving the recovery invariant that surviving files form a continuous sequence

wal-truncate-drops-after-corruption.text: During truncate, if a corrupt record is encountered in a WAL file, all subsequent records in that file are silently discarded regardless of their sequence number — even records with `seq_num > up_to_seq`

wal-truncate-fsyncs-before-scan.text: `truncate()` flushes and fsyncs the current WAL file before scanning for records to remove, preventing data loss from buffered writes that haven't reached disk

wal-truncate-inclusive-boundary.text: `truncate(n)` removes records with `seq_num <= n` (inclusive upper bound), keeping only records strictly greater than `n`

wal-truncate-is-inclusive.text: `truncate(seq)` removes all records with sequence number less than or equal to `seq`, keeping only records where `seq_num > seq`

wal-truncate-keeps-records-above-cutoff.text: truncate(up_to_seq) removes only records with seq_num <= up_to_seq; records with sequence numbers greater than the cutoff are preserved.

wal-truncate-no-bounds-check.text: `truncate` does not validate that `up_to_seq` is within range — passing a value beyond `current_seq_num()` silently deletes all records without error

wal-truncate-not-atomic.text: Duplicates existing `wal-truncate-not-crash-safe` — both describe the lack of atomic file operations (no temp-file-rename pattern) during truncation

wal-truncate-not-crash-safe.text: `truncate()` rewrites WAL files in place without atomic rename, so a crash during truncation can leave the log in an inconsistent state.

wal-truncate-preserves-records-above-seq.text: `WriteAheadLog.truncate(up_to_seq)` keeps records with `seq_num > up_to_seq` and deletes only those at or below, enabling partial log reclamation tied to checkpoint boundaries.

wal-truncate-removes-whole-segment-when-.text: During `truncate(up_to_seq)`, if a segment contains no records with `seq_num > up_to_seq`, the entire segment file is deleted with `os.remove(path)`.

wal-truncate-requires-explicit-seq.text: `truncate(up_to_seq)` takes an explicit sequence number parameter; the WAL never decides what to truncate on its own — the caller must provide the boundary

wal-truncate-requires-prior-checkpoint.text: WAL truncation is only safe because it is called after the data the WAL protects has been durably written to the main store (SSTable flush or data file fsync); violating this ordering loses committed data with no recovery path

wal-truncate-returns-none.text: `WriteAheadLog.truncate` returns `None`; success is silent and callers infer correctness from the absence of exceptions.

wal-truncate-rewrites-files.text: `WriteAheadLog.truncate()` reads and rewrites every segment file record-by-record rather than deleting whole segment files, making it O(total records) instead of O(segments)

wal-truncate-rewrites-in-place.text: `WriteAheadLog.truncate()` rewrites each WAL file in place with the kept records rather than writing to a temporary file and atomically renaming it.

wal-truncate-rewrites-in-place-with-wb.text: `write-ahead-log/wal.py:truncate` opens the WAL path with `open(path, "wb")`, truncating existing content before writing the filtered records.

wal-truncate-scans-segment-records-befor.text: `truncate()` reads and scans each WAL segment's records to build a `kept` list before deciding whether to delete or rewrite that segment.

wal-truncate-syncs-before-rewrite.text: The WAL's `truncate` method calls `os.fsync` before rewriting the file.

wal-truncate-uses-temp-fsync-rename-and-.text: The standalone WAL truncate() writes a temp file, fsyncs it, atomically renames it over the original, and fsyncs the directory.

wal-truncate-zero-is-noop.text: In `WriteAheadLog.truncate`, passing `up_to_seq=0` is a no-op because no records have sequence number 0.

wal-truncation-is-multi-failure-hazard.text: WAL truncation combines three independent failure modes: it blocks all concurrent operations for its entire duration, silently discards all records after encountering corruption in a file, and is not crash-safe due to in-place file rewriting without atomic rename.

justifications.label: Truncation is simultaneously blocking, data-losing on corruption, and crash-unsafe

wal-truncation-safe-when-linear.text: WAL truncation maintains data safety through two complementary mechanisms: segments are processed in oldest-first order (so a crash mid-truncation leaves a contiguous suffix of segments), and the current WAL file is flushed and fsynced before scanning for records to remove (preventing buffered data from being lost).

justifications.label: Oldest-first ordering plus pre-scan fsync provide truncation safety, gated on the truncation operation itself not being crash-safe (no atomic rename pattern)

wal-truncation-vs-corruption-distinction.text: `_read_record` returns `None` for short reads (truncation) but raises `ValueError` for CRC mismatch (corruption), giving callers two distinct failure modes to handle differently during recovery

wal-two-tier-durability-model.text: The WAL provides two distinct durability levels: individual appends respect the configured sync mode (potentially skipping fsync entirely), while batch operations always force fsync, meaning batch writes are strictly more durable than individual writes regardless of configuration.

justifications.label: The interaction between configurable sync mode and forced batch sync creates an implicit durability hierarchy that callers must understand

wal-uses-crc32-not-sha.text: WAL integrity uses `zlib.crc32` (32-bit, non-cryptographic); it detects accidental corruption but not intentional tampering

metadata.example: checksum = zlib.crc32(key + value) & 0xFFFFFFFF

write-amplification-pressure-requires-su.text: The SSTable selection heuristic only materially affects write amplification under sustained write load with background compaction; in a batch-then-compact model the total bytes rewritten to reach a clean state is roughly the same regardless of selection order.

write-meta-leaves-cursor-at-page-size.text: After `_write_meta` returns, the file cursor is positioned at byte `page_size`, just past page 0.

write-meta-no-fsync.text: `PageManager._write_meta` calls `flush()` but not `os.fsync()`, so metadata updates (`next_free_page`, `free_list_head`) are not durable against power loss — compounding the WAL bypass with a durability gap on the direct write path.

write-meta-page-size-under-20-overwrites.text: If `page_size` is less than 20, `_write_meta`'s packed 20-byte metadata is not padded and overwrites into page 1's territory.

write-page-pads-short-pages.text: PageManager.write_page pads data shorter than page_size to exactly page_size bytes.

write-page-silently-truncates.text: `PageManager.write_page` truncates data exceeding `page_size` to exactly `page_size` bytes without raising an error, which would corrupt the node header's `num_keys` count

write-record-advances-file-position.text: `_write_record` advances the active file position by the record size, and `put` uses `tell()` to detect when the segment exceeds `_max_segment_size` and needs rotation.

write-record-does-not-handle-rotation.text: `_write_record` does not perform file rotation; its caller must invoke `_maybe_rotate()` before writing if size limits matter.

write-record-header-format-iii.text: `_write_record` packs a 12-byte header as `[crc32 | key_size | value_size]` using `struct` format `!III` (network byte order, three unsigned 32-bit integers).

write-record-no-length-validation.text: `_write_record` performs no length validation on key or value; arbitrarily large keys and values are accepted until struct packing overflows at approximately 4 GB.

write-record-propagates-errors-unhandled.text: `_write_record` catches no exceptions; `UnicodeEncodeError`, `OSError`/`IOError`, and `struct.error` propagate to callers unhandled.

write-record-single-contiguous-write.text: `_write_record` writes the 12-byte header and the key+value payload as a single contiguous write.

write-record-timestamp-captured-before-i.text: `_write_record` captures `time.time()` before encoding and writing, so the record timestamp reflects the start of the write call rather than I/O completion.

write-returns-after-page-cache-copy-not-.text: `write()` returns successfully after copying data into the kernel page cache; the data is not on disk until writeback or `fsync()` flushes dirty pages.

write-skew-has-no-default-tests.text: The `write-skew-detection` module's tests exist only in `tester_test_ssi.py`, making it entirely untested under default `pytest` invocation since that filename does not match the `test_*.py` / `*_test.py` globs

write-time-durability-engineering-abando.text: The WAL's carefully engineered write-time durability infrastructure is systematically abandoned at recovery time: the two-tier durability model (per-write sync vs. batch-only fsync) loses all distinction during replay because recovery ignores tiers entirely, AND crash recovery is both broken (no safe path across any implementation) and unverified (no crash or async tests), meaning the engineering investment in write-time safety provides zero value when it is most needed.

justifications.label: Write-time durability engineering without matching recovery implementation is stranded investment; the most sophisticated half of the system is precisely the half that doesn't protect data.

wrong-digest-cannot-reach-quorum.text: PREPARE and COMMIT messages with non-matching digests are silently dropped and never count toward quorum thresholds; a Byzantine node sending bad digests cannot contribute to agreement

wrong-digest-is-node-specific.text: `WRONG_DIGEST` mode produces `"bad_digest_{node_id}"`, so two Byzantine nodes with this mode produce different invalid digests rather than accidentally colluding on the same forged value

wrong-sequence-adds-1000.text: `WRONG_SEQUENCE` Byzantine mode adds 1000 to every outbound message's sequence number so honest nodes reject them as matching no accepted pre-prepare.

xfs-historically-zero-length-file-bug.text: XFS was historically infamous for zero-length files after crash before barriers were required.

xfs-lacks-auto-da-alloc-equivalent.text: XFS provides no `auto_da_alloc` equivalent and aggressively delays allocation, fully exposing both rename and new-file directory-entry gaps.

xfs-requires-directory-fsync-for-rename-.text: XFS requires directory fsync for rename durability; without it, a crash can lose the rename and, on older kernels, even the file contents of newly allocated files.

xfs-requires-explicit-directory-fsync-fo.text: XFS provides no implicit durability for renames or new file creation without explicit `fsync` on the parent directory.

xxhash-about-3x-faster-than-crc32-withou.text: xxHash is about 3x faster than CRC32 on large inputs when no hardware acceleration is available.

zero-entries-stripped.text: `VectorClock.__init__` strips all entries with value 0, ensuring two clocks with identical non-zero entries are always equal and hash-equal.

zip-truncation-risk.text: If `keys` and `values` lists passed to `_serialize_leaf` have mismatched lengths, `zip` silently truncates to the shorter list while `num_keys` in the header reflects the longer, producing a corrupt page

zlib-crc32-is-iso3309.text: All 13 CRC call sites across the codebase use `zlib.crc32`, which implements the ISO 3309 polynomial (0xEDB88320); no module uses the Castagnoli polynomial (CRC-32C) that RocksDB and PostgreSQL prefer for hardware-accelerated checksumming.

zlib-crc32-supports-chaining-natively.text: Python's `zlib.crc32(data, initial_value)` accepts an initial CRC value, meaning chained checksums could be implemented in this codebase by passing the previous frame's CRC as the seed with no additional hashing infrastructure
